1. John Lewis – “Where Love Lives”

John Lewis returned with “Where Love Lives,” a rave-tinged story about a teenage son gifting his dad a 12-inch pressing of Alison Limerick’s 1990 house classic and reconnecting through shared club history. The Saatchi & Saatchi film leans on music and small gestures rather than a mascot, and the campaign extends into a real vinyl release whose profits support the retailer’s Building Happier Futures programme for care-experienced young people. (Creative Salon, DJ Mag)

  • Shows how a specific cultural reference can give a familiar gifting story more personality and emotional precision.
  • Extends the film into a product and charity action without making the emotional story depend on the purchase.

2. Waitrose – “The Perfect Gift”

Waitrose used “The Perfect Gift,” a four-minute romantic comedy starring Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson, to make food part of the plot rather than a product cutaway. The film follows a widower, a meet-cute over Sussex Charmer at the cheese counter, and a love confession spelled in pastry on a No.1 Festive Turkey Pie, supported by shorter TV and social edits. (Ads of the World, The Guardian) For a food brand, that is a useful food and beverage marketing lesson: the product is strongest when it belongs naturally to the occasion and story.

  • Shows how long-form seasonal storytelling can still work when the product and emotional idea are tightly connected.
  • Uses food as the emotional connector rather than interrupting the story with a separate sales message.

3. Amazon – “Joy Ride” Returns To The Top

Data firm System1 reported that Amazon’s reprisal of its “Joy Ride” ad, featuring three older women reliving their sledging days to a cover of “In My Life,” was the top-scoring Christmas ad in early testing for 2025, with a 5.9 Star Rating and very strong long-term brand-building potential. The spot is a rerun from a previous year, but its emotional resonance, subtle product role and focus on friendship made it one of the best holiday ads of 2025 and proof that not every winner has to be brand new. (Advanced Television, YouTube)

  • Kantar found that five of its top 10 performing Christmas ads were repeats, while System1 also ranked the returning “Joy Ride” highly, showing why holiday nostalgia marketing can benefit from familiar assets when the idea still feels relevant.
  • Shows how brands with the best holiday ads in 2025 leaned into warmth and memory rather than overcomplicated storytelling.

4. Cadbury – “Secret Santa” And The Power Of Repeats

Cadbury’s “Secret Santa,” first launched in 2018, was crowned the most effective Christmas ad of 2025 in Kantar’s consumer testing, sitting in the top percentile of its database for branding impact. The campaign’s simple mechanic of anonymous gifting via purple postboxes has become a ritual, and in 2025 it once again outperformed many glossy new productions, cementing its place among the best holiday marketing campaigns and best Christmas ads of 2025. (Marketing Week, Retail Times)

  • Illustrates that brands with the best holiday ads in 2025 often reused strong creative platforms rather than reinventing every year.
  • Demonstrates that a clear, generous idea can carry a brand across multiple seasons more effectively than changing slogans.

5. Coca Cola – “Holidays Are Coming” And The Truck Tour

Coca-Cola’s long-running “Holidays Are Coming” remained one of 2025’s strongest repeat performers in consumer testing. Kantar placed Cadbury and Coca-Cola in the upper end of its advertising database for branding, while System1’s early testing also gave the returning truck ad a maximum score. The campaign extends beyond television through Holiday Caravan stops and live experiences. (Advanced Television, Coca Cola Holiday Caravan)

  • Shows how brands with the best holiday ads in 2025 turned classic creative into live experiences and charity partnerships.
  • Highlights the value of a distinctive visual identity and recurring brand assets such as colour, music, and the truck, provided they keep being refreshed in relevant contexts.

6. Aldi – Kevin And Katie’s Carrot Wedding Finale

Aldi UK extended a decade of Kevin the Carrot storytelling with Kevin and Katie’s wedding, using a familiar character system rather than rebuilding its Christmas identity from scratch. Created by McCann Manchester, the campaign included a musical wedding story, merchandise, and supporting content. System1’s early 2025 testing scored Aldi’s “The Proposal” strongly, while Kantar later placed Aldi among its top-performing festive advertisers. (LBBOnline, Advanced Television)

  • Shows how a recurring character can become a distinctive brand asset when it is developed over years rather than treated as a one-season stunt.
  • Reinforces Aldi’s value and quality message with charm, helping the supermarket stand out among brands with the best holiday ads in 2025.

7. Apple – “A Critter Carol” And Practical Magic

Apple’s 2025 holiday film, “A Critter Carol,” used handcrafted puppets and practical effects as part of the creative idea. The woodland-creature story centers on an iPhone 17 Pro, and the accompanying behind-the-scenes material emphasized that the film was shot on iPhone. The craft choice stood out during a year when AI-generated advertising was itself part of the industry conversation. (The Verge)

  • Shows how practical craft can become a differentiating creative decision without implying that one production method is universally more effective.
  • Reinforces Apple’s product message in a soft way by showing, not telling, what the camera can do.

8. McDonald’s – “The Grinch Meal” Holiday Takeover

McDonald’s built its 2025 holiday campaign around Dr. Seuss’s The Grinch, pairing a themed meal, Dill Pickle McShaker Fries, collectible socks, television creative, creator-led gaming integrations, and a Times Square presence. Marketing Dive describes the work as part of a broader IP-takeover strategy, while the Canadian execution adapted the idea for its local market. (Marketing Dive, LBBOnline)

  • Demonstrates how holiday IP can refresh core menu items and create social-friendly moments that stand out among recent campaigns.
  • Shows that playful world-building is key when fast food brands compete for the best holiday ads of 2025.

9. Heathrow – “It Must Be Love” And The Return Of The Bears

Heathrow brought back teddy bear couple Doris and Edward Bair for “It Must Be Love,” their first appearance since 2018, and extended the idea into Terminal 4 with “Terminal Paw” signage and airport activations. The St Luke’s film focuses on festive crowds, travel, and reunion, while System1 later ranked Heathrow among its 5.9-Star Christmas performers. (Heathrow Media Centre, Creative Moment) The transferable travel and hospitality marketing lesson is to connect the emotional promise to the actual customer journey, not only the ad film.

  • Reinforces Heathrow’s brand as a place of reunion and emotion, not just a functional transport hub.
  • Uses returning characters to deliver one of the most charming best holiday marketing campaigns without heavy product messaging.

10. Boots – “Gift Happily Ever After” With Puss In Boots

Boots delivered one of the best holiday ads of 2025 by inviting DreamWorks’ Puss in Boots to do his Christmas shopping in a fairy tale campaign titled “Gift Happily Ever After.” The film, led by VML and DOM&NIC, sees Puss hunt for the perfect gifts ahead of the Snow Queen’s Ball, while Boots showcases beauty offers and its signature three for two deal. Marketing Week and Boots itself describe it as the retailer’s “most integrated” festive effort yet, with Puss acting as a character device designed to anchor future campaigns, similar to what Aldi has achieved with Kevin the Carrot. (Boots Newsroom, Marketing Week, LBBOnline)

  • Shows how brands with the best holiday ads in 2025 leaned into character fluent branding to build long-term recognition.
  • Balances price-led offers with a playful narrative, making it one of the standout best holiday marketing campaigns in high street retail.

FAQ

Which brands had the best holiday ads of 2025 overall?

This article is an editorial selection of ten standout campaigns, not a single objective ranking. Kantar and System1 published separate effectiveness lists with different methodologies, while trade press and audience-favourite studies highlighted other campaigns.

What did the best holiday marketing campaigns tend to have in common?

They used simple, human stories, strong recurring characters or assets, and linked the creative to retail, charity or experiential activity rather than treating the ad as a standalone moment.

Is it risky to repeat a previous Christmas ad rather than make a new one?

It can be a smart choice when the creative platform is still distinctive. Kantar found that five of its top 10 performing Christmas ads in 2025 were repeats, while System1 also found returning creative among its strongest performers.

How did AI influence the best holiday ads of 2025?

AI was part of the broader advertising debate in 2025, but the campaigns in this editorial list used a range of production approaches. Apple’s handcrafted puppetry was notable precisely because practical craft became part of the story; that does not establish that avoiding AI caused stronger effectiveness.

What can smaller brands learn from the best Christmas ads of 2025?

You do not need a huge budget, but you do need a clear idea: pick one emotional insight, one distinctive visual or character and one way to carry it into store or online, then build your holiday campaign around that instead of trying to do everything.

What the Best Holiday Ads of 2025 Suggest

Across these ten campaigns, the strongest pattern is coherence. John Lewis connected music, gifting, and charity. Waitrose made the product part of the plot. Cadbury, Coca-Cola, Aldi, and Amazon benefited from familiarity. Heathrow extended a reunion story into the airport itself. That is where integrated holiday marketing becomes more useful than treating the film as a standalone asset.

For Canadian teams, a Canadian marketing agency can help adapt seasonal offers, cultural references, media plans, and landing pages for the audiences actually seeing the campaign. The goal is not to copy one of these ads, but to identify the distinctive idea your own brand can repeat across channels.

McDonald’s advertising has spent decades turning simple products, slogans, promotions, and celebrity partnerships into recognizable cultural moments. The best McDonald’s advertisements are not all built the same way. Some rely on jingles, some on humor, some on collectibility, and others on the reach of a famous collaborator. What connects them is a clear understanding of how a restaurant brand can use repetition, entertainment, and familiarity to stay memorable.

That makes the campaigns useful beyond fast food. For brands working in food and beverage marketing, McDonald’s shows how product, packaging, promotion, media, and brand voice can reinforce one another. The eight examples below trace that evolution from early jingles to global celebrity meals.

1. “You Deserve a Break Today” (1971)

Launched in 1971, “You Deserve a Break Today” helped McDonald’s frame a visit as a reward rather than only a convenient meal. The commercial showed employees preparing a clean, welcoming restaurant while the jingle invited customers to take a break from their daily routine.

The campaign’s strength was emotional simplicity. Instead of explaining the menu in detail, it attached McDonald’s to a familiar feeling: relief, comfort, and an easy moment away from work or household responsibilities. That made the slogan adaptable across television, print, and restaurant messaging. It also gave McDonald’s a repeatable emotional promise that could sit above individual menu items. A promotion could change, but the broader idea of the restaurant as an easy, familiar break remained understandable.

2. Big Mac’s “Two All-Beef Patties…” Jingle (1974)

In 1974, McDonald’s introduced a fast, memorable description of the Big Mac: “two all-beef patties, special sauce, lettuce, cheese, pickles, onions on a sesame seed bun.” The line turned the ingredients themselves into a memory device rather than leaving them as ordinary product information.

McDonald’s used the phrase in promotions and challenges that encouraged customers to repeat it. That participation mattered. A product description became something people could recite, share, and recognize, showing how repetition can turn even basic menu information into a distinctive brand asset. It is also a reminder that memorable copy does not always need to be abstract. Sometimes the most useful creative move is to make a product truth unusually easy to repeat.

3. Happy Meal Launch (1979)

When McDonald’s unveiled the Happy Meal in 1979, it created a product format in which the food, packaging, and toy were part of one experience. Early advertising centered on the excitement of opening the box and discovering what came with the meal.

That packaging system gave McDonald’s a flexible platform for family marketing, character tie-ins, and later entertainment partnerships. It also shows how branding can extend beyond logos into the physical format of the product itself. The box, toy, and meal worked together as a recognizable unit. That combination created room for new themes without changing the basic experience customers recognized. In brand-system terms, the format stayed stable while the creative layer could keep changing around it.

4. “The Showdown” with Michael Jordan and Larry Bird (1993)

In 1993, McDonald’s aired a Super Bowl commercial that pitted NBA legends Michael Jordan and Larry Bird against each other in a trick-shot contest for a Big Mac and fries. The setup was simple enough to understand immediately: two famous competitors keep escalating the difficulty of the shots because neither wants to give up the meal.

The commercial combined celebrity recognition with a repeatable comedic structure. The product stayed at the center of the contest without needing a long sales pitch, while the escalating shots made the spot entertaining on its own. It is a useful example of using celebrity talent to strengthen an existing product story rather than letting the celebrity become the entire story. The audience still knows what is being competed for, and the meal remains visible throughout the premise. That balance is important whenever a partnership risks drawing more attention than the product itself.

5. “I’m Lovin’ It” (2003)

In 2003, McDonald’s introduced “I’m Lovin’ It,” its first global advertising campaign. The slogan gave McDonald’s one flexible phrase that could travel across markets while leaving room for local executions, products, languages, and media.

Fronted by Justin Timberlake’s involvement in some early music spots, the campaign connected the brand with contemporary music and youth culture. Its longevity demonstrates the value of a brand strategy that gives a global organization a recognizable core without requiring every advertisement to be identical. The phrase can sit beside different menu items, celebrities, markets, and media formats because it functions as a broad brand platform rather than a one-campaign headline.

6. McDonald’s Monopoly (First Launched in 1987)

Among McDonald’s recurring promotions, Monopoly stands out because the purchase becomes part of a game. Debuting in 1987, the “peel-and-win” game format invited customers to collect property stickers and instantly redeem prizes. The promotion gave customers another reason to inspect packaging, return, and compare pieces with other players. It also created anticipation after the purchase, extending the experience beyond the moment food was ordered. That extra layer of participation helped the campaign operate as both promotion and recurring ritual.

The marketing lesson is not simply to copy a contest. The stronger idea is to build participation into the product experience. When the mechanic is easy to understand and clearly connected to the purchase, packaging and promotion can become part of the entertainment rather than functioning only as containers or announcements.

7. The Travis Scott Meal (2020)

In September 2020, McDonald’s teamed up with rapper Travis Scott for a special “Travis Scott Meal,” bringing his usual McDonald’s order to participating restaurants across the U.S. McDonald’s described it as the first time since 1992 that a celebrity’s name had appeared on its menu.

The campaign worked as a product collaboration and a cultural signal at the same time. The order was familiar food, but attaching a specific celebrity preference gave fans a simple way to participate. Social content around ordering the meal extended the campaign beyond paid media and helped the collaboration travel through fan behavior. The collaboration also worked because the order itself was easy to imitate. Fans did not need access to a limited product design or special event to participate; they could order the same combination and share the experience.

8. The BTS Meal (2021)

Following the Famous Orders program’s earlier celebrity collaborations, McDonald’s launched the BTS Meal in May 2021 across 50 countries. The meal used familiar McDonald’s products plus Sweet Chili and Cajun dipping sauces inspired by McDonald’s South Korea, giving the collaboration both a global format and a specific connection to the group.

The rollout showed how a partnership can travel across markets without requiring each country to invent a completely separate campaign. Fans could recognize the same collaboration through menu items, packaging, sauces, and social content, while local availability and execution still varied by market. That balance between a global campaign idea and market-level execution is useful for any brand expanding across regions: the central concept should travel, but the way customers encounter it still needs local operational flexibility.

What These McDonald’s Ads Have in Common

These campaigns span very different eras, but several patterns repeat. McDonald’s often starts with something easy to understand, then gives it a memorable wrapper: a jingle, a challenge, a celebrity order, a game, or a family ritual. The strongest examples do not ask the audience to absorb a complicated message before participating.

From Brand Vision’s agency perspective, the useful lesson is the relationship between brand consistency and campaign flexibility. McDonald’s can change the creative format dramatically while keeping recognizable products, language, symbols, and customer expectations in place. For restaurant and retail operators, a broader marketing strategy should work the same way: campaigns can change, but they should still feel connected to one brand system.

How Businesses Can Apply the Lessons

First, build campaign ideas around behavior that is easy to explain. If customers need a paragraph of instructions before they understand the promotion, the concept may be doing too much. Second, make the product part of the idea. The Big Mac jingle, Happy Meal packaging, Monopoly pieces, and celebrity orders all give the product a visible role rather than treating it as an afterthought.

Third, choose media formats that fit how the idea spreads. A celebrity collaboration may depend heavily on social content, while a product demonstration may be better suited to video marketing. For a restaurant operator selecting outside support in a major market, choosing a branding agency in Chicago, or another relevant region, can add local market context while specialist campaign, web, and search needs remain separate.

The best McDonald’s advertisements show that longevity does not require repeating the same commercial forever. It comes from creating recognizable brand assets, then finding new formats that make them relevant to each generation. Nike’s long history of advertising includes campaigns that reach beyond typical sports marketing. Whether it is an 80-year-old runner introducing “Just Do It,” or a montage of athletes connected through split-screen editing, Nike ads have combined inspiration, cultural awareness, humor, and product storytelling. Some campaigns have also coincided with major commercial results and broader cultural conversations, including the rise of sneaker culture around Air Jordans. More than product showcases, many Nike ads use personal ambition, inclusion, and social themes to give the brand a recognizable point of view.

Despite new platforms and evolving consumer tastes, Nike ads remain powerful statements that speak to both casual sports enthusiasts and die-hard fans especially those who love Nike's athletes. In the sections below, we’ll revisit ten remarkable moments in Nike’s advertising evolution: campaigns that have become cultural touchpoints, pushed athletic storytelling, and, most importantly, kept us talking about Nike ads for years to come.

From Brand Vision’s agency perspective, this breakdown is designed to help founders and marketers translate Nike’s advertising choices into decisions they can apply to their own brands. Nike ads are worth studying because they show how a message, a moment, and a media plan can work together to build long-term brand meaning, not just short-term attention.

1. “Just Do It” – The Birth of an Iconic Slogan (1988)

When asked to pick the most influential Nike ads, most people point to the 1988 debut of “Just Do It.” First airing on July 1 of that year, the ad featured 80-year-old runner Walt Stack crossing the Golden Gate Bridge while a voiceover urged viewers to seize the day. This seemingly simple scenario introduced an evergreen rallying cry, “Just Do It.” Since then, “Just Do It” has united multiple Nike ads under a cohesive motivation, turning casual joggers, pro athletes, and everyday dreamers into a single community.

Over the following years, Nike’s U.S. market share rose from 18% to 43%, during the period in which “Just Do It” became central to the brand’s advertising. The slogan proved so broad that it appealed to virtually anyone with a desire to move. From high school track runners to seasoned marathoners, each new wave of Nike ads bearing “Just Do It” reminded audiences that pushing your own boundaries is a universal quest. Advertising Age would later name it a top-five slogan of the 20th century, underscoring the enduring impact of Nike’s simple yet urgent words.

2. Air Jordan & Mars Blackmon – Sneaker Culture Takes Flight (1988–1991)

Among the many Nike ads that define sneaker culture, the Air Jordan and Mars Blackmon series stand out. Sparked in 1988, these TV spots teamed Michael Jordan with Spike Lee’s movie character, Mars Blackmon, known for his comedic obsession with Jordan’s shoes. Each year, a fresh commercial arrived, often debuting during All-Star Weekend to unveil the newest Air Jordan. Over time, these fun, quick-witted Nike ads expanded Jordans from mere basketball gear into must-have style icons, a phenomenon that redefined how sports endorsements shaped popular culture.

The storyline of “Is it the shoes?!” famously blurred lines between comedic banter and star-powered swagger, helping Nike connect to younger audiences in unprecedented ways. Industry insiders credit these Nike ads with kickstarting modern sneaker mania, proving that a charismatic athlete, a creative director, and an irreverent fictional sidekick can combine to move millions of products. Today, the Air Jordan brand remains an empire of its own, and these early Nike ads remain timeless references for how an athlete endorsement can revolutionize an entire industry.

3. “Bo Knows” – Multi-Sport Greatness Goes Mainstream (1989)

In 1989, Nike showcased two-sport phenom Bo Jackson in one of the funniest and most memorable Nike ads from the late ’80s: “Bo Knows.” As Bo dabbled in football and baseball stardom, the commercial humorously depicted him trying his hand at a multitude of sports—from basketball to hockey—while icons like Michael Jordan and Wayne Gretzky watched. Each scene bore the tagline “Bo Knows,” culminating in music legend Bo Diddley quipping, “Bo, you don’t know Diddley!”

The ad’s universal catchphrase “Bo Knows” became a cultural staple, fueling demand for Nike’s cross-training shoes. According to Nike co-founder Phil Knight, this series of Nike ads stands among the most critical in the brand’s history, second only to Air Jordan. Sales soared, mainstream audiences fell in love with Bo’s everyman appeal, and “Bo Knows” was parodied in countless jokes. By creatively showing off the versatility of cross-training sneakers, Nike built unstoppable momentum that cemented Bo Jackson’s name—and the brand’s—into sports marketing legend.

4. “If You Let Me Play” – Empowering Girls in Sports (1995)

Among the most socially impactful Nike ads is 1995’s “If You Let Me Play.” Rather than featuring big-name athletes, this ad highlights young girls explaining how sports benefit them mentally, physically, and emotionally. Each line underscores how participation can reduce rates of teenage pregnancy, boost self-confidence, and foster resilience. By emphasizing these long-term gains, the campaign signaled Nike’s willingness to champion advocacy beyond product promotion.

Consumer response was overwhelmingly positive, with audience approval ratings hovering above 90%. Advocacy groups lauded the ad, celebrating it as a pivotal statement on the importance of youth athletics. “If You Let Me Play” helped broaden the scope of Nike ads, showing they could serve as mini public service messages. Over time, it became a template for sports marketing that moves beyond game highlights, blending corporate messaging with genuine social empowerment.

5. Global Football Spectacles – From “Good vs Evil” to “Write the Future” (1996–2010)

Nike’s flair for epic cinematic experiences shines in its global football (soccer) campaigns. Early Nike ads like “Good vs Evil” (1996) pitted iconic athletes like Eric Cantona against demon-like opponents in a Roman colosseum, dramatizing the sport’s stakes and star power. By 1998, “Brazil Airport” had the Brazilian national team dribbling a football through an entire terminal, enchanting viewers with playful spontaneity.

The pinnacle arrived with “Write the Future” (2010), a three-minute short featuring Wayne Rooney, Cristiano Ronaldo, and others imagining the ripple effects of a single game-changing play. The ad was helmed by Oscar-winning director Alejandro Iñárritu and garnered massive online buzz, exemplifying how Nike ads often become more like blockbuster events than mere commercials. Winning Cannes Lions Film Grand Prix, “Write the Future” cemented Nike’s leadership in global sports marketing.

6. “Freestyle” and “Tag” – Creative Masterpieces of the Early 2000s

In 2001, two very different Nike ads showed the brand’s unmatched creative range: “Nike Freestyle” and “Tag.” “Freestyle” was a 60-second spot that married basketball dribbling with hip-hop elements, forging an ad reminiscent of a music video. It featured NBA players and streetball stars performing choreographed moves to a percussive beat generated by the bouncing ball itself, achieving a cultural moment that enthralled young hoops fans.

Meanwhile, “Tag” took a whimsical approach, showcasing a chain reaction of citywide tag that eventually swept up hundreds of people. Its almost cinematic ambition yielded multiple advertising awards, including a Cannes Lions Grand Prix. By juxtaposing edgy street-culture vibes in “Freestyle” with lighthearted urban fantasy in “Tag,” these Nike ads underlined the brand’s capacity to craft equally compelling sports narratives and comedic escapades.

7. The Digital Revolution – Nike’s Viral and Interactive Campaigns

As online platforms flourished, Nike ads evolved with them, pioneering interactive experiences. A prime example is the “Chalkbot” from 2009, part of a Livestrong campaign. Fans sent motivational messages via Twitter, which a robot then spray-painted along the Tour de France route in real time—blending digital outreach with tangible presence. By winning major ad awards, “Chalkbot” highlighted how Nike ads could transcend traditional screens and truly engage participants.

Subsequently, viral hits like “Make It Count” (2012) showcased Casey Neistat’s spontaneous world travel, flipping typical product demos into raw storytelling. Meanwhile, #Breaking2 (2017) turned an attempt to break the two-hour marathon barrier into a globally streamed spectacle, uniting millions of online viewers. In each instance, these Nike ads used digital innovation and real-time engagement, reinforcing that the brand’s “Just Do It” spirit could thrive in evolving media ecosystems.

8. “Dream Crazy” – Controversy Meets Inspiration (2018)

“Dream Crazy,” narrated by Colin Kaepernick, became one of the most talked-about Nike ads in recent memory. The 2018 spot featured iconic athletes: Serena Williams, LeBron James, and more, championing the idea that chasing impossible dreams can reshape one’s life. The tagline “Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything.” directly referenced Kaepernick’s NFL protests, igniting praise and backlash alike.

Despite the initial uproar, Nike’s sales soared 31% the weekend after the ad debuted, and the brand’s market value surged by billions. Critically, “Dream Crazy” swept top awards, including multiple Cannes Lions and an Emmy for Outstanding Commercial. Beyond trophies, the campaign showed that Nike could place a polarizing social issue inside a major brand platform while remaining commercially visible. The short-term sales figures reported after launch are notable, but they do not by themselves establish that the campaign caused longer-term business performance or consumer loyalty.

9. “Dream Crazier” – Celebrating Women Athletes (2019)

A year after “Dream Crazy,” “Dream Crazier” carried the same spirit of activism into women’s sports. Narrated by Serena Williams, this powerful piece called out double standards by highlighting how emotional female athletes are often labeled “crazy.” The ad then flipped the word “crazy” into a signifier of courage, featuring WNBA players, gymnasts, and other female stars confidently breaking barriers.

Released during the Oscars broadcast, “Dream Crazier” enjoyed viral momentum among viewers applauding its inclusive message. Many pointed out that these Nike ads continue the brand’s longstanding focus on women’s empowerment, dating back to 1995’s “If You Let Me Play.” Through moving visuals and direct narrative, Nike’s approach once again demonstrated that certain Nike ads can shift cultural conversations far beyond sports footwear, reinforcing “Just Do It” as a universal call to overcome bias.

10. “You Can’t Stop Us” – Unity and Hope Amid Adversity (2020)

In 2020, with a global pandemic reshaping the world, Nike released “You Can’t Stop Us,” a stunning split-screen montage directed by Oscar nominee Kim Gehrig. Over 70 clips of different athletes were paired so that each half of the screen matched seamlessly, creating visuals of unity across sports, genders, and backgrounds. Narrated by soccer star Megan Rapinoe, the ad illustrated how Nike ads can fuse top-tier editing with an uplifting call for solidarity during turbulent times.

The emotional resonance was immediate. Within days, it racked up tens of millions of views across platforms, showing how quickly the campaign traveled while drawing on themes of disruption, resilience, and social solidarity. Critically, “You Can’t Stop Us” swept awards, including the Cannes Lions Grand Prix for Film. It’s a testament to how Nike ads remain potent tools for forging global unity, confirming the brand’s relevance in an era craving messages of resilience.

What Business Owners Can Learn From Nike Ads

From Brand Vision’s agency perspective, Nike ads are useful to study because they’re built like systems. The best ones pair a clear belief with a repeatable creative language, then distribute it in a way that makes the story feel unavoidable. For business owners, the takeaway is not to imitate Nike’s scale. It is to copy the structure behind the work: a clear brand system, tight positioning, consistent craft, and a message that holds up across channels. That same discipline matters in B2C marketing, where recognition and distribution need to work together.

  • Pressure test your positioning before you ship creative. If your “why us” is vague, your campaign will be too. This is where focused brand strategy and brand research make the difference.
  • Design for recognizability, not novelty. Nike’s strongest ads feel like Nike in the first two seconds. Build that same consistency through visual identity and a clear brand voice system.
  • Treat your website like the conversion layer of the campaign. Great ads create interest, but your site has to close the loop with speed, clarity, and trust. If you’re updating your messaging or offers, pair it with a modern web design agency approach and a sharper UI UX design agency mindset.
  • Make distribution part of the creative, not an afterthought. Nike’s campaigns are designed to travel. That means building content that works in search, social, and short-form, supported by an SEO agency plan that can strengthen discoverability over time.
  • Audit your marketing the way Nike audits its story. Ask: what do people repeat, what do they feel, and what do they do next? A structured marketing consultation can help you identify what’s working, what’s noise, and what needs to be rebuilt. Pair that qualitative review with marketing metrics tied to acquisition, demand, conversion, and retention.

Changing Sports Advertising Forever

From the debut of “Just Do It” through “You Can’t Stop Us,” Nike ads have exemplified marketing that transcends basic product pitches to become cultural touchstones. Whether harnessing the star power of Bo Jackson and Michael Jordan, championing female participation in sports, or boldly aligning with social causes, Nike ads communicate a brand ethos rooted in possibility and personal conviction. Their influence isn’t just measured in sales spikes, though Nike has certainly benefited, but in how these ads shift dialogues, inspire communities, and demonstrate the potential for commercial art to reflect pressing social themes.

Across multiple decades, mediums, and controversies, Nike ads consistently pivot back to a simple message: pushing yourself can lead to surprising outcomes, whether in sports or life. By blending storytelling, cinematic style, and human-centric narratives, these commercials have achieved the rare feat of being simultaneously promotional and inspirational. From the comedic Mars Blackmon sketches of the 80s to the modern digital spectacles that trend on social media, Nike ads remain benchmarks for emotional resonance in brand communications. As new generations of athletes and viewers emerge, Nike’s advertising will keep providing useful material for studying how brand systems evolve across media. Treat a course as a structured starting point, then validate tactics against current documentation and real campaign data. Before choosing a program, separate three questions: what skill do you need, what evidence of learning do you want, and how much guided practice do you need to become useful at the task. A badge can document completion, but it does not replace a portfolio, campaign result, or demonstrated ability to diagnose a marketing problem.

1) Google Skillshop – Fundamentals of Digital Marketing

Google’s Fundamentals of Digital Marketing remains a broad beginner option, but it now lives in Skillshop rather than the older Digital Garage experience. Google currently lists it as a 40-hour beginner course with 17 modules covering modern digital marketing topics, including AI tools and video marketing. Learners can still review the legacy Digital Garage material through the existing Fundamentals of Digital Marketing playlist, but current completion recognition is handled through Skillshop.

The credential language has also changed. Google now awards a digital award or badge for completing all required activities rather than the traditional Digital Garage certificate. The current Skillshop course is therefore a good fit for beginners who want a long-form overview from Google, but learners should describe the credential accurately rather than presenting it as an accredited qualification.

Because the course is broad, use it to build vocabulary and understand how channels fit together, then deepen the area that matters most to your role. Someone responsible for search should move into current Google Ads, Analytics, and SEO documentation; a content marketer should pair the overview with actual editorial planning and measurement work. The award is useful evidence of completion, not proof that the learner can independently run every channel covered.

2) HubSpot Academy – Inbound Marketing Certification

HubSpot Academy’s Inbound Marketing Certification remains one of the clearest no-cost options for learning the inbound methodology. The current course includes nine lessons, 24 videos, seven quizzes, and just under five hours of content. Topics include content marketing, lead generation, automation, customer understanding, and reporting.

It is especially useful for marketers who want a compact, structured credential rather than a broad survey of every digital channel. HubSpot describes the certification as free and designed for marketing managers, inbound professionals, and small-business owners. Because the course is built around HubSpot’s own methodology and ecosystem, learners should separate general inbound principles from workflows that are most natural inside HubSpot products.

The best way to apply the course is to build one complete buyer journey after finishing it. Define a target customer, map questions by stage, create one useful content asset, decide how a lead should be nurtured, and identify the metric that would show whether the sequence is working. That exercise exposes the difference between knowing inbound terminology and being able to design a coherent customer experience.

3) Coursera – Digital Marketing Specialization from the University of Illinois

The University of Illinois Digital Marketing Specialization on Coursera remains available and is currently presented as a seven-course series. It covers strategic marketing, digital analytics, social media, customer behavior, and related digital topics, with a shareable career certificate and a capstone-style applied learning component.

This path is a better fit for someone who wants university-led structure and a broader academic framework than a short platform tutorial. Coursera currently estimates roughly three months at about ten hours a week, though self-paced completion varies. It is also connected to University of Illinois degree pathways, which makes it meaningfully different from a vendor badge or a single standalone course.

Academic structure can be an advantage when you want durable concepts such as consumer behavior, measurement, and strategy rather than only interface instructions. The tradeoff is that any long-running specialization may contain examples or tool references that age at different speeds. Learners should treat the strategic framework as the durable layer and verify current platform mechanics separately whenever an assignment depends on a live advertising or analytics product.

4) Udemy – The Complete Digital Marketing Course: 12 Courses in 1

The Complete Digital Marketing Course – 12 Courses in 1 remains live on Udemy. The course page currently lists more than 22 hours of content across 247 lectures and shows an April 2026 update. Its curriculum spans market research, website setup, email marketing, SEO, social media, paid advertising, copywriting, and analytics.

Udemy’s strength is flexible, self-paced access rather than institutional accreditation. This course includes a Udemy certificate of completion, but that is different from a university credential or a professional certification exam. It can suit learners who want a wide practical survey and lifetime access to course materials. As with any marketplace course, check the current update date, instructor, syllabus, and recent learner feedback before enrolling because the quality and maintenance cadence varies by course.

Broad marketplace courses are most valuable when you use them selectively. If you already know email marketing but need a stronger grounding in copywriting or paid search, you do not have to treat every module as equally important. Build a short learning plan around the weak areas, complete the related exercises, and compare the teaching against current platform documentation before using an older workflow in a live account.

5) Meta Blueprint

Meta Blueprint remains Meta’s official learning ecosystem for skills tied to Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, advertising, measurement, and related Meta tools. Its value is specificity: when the goal is to understand Meta campaign setup, targeting, creative formats, or platform operations, first-party training is usually more dependable than an old third-party tutorial that may show an outdated interface.

Meta also maintains professional certification pathways separate from individual learning modules. That distinction matters when comparing credentials. Completing training material is not automatically the same as passing a certification exam. This option is most relevant for marketers who already know general marketing fundamentals and want platform-specific knowledge they can apply to Meta campaigns.

Platform training should be paired with skills that Meta cannot teach for you: offer design, positioning, creative judgment, landing-page quality, economics, and experimentation. A person can know where every button sits in Ads Manager and still run a weak campaign. Use Blueprint to reduce operational mistakes, then judge campaign quality through business outcomes and disciplined testing rather than interface fluency alone.

6) LinkedIn Learning – Advance as a Digital Marketing Specialist

LinkedIn Learning’s Advance as a Digital Marketing Specialist path remains active and was updated in September 2026. It currently contains nine courses and about eleven hours of material, including digital marketing foundations, SEO, social media, content marketing, analytics, and related skills.

This format works well for professionals who want short, modular courses rather than one large cohort program. LinkedIn Learning issues a badge or certificate of completion for the learning path, which can be displayed on a LinkedIn profile. The tradeoff is depth: the path spans several disciplines in a relatively compact runtime, so it is better used as a structured overview or refresher than as proof of advanced mastery in every channel.

Its biggest practical advantage is convenience. A learner can identify one job-relevant gap, finish a compact course, and immediately test the concept at work. The risk is passive consumption: completing eleven hours of video without producing anything creates little evidence of skill. Pair the path with a campaign brief, content plan, analytics review, or other artifact that shows how you apply the material.

7) Semrush Academy

Semrush Academy remains a strong specialist resource for SEO, content marketing, paid search, analytics, and workflows connected to Semrush tools. Semrush states that its Academy courses are free and led by digital marketing practitioners. Many courses pair conceptual instruction with product demonstrations, which can make abstract search and competitive-research tasks easier to understand.

The fit is strongest when you want search-focused training or already use Semrush in your work. The Academy also offers certifications, but credential terms can change, so check the current course page and certification FAQ before presenting a credential as permanent. Tool-specific instruction is useful when it supports sound strategy, not when the tool becomes a substitute for understanding search intent, measurement, or content quality.

Use the demonstrations as practice prompts rather than recipes. Recreate a keyword analysis, competitive gap review, or technical audit on a site you know, then explain what decision the data should change. The ability to turn a dashboard into a prioritized recommendation is more valuable than memorizing where a report lives in the interface.

8) Hootsuite Academy

Hootsuite Academy continues to operate as Hootsuite’s learning hub for social media and Hootsuite product skills. Its current public Academy page directs learners into the company’s training portal, while Hootsuite continues to position the Academy as a resource for social marketing education.

This option makes the most sense for social media managers who want structured practice around planning, publishing, engagement, listening, analytics, and workflows inside a social management platform. Before paying for any certificate or enrolling through an employer account, confirm the current access model and credential details. Social platforms evolve rapidly, so the course’s update cadence is as important as the brand name attached to it.

For a working social team, the value can extend beyond individual certification. Training can help standardize naming conventions, scheduling, approvals, community management, and reporting across multiple people. The strongest outcome is not simply knowing Hootsuite features; it is creating a clearer operating process for how content moves from idea to approval, publication, response, and measurement.

9) Simplilearn – Current Digital Marketing Programs

Simplilearn’s digital marketing catalog has evolved since this list was first framed in 2025. The current catalog highlights a broader mix of paid learning paths and shorter free courses rather than relying on one “Digital Marketing Specialist” label. Its offerings now cover SEO, paid media, content, analytics, automation, AI-assisted marketing, social media, and campaign strategy.

This is still worth considering for learners who prefer a more guided program and want projects or a learning path rather than a handful of isolated videos. The key is to evaluate the exact program currently offered in your region: duration, live instruction, included certifications, partner branding, and pricing can change. Do not assume a course name or partnership from an older version of the catalog still applies to the program you are about to buy.

When comparing a paid cohort or longer learning path, ask for the actual weekly commitment, instructor access, project feedback process, cancellation terms, and examples of the portfolio work learners create. A long program is not automatically deeper if most of the time is spent watching recordings. Guided feedback and project review are usually more important than the raw number of course hours.

10) edX – Current Digital Marketing Programs

edX continues to offer university-backed digital marketing study, but its current catalog should be checked rather than assuming the 2025 University of Queensland Digital Marketing MicroMasters is still the active option. The general MicroMasters directory remains useful for understanding that credential format, while the current edX digital marketing catalog prominently lists Professional Certificates from several universities and institutions.

One current example is the University of Edinburgh’s Digital Marketing Fundamentals Professional Certificate, a two-course, self-paced program that covers marketing principles and digital marketing strategy. This route is best for learners who value university-led instruction and a more formal certificate structure. Always confirm the current institution, course count, price, and credit treatment on the live program page before enrolling.

edX can also offer audit and verified-certificate paths depending on the course, so compare what access each path includes. If your reason for enrolling is academic progression, check whether a specific program actually carries credit or admission value before paying. If the goal is simply practical upskilling, the curriculum, assessments, and applied project may matter more than whether the credential sits inside a larger academic ecosystem.

How to Choose an Online Marketing Course

Start with the skill gap rather than the logo on the certificate. A beginner who needs a broad map of digital marketing has different needs from an SEO specialist learning a new tool, a social manager preparing for Meta campaigns, or a manager who wants a university-led strategy program. Compare the syllabus against the work you actually expect to do after the course.

Then compare credential type. A completion badge, vendor certification, marketplace certificate, university career certificate, and graduate-credit pathway are not interchangeable. Ask what assessment is required, whether the credential expires, whether the course can count toward another program, and whether the provider clearly explains those conditions. A credential can support a résumé, but it does not guarantee a job, promotion, or campaign result.

Finally, check practical details on the live provider page: current duration, update date, teaching format, refund terms, price, prerequisites, and access period. Platform-specific courses are often best for current interfaces and workflows; broader programs can be stronger for strategy and transferable concepts. If your goal is to build a portfolio, prioritize programs that require projects or let you apply the material to a real business problem.

For employers choosing training for a team, add another layer: identify the behavior that should change after training. A course on analytics might be intended to improve reporting quality; a paid-media course might reduce campaign setup errors; a strategy program might give managers a common planning framework. Defining that expected change makes it easier to decide whether the training worked.

From Learning Marketing to Applying It

Courses are most valuable when the material turns into a repeatable operating habit. Build a small project, define an audience, create an offer or message, choose a channel, set a measurement plan, and review the outcome. That process will reveal gaps much faster than collecting certificates without applying the material.

For education providers, the same principle works in reverse: prospective students need clear information about curriculum, credential type, delivery format, outcomes, price, and prerequisites. Sector-specific education marketing can help training organizations communicate those differences without overstating what a credential guarantees.

If an organization already has capable marketers but needs help translating skills into a coordinated growth plan, a marketing consultation can clarify priorities before committing to new channels or tools. Expanding an IT team isn’t just about hiring more people—it’s about growing with intention. Rapid team scaling can strain communication, dilute company culture, or even slow progress if not managed carefully. That’s why aligning team structure with strategic goals and investing in knowledge-sharing practices is just as important as headcount. Many organizations find that partnering with an IT staff augmentation company helps bridge growth phases, offering immediate access to experienced professionals without compromising team dynamics. With the right approach, scaling becomes a structured evolution, not a disruptive leap.

Understanding the Need for Scaling IT Teams

Scaling IT teams helps adapt to the rapid pace of market demands and technological changes. As businesses grow and evolve, the need for more specialized roles and increased workforce capacity becomes apparent. However, rapid hiring during scaling can lead to quality trade-offs if not managed carefully. Striking a balance between speed and maintaining high standards is vital.

Ensuring team cultures remains intact during scaling is another significant challenge. A cohesive and productive team culture fosters collaboration and innovation, which are vital for success. As teams expand, it’s essential to ensure that new hires align with the existing culture and values of the organization.

Embracing Agile methodologies supports rapid adaptation to changing business priorities, helping maintain alignment between agile teams. Agile frameworks such as the scrum framework can facilitate better team collaboration and efficiency, ensuring that scrum masters and teams remain focused on delivering value to the business.

Understanding the importance of scaling teams in IT is the first step. The next step involves aligning team structures with the big picture of business goals for strategic success.

Aligning Team Structure with Business Goals

Aligning software engineering with business objectives enhances project efficiency and supports overall strategic goals. Regular reviews of software projects and business goals allow for timely adjustments to keep pace with market changes. This ongoing review process helps ensure that teams remain focused on delivering solutions that address real business problems.

Effective alignment reduces the risk of project failures by ensuring that software solutions address real business problems. Regular meetings between business stakeholders and engineering teams enhance communication and understanding of project priorities. These meetings serve as a platform for discussing project scopes, timelines, and potential roadblocks.

Setting SMART goals ensures that engineering objectives are specific, measurable, and aligned with business outcomes. This approach provides clarity and direction for teams, enabling them to stay focused on what matters most. Organizations should adapt work management strategies to allow for more fluid project scopes, promoting adaptability and rapid feedback.

Effective knowledge management offers a competitive edge by fostering faster innovation and enhancing operational efficiency. By aligning team structures with business goals, companies can create a solid foundation for scaling their IT teams effectively, leveraging explicit knowledge and management support.

Creating High-Performance Cross-Functional Teams

Cross-functional teams encourage collaboration across disciplines, promoting a shared understanding of business and technical goals. These teams bring together diverse skill sets and perspectives, enabling them to tackle complex challenges more effectively. Involving the engineering team and product owners in user research helps them understand customer needs, driving the development of solutions that solve real-world problems.

Building trust among departments is vital for successful collaboration in cross-functional teams. Trust fosters open communication and a willingness to share ideas and feedback. Training in soft skills helps team members navigate negotiation and collaboration effectively. Soft skills like communication, empathy, and conflict resolution are essential for maintaining a positive team dynamic.

Key principles for effective cross-functional teams include:

  • Staffing based on required skills rather than existing relationships to ensure the right expertise.
  • Ensuring the team has the right expertise to achieve its goals.
  • Maintaining momentum and clarity through effective project management.
  • Using clear planning, regular check-ins, and transparent communication to keep the team on track and focused on objectives.

By creating high-performance cross-functional teams at the team level, many organizations can harness the collective strengths of their workforce, driving innovation and achieving better outcomes for the company, which can lead to significant benefit. This idea can transform how teams operate.

Establishing Clear Communication Channels

Robust communication processes are vital for overcoming the challenges of team expansion. As teams grow, managing communication and cultural dynamics becomes increasingly complex. Effective communication begins with trust and engagement among team members. When team members feel valued and heard, they are more likely to contribute actively and share their ideas.

Good group communication requires understanding various communication styles among team members. Key characteristics and practices include:

  • Clarity and conciseness: Team members should clearly articulate their thoughts and avoid unnecessary jargon.
  • Active listening: Ensures team members understand each other’s messages.
  • Attentive listening: Helps avoid misunderstandings and fosters a collaborative environment. Additionally, the practice of effective communication is essential for success.

Encouraging feedback enhances communication effectiveness within teams. Key aspects include:

  • Constructive feedback improves team performance and fosters a culture of continuous improvement.
  • Celebrating team and individual successes creates a positive communication environment.
  • Recognizing achievements boosts morale and encouraged collaboration.

Project management tools can centralize communication and improve collaboration among team members. These tools provide:

  • A platform for sharing updates
  • Tracking progress
  • Coordinating tasks Technology solutions should support visibility and improving collaboration across teams to overcome scaling hindrances.

By establishing clear communication channels, organizations can ensure that their teams are created to remain connected, engaged, and focused on achieving their goals throughout the entire organization in an organizational context.

Implementing Effective Knowledge Sharing Systems

Creating physical and virtual collaboration spaces enhances knowledge sharing among employees. A centralized internal knowledge base, powered by knowledge base software, allows employees to access and contribute valuable information easily. This library serves as a repository for best practices, lessons learned, and other critical knowledge assets.

Removing barriers to knowledge sharing encourages broader participation among employees, and overcoming barriers to knowledge sharing is essential. Key strategies include:

  • Clear knowledge sharing guidelines to prevent frustration and duplication of effort.
  • Designating knowledge approvers to prevent bottlenecks and encourage timely contributions.
  • Providing incentives for knowledge sharing, such as public recognition, to enhance employee engagement in sharing expertise and encourage employees.

A systematic approach to knowledge sharing saves time. It ensures the correct information reaches the appropriate individuals. A knowledge management system is more effective for sharing knowledge than verbal repetition. Knowledge sharing facilitates the transfer of information and expertise, increasing collective organizational knowledge. The benefits of knowledge sharing include improved collaboration, enhanced innovation, and reduced redundancy.

By implementing an effective knowledge sharing system, organizations can foster a knowledge sharing culture of continuous learning and innovation, ensuring that valuable insights and expertise are accessible to all knowledge workers through a knowledge sharing tool that includes embedded knowledge, new ideas, tacit knowledge, collective knowledge, knowledge hoarding, documenting knowledge, knowledge sharing activities, and knowledge transfer. Additionally, organizations should prioritize efforts to share knowledge effectively.

Measuring and Managing Cognitive Load

Assessing cognitive load involves evaluating the complexity of the service. It can also be determined by examining the module or product pillar managed by the team. Understanding the sources of cognitive load is key to managing it effectively. Cognitive load can be broken down into intrinsic, extraneous, and germane loads, each representing different sources of mental strain.

High cognitive burden can lead to decreased team effectiveness, as it exceeds the collective processing capacity. Managing cognitive load should be a continuous process to effectively address team mental strain. Regularly assessing and adjusting workloads helps prevent burnout and ensures teams remain productive and focused in this challenging environment.

Measuring and managing cognitive load creates a more sustainable and supportive work environment for teams.

Summary

Scaling IT teams effectively requires a strategic approach that encompasses alignment with business goals, creating high-performance cross-functional teams, establishing clear communication channels, implementing effective knowledge-sharing systems, and managing cognitive load. Each of these practices plays a crucial role in ensuring that teams can grow and adapt without compromising quality or productivity.

By following these best practices, organizations can build resilient and agile IT teams capable of meeting the challenges of today’s fast-paced business environment. Remember, the key to successful scaling lies in fostering a culture of collaboration, continuous learning, and adaptability.

This 2025 comparison covers ten widely used project management tools for teams that need to plan work, assign owners, track deadlines, and report progress. The original article described a standardized hands-on test, but there is no project record supporting that methodology. This repaired version is based on vendor pricing and feature pages, preserved product imagery, and user-review themes from the linked sources rather than invented first-hand testing.

Pricing below is a June 2025 snapshot unless a current-plan note is included. Vendors change packaging often, so use the linked pricing pages to confirm today's limits before buying. The most important differences are workflow depth, reporting, client access, automation, documentation, and how much setup a team can realistically maintain.

How to Compare Project Management Software

  • Workflow fit: Match the tool to the way work actually moves, not the longest feature list.
  • Reporting: Check whether dashboards, workload views, goals, and portfolio reporting sit in the tier you can afford.
  • External collaboration: Agencies and service teams should review guest permissions, proofing, time tracking, and client visibility.
  • Automation: Confirm action limits and integration rules. A cheap entry tier can become expensive if core automation sits higher up the plan ladder.
  • Adoption: Pilot one real project with several roles before migrating the whole organization.

1. Monday.com

2025 entry price: Basic at about $9 per seat per month when billed annually.

Monday.com is strong for teams that want visual boards, configurable fields, dashboards, and multiple ways to view the same work. User-review themes on g2.com commonly emphasize visual clarity and customization. The main caution is plan packaging: the current monday.com Basic price is still $9 annually, but automations, integrations, Timeline, and Gantt now begin on Standard rather than Basic. The original claim that Basic included thousands of monthly automation actions should not be used as a buying assumption.

For teams running visual identity projects, boards can make asset status, approvals, and handoffs easier to scan, provided the workspace has naming and ownership rules.

2. Asana

2025 entry price: Starter at $10.99 per user per month billed annually.

Asana combines task lists, boards, Timeline, Gantt, forms, rules, dashboards, and project templates in a polished interface. Reviewers on g2.com frequently highlight ease of use, while larger teams can find notification and governance settings demanding if projects multiply. The current asana.com Starter plan remains $10.99 annually and includes Timeline, Gantt, dashboards, forms, and unlimited automations; company-level Goals sit in Advanced.

3. ClickUp

2025 entry price: Unlimited at $7 per user per month billed annually.

ClickUp is designed as a broad work platform, combining tasks, docs, whiteboards, time tracking, dashboards, chat, goals, and integrations. Review themes on g2.com often praise flexibility while also noting that the interface can take time to learn. The current clickup.com Unlimited plan is still $7 annually and includes unlimited integrations, Gantt charts, storage, custom fields, time tracking, and resource management.

4. Notion

2025 entry price: Plus at $10 per member per month.

Notion is especially useful when documentation and project tracking need to live together. Databases can represent tasks, projects, editorial calendars, and knowledge-base content on the same workspace. User feedback on g2.com often praises flexibility but can flag setup complexity for teams that need stricter workflow controls. Current notion.com pricing still lists Plus at $10 per member per month, while offline support is now available for selected pages rather than being absent altogether.

5. Trello

2025 entry price: Standard at $5 per user per month billed annually.

Trello remains one of the simplest Kanban-style options for teams that primarily need cards, lists, due dates, checklists, and lightweight automation. Reviews on g2.com commonly highlight its approachable board model. The current trello.com Standard plan remains $5 annually, but Timeline, Table, Dashboard, and Map views belong to Premium, so teams needing cross-project reporting should price the correct tier.

6. Wrike

Current entry reference: Team at $10 per user per month for new purchases.

Wrike suits teams that need request forms, approvals, dashboards, Gantt planning, and configurable work types. The preserved g2.com review source reflects the trade-off between customization and setup effort. Current wrike.com pricing lists Team at $10 and Business at $25 for new purchases from January 2026. For B2B marketing teams, Wrike can be useful when campaigns require formal intake, proofing, approvals, and reporting across multiple stakeholders.

7. Smartsheet

Current entry reference: Pro at $9 per member per month billed annually, or $12 monthly.

Smartsheet combines spreadsheet-style grids with Gantt, board, calendar, formulas, reports, and automation. Review themes on g2.com often praise workflow flexibility while noting a learning curve for teams that are not comfortable with spreadsheet logic. Current smartsheet.com pricing corrects the old article's annual-billing statement: Pro is $9 annually, while $12 is the monthly rate.

8. Teamwork.com

2025 snapshot: Deliver at $10.99 per user per month billed annually. Teamwork has since changed its plan names.

Teamwork.com is built around client work, with time tracking, billable rates, project budgets, client permissions, and invoicing features. User-review summaries linked through g2.com frequently emphasize visibility and time tracking. The current teamwork.com lineup uses Basics, Accelerate, Optimize, and Enterprise; Basics is $9.99 per user per month billed yearly.

A Montreal branding agency, or any client-service team with similar approval and handoff needs, should test guest access, time budgets, invoicing, and client visibility before committing to a plan.

9. Basecamp

2025 snapshot: The original article listed $15 per user per month or $299 per month for Pro Unlimited.

Basecamp focuses on a calmer, bundled collaboration model built around messages, to-dos, files, schedules, chat, and card tables. The preserved g2.com source reflects its appeal to teams that value simplicity over deep portfolio controls. Current basecamp.com packaging has changed: Basecamp now offers several fixed-price tiers, while Unlimited remains $299 per month billed annually. Teams should therefore treat the 2025 per-user price as historical.

10. Jira

2025 snapshot: Standard was listed at $8.60 per user per month in the original article. Current Jira Cloud pricing has changed.

Jira remains a strong fit for teams using backlogs, sprints, workflows, issue types, and software-development integrations. User feedback on g2.com often cites depth as both its strength and its learning curve. The existing atlassian.com licensing source is preserved. Atlassian's current Jira pricing lists Standard at $7.91 per user per month. The original Atlassian image credit is preserved below.

For SaaS marketing teams coordinating launches with product and engineering, Jira can provide visibility into release dependencies without implying that the marketing team itself should adopt a developer workflow for every campaign.

Which Tool Fits Which Team?

  • Visual campaign and creative teams: Monday.com or Trello can make status easy to scan, while Asana adds stronger cross-project structure.
  • Cross-functional organizations: Asana, ClickUp, and Wrike offer more reporting and workflow depth as complexity increases.
  • Documentation-heavy teams: Notion is strong when project work and knowledge management should live together.
  • Spreadsheet-oriented operations: Smartsheet suits teams that want formulas and grid logic inside a collaborative system.
  • Client-service businesses: Teamwork.com is built around time, budgets, profitability, and client access.
  • Software product teams: Jira remains purpose-built for backlog and sprint workflows.
  • Teams prioritizing simplicity: Basecamp keeps the collaboration model intentionally constrained.

Do not assume every vendor offers the same trial or free-plan structure. Current pages show a mix of free tiers, short trials, and paid-only options, and those policies change. A pilot should use a real deadline, real owners, one reporting need, and at least one handoff to an external collaborator.

Project management software also should not be confused with marketing automation software. Project tools organize people and work; automation platforms coordinate customer data, campaigns, and lifecycle actions. Teams may need both, but for different jobs.
