How to Create a Brand Voice in 7 Steps

Step 1: Anchor the Voice to Brand Strategy

Do not begin by choosing adjectives that sound appealing.

Start with the strategic decisions the voice needs to express.

Clarify:

  • Who the brand is for
  • What problem it solves
  • How it is positioned
  • What makes it different
  • What it believes
  • What it can credibly prove
  • How customers should perceive it
  • What it should never sound like

A premium legal firm, a youth entertainment platform, and a technical software company may all want to sound “confident,” but confidence should look different for each one. In law firm marketing, for example, confidence often needs to sound precise and credible rather than promotional.

The voice must fit the brand’s actual market position.

Use Brand Vision’s brand strategy framework if these foundational decisions have not been documented.

Step 2: Audit Your Current Communication

Before inventing a new voice, identify what already works.

Collect examples from:

  • Homepage copy
  • Product or service pages
  • Blog posts
  • Sales emails
  • Marketing emails
  • Social media
  • Advertisements
  • Proposals
  • Customer support replies
  • Product notifications
  • Error messages
  • Internal presentations

Review the examples and ask:

  • Which pieces already sound recognizable?
  • Which phrases feel specific to the company?
  • Where does the communication become generic?
  • Which channels sound disconnected from the others?
  • Which examples feel clear and credible?
  • Which examples feel exaggerated, stiff, or overly casual?
  • What language do team members consistently disagree about?

Keep the strongest existing patterns when they support the strategy.

Do not discard useful brand equity simply because the company is formalizing its voice for the first time.

Step 3: Research Your Audience and Category Language

A brand voice should be distinctive, but it should also be understandable and credible to the intended audience.

Use evidence from:

  • Customer interviews
  • Sales calls
  • Support conversations
  • Customer reviews
  • Surveys
  • Search queries
  • Social comments
  • Community discussions
  • Competitor websites
  • Category publications
  • Existing customer emails

Look for:

  • Words customers naturally use
  • Problems they describe repeatedly
  • Technical terms they understand
  • Technical terms that create confusion
  • Emotional concerns behind their decisions
  • Claims they trust
  • Claims they question
  • Phrases every competitor repeats

Do not imitate every phrase, trend, or piece of slang the audience uses.

The goal is to understand the audience well enough to communicate naturally, not to impersonate them.

If internal evidence is limited, Brand Vision’s audience and competitor research can supply the interviews, category analysis, and customer language this step depends on.

Step 4: Choose Three to Five Brand Voice Attributes

Choose a small number of characteristics that describe how the brand should communicate consistently.

Possible attributes include:

  • Clear
  • Confident
  • Helpful
  • Direct
  • Warm
  • Practical
  • Optimistic
  • Sophisticated
  • Curious
  • Bold
  • Empathetic
  • Precise
  • Playful
  • Educational

Three to five attributes are practical for most teams. A longer list becomes difficult to remember and may contain characteristics that conflict.

Each attribute should be:

Strategically Relevant

It should support the brand’s positioning and customer expectations.

Credible

The company should be able to communicate this way naturally.

Distinctive

The combination should create a personality that does not sound interchangeable with every competitor.

Usable

Writers should be able to translate the attribute into observable language choices.

Compatible

The attributes should work together as one personality.

Avoid relying on broad words such as:

  • Professional
  • Authentic
  • Innovative
  • Modern
  • Friendly

These words are not necessarily wrong, but they are incomplete without specific definitions and rules.

Step 5: Add “We Are, but We Are Not” Guardrails

Every voice attribute needs a boundary.

Guardrails prevent teams from exaggerating a characteristic until it becomes a different personality.

For example:

  • We are confident, but not arrogant.
  • We are warm, but not overly familiar.
  • We are expert, but not jargon-heavy.
  • We are direct, but not abrupt.
  • We are playful, but not careless.
  • We are sophisticated, but not pretentious.
  • We are optimistic, but not unrealistic.

For each voice attribute, document:

  • What the attribute means
  • What the attribute does not mean
  • How it affects writing
  • Where it should be dialed back
  • An on-brand example
  • An off-brand example

These boundaries make abstract personality characteristics easier to apply.

Step 6: Translate Attributes Into Writing Rules

A usable brand voice needs rules, not only descriptions.

For example:

Voice attribute: Clear

Change the abstract direction, write clearly, into specific rules:

  • Lead with the answer or most important information.
  • Use everyday words when they are as accurate as technical terms.
  • Define necessary technical language.
  • Keep each sentence focused on one main idea.
  • Replace vague claims with specific information.
  • Make the next action obvious.
  • Remove introductory language that delays the point.

Another example:

Voice attribute: Confident

Translate it into rules such as:

  • State the recommendation directly.
  • Support important claims with evidence.
  • Avoid unnecessary qualifiers.
  • Acknowledge uncertainty when it genuinely exists.
  • Do not use superiority claims the company cannot prove.
  • Do not insult competitors or pressure the reader.

Another example:

Voice attribute: Human

Translate it into rules such as:

  • Use natural sentence structures.
  • Use contractions when appropriate.
  • Address the reader directly when it improves clarity.
  • Avoid corporate filler and scripted enthusiasm.
  • Explain what happens next.
  • Do not force jokes into serious situations.

Every attribute should produce a repeatable set of writing decisions.

Step 7: Test and Document the Voice

Test the proposed voice before finalizing it.

Apply the voice to several different content types:

  • Homepage headline
  • Service description
  • Sales email
  • Social post
  • Product announcement
  • Customer complaint response
  • Payment reminder
  • Error message
  • Policy explanation

The voice should remain recognizable across all of them.

If one characteristic only works in advertising or social media, it may be a tone choice rather than a core voice attribute.

Once the system works across contexts, document it.

How to Choose Strong Brand Voice Attributes

The best brand voice characteristics create meaningful communication choices.

Use these tests before approving an attribute.

Can It Be Defined?

A writer should be able to explain what the attribute means in one or two sentences.

Can It Be Observed?

The characteristic should affect vocabulary, sentence structure, formality, rhythm, or another visible part of the writing.

Can It Be Distinguished From Its Opposite?

If “confident” and “not confident” produce the same copy, the attribute has not been defined clearly enough.

Does It Fit the Audience?

The voice should help the audience understand and trust the brand.

Does It Fit the Category?

The characteristic should make sense within the expectations and risks of the industry.

Is the Combination Distinctive?

One attribute may be common. The combination should create a more specific personality.

For example, clear + confident + practical creates a different communication style from clear + warm + curious or clear + bold + irreverent.

Do not choose characteristics independently. Evaluate how they work together.

Brand Voice Examples: Before and After

Assume a fictional software company has defined its voice as clear, confident, practical, and helpful.

Homepage Example

Change this generic copy:

Our innovative, cutting-edge platform empowers modern organizations to unlock next-level productivity and transform the way they work.

To this on-brand copy:

Plan the work, assign owners, and see what is blocked before deadlines slip.

Why it works: the second version explains the product in specific language and removes unsupported promotional claims.

Call-to-Action Example

Change this:

Unlock Your Potential

To this:

Create Your First Project

Why it works: the revised call to action tells the reader exactly what will happen next.

Customer Support Example

Change this:

Oops! Something went wrong. Please try again later.

To this:

We couldn’t save your changes. Try again in a moment. Your previous version is still available.

Why it works: the revised message explains what happened, gives a next step, and reduces uncertainty.

Sales Example

Change this:

We would be delighted to schedule some time to explore how our world-class solution could potentially support your organization.

To this:

Book a 30-minute call to review your current process and see whether the platform fits your team.

Why it works: the revised message is direct, specific, and clear about what the conversation will cover.

Social Media Example

Change this:

We are beyond thrilled and incredibly excited to announce the launch of our amazing new feature!

To this:

Project templates are live. Save your best workflow once, then reuse it with every new project.

Why it works: the second version leads with the change and explains its practical benefit.

Brand Voice Examples From Public Style Guides

Microsoft: Simple, Human, and Helpful

Microsoft’s official brand voice guidance defines three primary voice principles:

  • Warm and relaxed
  • Crisp and clear
  • Ready to lend a hand

The guide turns those characteristics into practical writing decisions, such as getting to the point quickly, using natural language, reducing jargon, and making choices and next steps obvious.

What to learn from Microsoft: do not stop at personality adjectives. Explain how each characteristic changes the writing.

Mailchimp: Plainspoken With Controlled Humor

Mailchimp’s public Voice and Tone guide describes its voice through practical characteristics such as being plainspoken, genuine, helpful at translating complexity, and capable of dry humor.

The guide also establishes an important boundary. Clarity is more important than entertainment, and humor should depend on the reader’s situation.

What to learn from Mailchimp: a distinctive brand can use humor without forcing jokes into every message. Define where personality belongs and where clarity must come first.

Atlassian: Bold, Optimistic, and Practical

Atlassian’s public voice and tone guidance defines its personality as:

  • Bold
  • Optimistic
  • Practical, with a wink

Its guidance then explains how those characteristics should be adjusted according to what the user is doing and feeling.

What to learn from Atlassian: a strong voice can stay recognizable while the intensity of individual traits changes according to context.

How to Test Your Brand Voice

Before approving the voice, test it against six standards.

Recognition Test

Remove the logo and company name from several examples.

Ask whether the language still feels connected and recognizable.

Relevance Test

Ask whether the voice fits the company’s positioning, audience, industry, and level of customer risk.

Distinction Test

Compare the writing with several direct competitors.

Look for language, claims, and sentence patterns that feel interchangeable.

Repeatability Test

Give the guidelines to two writers.

Ask them to write the same type of message independently.

If the outputs feel like completely different brands, the rules need more detail.

Flexibility Test

Apply the voice to:

  • A celebration
  • A sales page
  • A complaint
  • An error
  • A policy
  • An educational article

The personality should remain recognizable without making every message emotionally identical.

Credibility Test

Read the copy aloud and ask:

  • Does this sound natural?
  • Would the company actually speak this way?
  • Can the claims be supported?
  • Is the personality appropriate for the audience?
  • Does any part feel forced or performative?

A distinctive voice should still feel credible.

What to Include in Brand Voice Guidelines

Once the voice has been defined, document it in a practical reference.

Include:

Brand Voice Summary

A short explanation of the personality and the strategic reason behind it.

Audience Summary

Who the brand is speaking to, what the audience needs, and what language it understands.

Voice Attributes

Three to five characteristics with clear definitions.

Guardrails

A “we are, but we are not” statement for every attribute.

Writing Principles

Specific rules for vocabulary, structure, claims, formality, point of view, and clarity.

Preferred and Avoided Language

Approved terms, terminology rules, generic phrases to remove, and words that conflict with the voice.

Tone Guidance

Instructions for adapting the voice during common situations such as sales, support, complaints, billing, announcements, and errors.

On-Brand and Off-Brand Examples

Examples from the company’s actual communication, not only invented sentences.

Channel Guidance

Any meaningful differences between the website, social media, email, product, sales, and support.

Ownership

Who maintains the guidelines, approves exceptions, and decides when the system needs to change.

How to Keep Brand Voice Consistent

A brand voice becomes valuable when different people can apply it without recreating the personality every time.

Create One Source of Truth

Keep the current guidelines, examples, vocabulary, and templates in one location.

Do not allow multiple outdated versions to circulate.

Use Real Examples

Save strong examples from:

  • Website pages
  • Emails
  • Social posts
  • Sales communication
  • Product copy
  • Customer support

Real examples make the system easier to understand than abstract descriptions alone.

Train Everyone Who Communicates Externally

Voice training should include more than writers.

It may also involve:

  • Marketing
  • Sales
  • Customer support
  • Product teams
  • Executives
  • Freelancers
  • Agencies

For organizations rolling voice standards across multiple offices, outside partners, or regional teams, governance is part of implementation. Canadian companies that need help coordinating that rollout can work with Brand Vision’s marketing team in Canada to connect the brand system to the channels where it is used.

Build Voice Rules Into Templates

Add voice guidance to:

  • Content briefs
  • Email templates
  • Sales scripts
  • Support macros
  • CMS instructions
  • AI prompts
  • Design systems
  • Approval workflows

Review Samples Regularly

Review a selection of communication across major channels.

Look for repeated drift rather than editing every sentence individually.

Change the Voice Deliberately

A brand voice can evolve when the positioning, audience, market, or company changes.

Do not change the voice every time a new trend, platform, or campaign appears.

How to Use Brand Voice With AI

Do not ask an AI writing tool to “sound confident, authentic, and professional” and expect consistent results.

Provide a structured voice brief containing:

  • The audience
  • The communication goal
  • The approved voice attributes
  • A definition of each attribute
  • “We are, but we are not” guardrails
  • Preferred vocabulary
  • Prohibited or overused phrases
  • Approved examples
  • Off-brand examples
  • The tone required for the specific situation
  • Factual and legal constraints
  • The desired format and length

For example:

Voice: Clear, confident, practical, and helpful.

Clear means: Lead with the answer, use everyday language, and explain necessary technical terms.

Confident does not mean: Arrogant, absolute, or dismissive of uncertainty.

Avoid: “Revolutionary,” “game-changing,” “seamless,” “unlock your potential,” and unsupported superiority claims.

Situation: A customer is reporting a failed payment.

Required tone: Calm, direct, and nonjudgmental.

Output requirement: Explain what happened, what remains secure, and the next action.

AI-assisted content should still be reviewed for accuracy, context, originality, and alignment with the approved voice.

Common Brand Voice Mistakes

Mistake 1: Choosing a Voice Before Defining the Brand

A voice built without positioning usually becomes a list of generic adjectives.

Change the approach: Define the audience, position, difference, and point of view first.

Mistake 2: Copying a Famous Brand

A playful social voice may work for another company because of its audience, category, product, and existing reputation.

Change the approach: Study examples for structure, not imitation.

Mistake 3: Treating “Authentic” as a Complete Direction

Authenticity does not tell writers which words, structures, or claims to use.

Change the approach: Define observable rules that align the language with the company’s real identity and behavior.

Mistake 4: Using Generic Attributes Without Definitions

“Professional,” “friendly,” and “innovative” can mean almost anything.

Change the approach: Define every attribute with rules, guardrails, and examples.

Mistake 5: Confusing Voice With Tone

This can make the brand rigid or inconsistent.

Change the approach: Keep the personality stable and adjust the emotional delivery according to context.

Mistake 6: Mimicking Customer Slang

Audience research should improve understanding, not lead to forced imitation.

Change the approach: Use language customers understand while preserving the brand’s own identity.

Mistake 7: Creating Guidelines Without Off-Brand Examples

Writers need to understand the boundaries, not only the ideal.

Change the approach: Show both on-brand and off-brand executions.

Mistake 8: Applying the Voice Only to Marketing

Customers also experience the brand through sales, product, billing, policies, and support.

Change the approach: Test the voice across the entire customer journey.

Mistake 9: Using the Same Tone Everywhere

A product celebration and a serious customer complaint require different emotional delivery.

Change the approach: Create situational tone guidance.

Mistake 10: Giving AI Vague Personality Prompts

Three adjectives do not provide enough operational direction.

Change the approach: Include definitions, rules, examples, prohibited language, and contextual tone.

Frequently Asked Questions About Brand Voice

What is brand voice?

Brand voice is the consistent personality a company expresses through written and spoken communication.

It influences vocabulary, sentence structure, formality, point of view, humor, pacing, and the way the brand relates to its audience.

How do I find my brand voice?

Start with your positioning, values, audience, and competitive difference.

Then audit your current communication, research the language your customers use, choose three to five credible voice attributes, and translate those attributes into rules and examples.

How do I create a brand voice?

Use this process:

  1. Define the strategic foundation.
  2. Audit existing communication.
  3. Research the audience and category.
  4. Choose three to five attributes.
  5. Add guardrails.
  6. Create writing rules and examples.
  7. Test and document the system.

How many brand voice attributes should I choose?

Three to five is practical for most teams.

Use enough characteristics to create a specific personality without making the system difficult to remember or apply.

What is the difference between brand voice and tone of voice?

Brand voice is the consistent personality behind the communication.

Tone of voice is how that personality adjusts according to the audience, channel, situation, or emotional context.

What are some brand voice examples?

Microsoft, Mailchimp, and Atlassian publish public guidance showing how they define their communication styles.

Microsoft emphasizes simplicity and helpfulness. Mailchimp combines plain language with controlled humor. Atlassian defines a bold, optimistic, and practical personality that adjusts according to the user’s situation.

Can a brand voice change?

Burberry’s marketing strategy works best when the brand treats British heritage as a living system rather than a museum display. The trench coat, gabardine, the Burberry Check, weather, London, and outerwear are more than visual references. Together, they give the brand a small set of recognisable signals that can carry across product, campaigns, stores, and digital channels.

That focus is especially important during Burberry’s current turnaround. The company’s Burberry Forward strategy centres on “Timeless British Luxury,” category authority in outerwear and scarves, customer relevance, and more disciplined execution. The latest results suggest that this sharper positioning is gaining traction rather than remaining a presentation-level idea.

For founders and marketers, the useful lesson is not to imitate Burberry’s British aesthetic. It is to identify the few assets, products, stories, and experiences that customers should immediately associate with the brand, then repeat them with enough discipline that every channel reinforces the same meaning.

Brand Image: Turning British Heritage Into a Clear Position

Burberry has always sold a version of Britishness, but the strongest expression is specific rather than generic. British weather, outerwear, London streets, countryside, wit, music, and a certain practical elegance all give the brand a richer creative system than simply saying “heritage.”

Burberry’s own history gives that positioning factual depth. Thomas Burberry founded the business in 1856 and invented gabardine in 1879, a breathable, weatherproof fabric that became central to the house’s outerwear story. The company still links its trench coats to specialist manufacturing in Castleford, Yorkshire, and says the gabardine used in Heritage Trench and Car Coats is woven at its mill in Keighley.

That makes heritage useful because it is visible in the product. A strong brand strategy should work the same way: positioning is more credible when the business can show where the promise comes from, how it is delivered, and which assets make it hard to copy.

  • British identity gives campaigns a recognisable mood and place.
  • Outerwear authority ties the story to a product category Burberry can credibly own.
  • Heritage materials and manufacturing give marketing claims operational proof.

Burberry’s own history of the Burberry trench coat is especially useful because it connects the icon to material, construction, purpose, and manufacturing rather than treating it as a celebrity prop.

Pricing Strategy: Keep the Icons Premium While Maintaining Entry Points

Burberry’s pricing strategy is a ladder rather than a single price tier. Trench coats and cashmere scarves act as high-visibility proof pieces, while categories such as smaller accessories, eyewear, fragrance, and selected ready-to-wear give customers lower-cost ways to enter the brand.

The important part is not “accessibility” by itself. Entry products still need to feel connected to the same brand world. If lower-priced categories become visually generic or too promotional, they can weaken the premium meaning of the hero products.

  • Hero products such as trench coats and cashmere scarves carry the clearest heritage and status cues.
  • Entry categories can broaden participation without redefining the parent brand.
  • Price segmentation works when each tier still reinforces the same design language and service expectations.

The Trench Coat: Burberry’s Most Efficient Marketing Asset

The trench coat is not simply Burberry’s best-known product. It is the brand’s clearest shorthand. It communicates history, technical function, British weather, tailoring, and cultural familiarity in a single silhouette.

Gabardine makes that story more defensible. Burberry’s current history says Thomas Burberry invented the fabric in 1879, and the company continues to use it in Heritage Trench and Car Coats. Burberry also says specialist craftspeople may take up to a year to learn the collar-stitching technique used on the trench.

This is where product design becomes visual identity. The silhouette, collar, storm flap, belt, epaulettes, fabric, and check lining all help the product communicate the brand before a customer sees a campaign headline.

In 2026, Burberry leaned further into that asset for its 170th anniversary with “The Trench, Portraits of an Icon,” a global campaign centred on the trench and photographed by Tim Walker. The campaign is a strong example of updating the cast and creative treatment while leaving the core product meaning intact.

Burberry’s History also connects the trench to the earlier Tielocken coat, exploration, military use, and protection from the elements. That continuity is difficult for competitors to reproduce because the story is attached to a real design lineage.

Timeless British Luxury, Not Costume Heritage

Burberry’s recent strategy is more useful when understood as a tone rather than a “gentleman and lady” persona. The company describes Timeless British Luxury as a combination of heritage and innovation, recognisable London imagery, British countryside, wit, and style.

That gives the brand room to move between polished tailoring, music, humour, weather, nightlife, countryside, and modern casting without losing the British frame. The point is not to recreate an old aristocratic stereotype. It is to make the brand feel unmistakably British while still relevant to current luxury customers.

Recent campaigns such as Burberry Weather: Postcards from London show how the company continues to use weather and place as recurring creative assets. In 2026, the 170th anniversary campaign and V&A partnership extended the same approach by treating the trench as both product and cultural object.

For another premium brand, the lesson is to avoid overloading the identity with too many ideas. A clear luxury brand marketing system is easier to remember when several campaigns are different expressions of the same core position.

The Burberry Check: Recognition Requires Control

The Burberry Check is one of the brand’s most recognisable assets, which is exactly why it needs discipline. Burberry says the check first lined raincoats in the 1920s and became a broader icon in the 1960s. The cashmere check scarf followed in the 1970s.

The check can signal the brand without a logo, but recognisability becomes a liability when an asset is overused or disconnected from the premium product experience. Burberry’s history with counterfeiting and overexposure makes the check a useful case study in why strong codes need controlled application.

  • Use signature assets often enough to build memory.
  • Vary scale, placement, material, and context rather than repeating the same treatment everywhere.
  • Protect the connection between the asset and the product quality it is supposed to represent.

Burberry documents the asset in The Burberry Check, framing it as history, craftsmanship, and enduring British style rather than a short-lived pattern trend.

Digital Strategy: Extend the Physical Brand World

Burberry was an early luxury adopter of digital channels, but the more useful question now is how digital supports the current positioning. The strongest online work makes outerwear, materials, casting, location, and British atmosphere feel more tangible rather than turning the brand into a constant promotion feed.

For a premium consumer brand, B2C marketing should connect discovery, storytelling, product information, and conversion without giving each platform a different identity. A focused content strategy can help decide which stories deserve depth, while product and campaign pages give search and social traffic somewhere coherent to land.

  • Social media should repeat the brand’s strongest visual and cultural codes.
  • Interactive features should help customers understand product, material, fit, provenance, or care.
  • Sustainability claims should connect to specific practices such as longevity, repair, materials, or manufacturing rather than vague virtue language.
  • Burberry’s own Burberry Forward strategy keeps the digital work tied to outerwear, scarves, and Timeless British Luxury rather than treating channels as the strategy itself.

Retail and Experience: Make the Brand Physical

Luxury positioning is tested most directly in the buying experience. Texture, tailoring, service, product knowledge, store design, appointment flow, packaging, and aftercare all affect whether the promise feels real.

That makes retail a proof point rather than only a distribution channel. The more important the product and price, the more the customer experience needs to support confidence. For digital journeys, UX research can identify which information or interactions customers need before they are ready to visit, book, or buy.

The original article captured an earlier point in the turnaround through Burberry’s interim reporting for the 26 weeks ended September 27, 2025, which listed £1,032 million in revenue and £19 million in adjusted operating profit. Those historical references remain available in the interim results announcement and the FY26 Interim Results Press Release. The later FY2026 and Q1 FY2027 figures show the recovery has progressed beyond that interim snapshot.

What Business Owners Can Learn From Burberry

The biggest lesson is that customers do not remember strategy decks. They remember signals. Burberry is strongest when it owns a small set of recognisable assets and repeats them with discipline across product, content, retail, and tone.

  • Identify a “hero proof.” For Burberry, the trench and gabardine give the brand something tangible to build around.
  • Protect recognisable assets. A branding agency should help determine which visual and verbal codes need consistency and which can flex.
  • Design the website around the proof, not around internal company structure. Strong web design should make the most persuasive product, evidence, and next step easy to find.
  • Use SEO to capture demand created by campaigns, editorial, social attention, and branded search rather than treating organic visibility as a separate brand universe.
  • Use UI UX design to make premium journeys clear and usable without stripping away personality.

Burberry’s recent results suggest that narrowing the strategy around outerwear, scarves, British identity, and disciplined execution is helping the business recover. In Q1 FY2027, comparable retail sales grew 5%, with outerwear outperforming and all major product divisions growing year over year.

For another company, that is a useful reminder that brand work should eventually show up in behavior: stronger demand for priority products, better conversion, more repeat purchase, clearer search interest, or improved customer acquisition. Creative consistency matters, but it becomes strategically valuable when the operating and commercial signals move with it.

The broader lesson is simple: heritage creates value only when the current product and customer experience continue to prove it. If your own brand has accumulated too many messages or lost sight of its strongest proof, a focused marketing consultation can help identify what should stay, what should change, and what customers need to understand first.

Burj Khalifa advertising turns a media placement into a landmark event. At 828 metres, the Emaar-developed tower remains the world’s tallest building and one of Dubai’s most recognizable symbols. When its facade becomes a giant illuminated canvas, the value is not only the number of people who see it in person. The display can also become content for social media, press coverage, launch videos, and wider campaign distribution.

That makes marketing on the Burj Khalifa different from buying an ordinary digital billboard. Brands are paying for scale, location, cultural association, and the possibility that the creative will travel beyond Downtown Dubai. The format is particularly relevant to entertainment marketing, major launches, national moments, and brands that can justify a high-profile awareness investment.

Why Brands Use the Burj Khalifa as an Advertising Canvas

The attraction begins with the building itself. Emaar describes Burj Khalifa as 828 metres tall, with its status as the world’s tallest building forming part of Dubai’s global identity. A campaign displayed across that surface can borrow some of the landmark’s prestige, ambition, and recognizability.

That association can strengthen brand development when the placement fits the message. A luxury launch, entertainment release, tourism campaign, or technology announcement can use the building’s scale as part of the story. The same placement would make less sense for a brand that has no reason to connect itself with spectacle or global visibility.

The medium also changes how the creative is judged. A design has to work from a distance, around the proportions of a very tall facade, and in photographs or short videos captured by spectators. Strong campaign graphics therefore need simple hierarchy, recognizable shapes, legible branding, and motion that can be understood quickly.

Examples of Burj Khalifa Advertising

The tower has hosted campaigns from entertainment, technology, retail, social media, and other sectors. A 2019 report from The National cited Burj Khalifa campaigns tied to Avengers, The Lion King, Huawei, and Samsung. TikTok also used the building around its UAE launch and New Year activity, turning the facade into a media moment that matched the platform’s emphasis on short-form visual content.

Noon has used Burj Khalifa as part of regional retail campaigns, while the landmark is also frequently illuminated for cultural and national occasions. The range of uses matters because it shows that the building is not tied to one category. The common requirement is a message that can benefit from being made physically monumental.

More recent campaigns continue to use the tower as a launch signal rather than an isolated screen. In January 2026, Campaign Middle East reported that du premiered its “Bridging the Spaces Between Us” campaign on Burj Khalifa before extending the work across out-of-home, digital, social, and film. That is a useful model for advertisers: the landmark moment creates attention, while the wider media plan gives the idea somewhere to go after the display ends.

How the Advertising Process Has Worked

Public information about the booking process is limited, and brands should confirm current requirements directly with the relevant Burj Khalifa and Emaar contacts before budgeting. Historical reporting provides a useful outline of how the process has worked, but it should not be treated as a current booking manual.

In 2019, The National reported that advertisers submitted requests through MullenLowe MENA, with Emaar providing final approval. The same report said a detailed storyboard had to be finalized four weeks before the display date, payment was required upfront, and music could accompany the facade display but could not be synchronized with the Dubai Fountain show.

The operational lesson remains useful even if vendors, specifications, and lead times have changed. A Burj Khalifa activation needs more planning than a standard media placement. Creative development, technical formatting, approvals, timing, filming, and secondary distribution should be considered before the display date is booked.

What Does Burj Khalifa Advertising Cost?

The figures most often repeated online come from a 2019 rate card, so they should be treated as historical context, not as current pricing. The National reported AED 250,000 for one three-minute weekday display between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m., AED 350,000 for the comparable weekend slot, AED 500,000 for two three-minute displays, and AED 1 million for five three-minute appearances within a broader evening window.

Those numbers are useful for understanding the order of magnitude, but a brand planning a campaign in 2026 should request a current quote. Date, event timing, number of plays, production requirements, filming, and creative adaptation can affect the real project budget. A historic rate card is not a substitute for a live media proposal.

That distinction also matters when comparing the Burj Khalifa with other landmark formats. The Las Vegas Sphere marketing model similarly combines an unusual media surface with the possibility of earned social reach. In both cases, marketers should compare the total campaign cost and expected business outcome rather than judging value by the screen price alone.

Creative Scale Does Not Guarantee Campaign Effectiveness

The Burj Khalifa can create a spectacular image, but spectacle by itself is not proof of effectiveness. A campaign still needs a clear objective. Brand awareness, product launch attention, earned media, search interest, social engagement, store traffic, or sales are different outcomes and should be measured differently.

The strongest executions usually have an idea that survives beyond the facade. A reveal, transformation, recognizable object, product silhouette, or simple visual can become a photograph or short clip that still makes sense after it leaves Dubai. Complicated copy or fine details are much harder to carry into secondary distribution.

This is why the media plan should be connected to the broader brand strategy. The building can amplify a message, but it cannot decide what the message should be. A visually impressive activation that feels unrelated to the brand may generate attention without creating useful memory.

Online Distribution Extends the Value of the Display

A Burj Khalifa campaign can reach audiences who never see the building in person if the team plans the content around it. Teasers, creator coverage, behind-the-scenes footage, launch edits, photography, interviews, and paid social cutdowns can extend the activation into a longer campaign.

A strong content strategy helps decide which pieces need to exist before, during, and after the display. The goal is not to publish the same tower clip everywhere. Different channels may need a short reveal, a longer explanation, a press image, a landing page, or a creator-led reaction.

SEO can support the campaign when there is real search demand around the launch, but it should not be treated as automatic amplification. Search visibility depends on useful pages and relevant queries, while social sharing depends on the creative and distribution. These channels should support the same campaign without being confused with one another.

How to Evaluate the Return on a Landmark Campaign

The return on Burj Khalifa advertising should be assessed against the original objective. If the goal is awareness, marketers can look at qualified reach, branded search movement, earned media, video views, and share of conversation. If the goal is a product launch, site traffic, retailer searches, enquiries, or sales may matter more.

Brands should also separate the physical display from the secondary distribution it generates. A widely shared tower clip may outperform the in-person exposure, but that does not mean the display itself should receive all the credit. Use campaign-specific links, time-based baselines, platform analytics, and post-campaign reporting to understand which parts of the launch created the strongest response.

What Marketers Can Learn From Burj Khalifa Advertising

Burj Khalifa advertising works best when the landmark is part of the idea rather than simply the most expensive screen available. The campaign should have a reason to use the building’s scale, a visual concept that can be understood quickly, and a distribution plan that extends the moment beyond the facade.

The practical lesson is to plan the tower, the creative, and the digital campaign as one system. Historical pricing shows that the media commitment can be substantial, so the surrounding content and measurement should be planned with the same care as the display itself.

If your team is evaluating a large launch or high-visibility campaign, Brand Vision can help clarify the positioning, creative priorities, channel plan, and measurement approach through a marketing consultation.

A buy now, pay later marketing strategy is less about adding another payment button and more about how affordability, conversion economics, and trust are handled across the buying journey. BNPL can change how a price is evaluated at the decision moment, but the commercial upside depends on approval rates, fees, customer mix, and the experience around the offer.

That is why BNPL work now spans product pages, creative, checkout UX, analytics, and finance. The goal is not to make a purchase look cheaper than it is. It is to present payment flexibility clearly enough that customers can evaluate the option without forcing the brand to rely on constant discounting.

At a Glance

  • BNPL is an affordability message first, and a payment method second.
  • Potential lift can come from reduced sticker shock, more payment flexibility, and fewer affordability-related drop-offs.
  • BNPL conversion rate gains depend on placement, approval rates, and the product’s consideration cycle.
  • Strong implementations treat BNPL checkout UX as a design system element, with clear microcopy and accessible disclosures.
  • BNPL regulation and credit reporting continue to evolve, so responsible messaging, current legal review, and clear disclosures are part of the implementation.

Why Brands Offer Buy Now, Pay Later: The Affordability Message

Buy now, pay later is typically presented as installments, including short pay-in-four products and longer-term installment loans. Some pay-in-four products charge no interest when payments are made as agreed, while longer-term products may carry interest or other costs. In marketing, BNPL functions as a pricing translation layer because it turns one larger price into a series of smaller scheduled payments.

That is the marketing tactic. BNPL is a way to meet price sensitivity without touching your price. It can widen the set of buyers who feel comfortable purchasing today, especially for higher-consideration products and services.

This is also why ecommerce teams talk about BNPL in the same breath as product positioning. In B2C marketing, the payment option can influence how the offer is evaluated at the exact point where buyers hesitate, so the message needs to stay consistent from product page to checkout.

Two implications follow:

  • BNPL should be designed and messaged like a core product element, not a footer badge.
  • Your site experience is the real surface area. The decision is usually made before the payment step.

For teams that already invest in psychology of pricing strategies, BNPL is a practical application. It is pricing perception, operationalized inside the funnel.

The Behavioral Mechanics Behind BNPL

BNPL can change how a purchase is evaluated without changing the underlying product value. For some interest-free pay-in-four purchases, the buyer may pay the same purchase price if payments are made on time and no extra fees apply. That is not universal, especially for longer-term installment products, so marketers should avoid implying that every BNPL option is cost-free.

Installment Price Framing Reduces Sticker Shock

The simplest mechanism is installment framing. A $600 total may feel like a larger immediate commitment than four payments of $150, even when the arithmetic is identical for a no-interest, no-fee plan.

This effect is stronger when:

  • The product is discretionary.
  • The buyer is comparing multiple alternatives.
  • The buyer is uncertain about timing, cash flow, or return risk.

Your product page is where this happens. If BNPL appears only at checkout, the buyer has already decided whether the item feels affordable. That is why BNPL placement is a marketing concern, not a payments-only concern.

Perceived Control Changes The Buying Moment

Buy now, pay later can increase perceived control by letting buyers align a purchase with their cash-flow timing. That may mean shorter installment schedules or longer repayment periods, depending on the product.

For the brand, this is a way to reduce decision friction without using urgency tactics. It is a calmer form of persuasion.

Installment framing can also change how upgrades, bundles, or add-ons are compared because the incremental scheduled payment may appear smaller than the incremental total price. That does not guarantee a larger basket, so AOV still needs to be measured against returns and margin.

Payment Salience Changes When Costs Are Split

Splitting a purchase into installments can reduce the salience of the full upfront amount at checkout. That is one reason BNPL can affect purchase behavior, and also why clear risk and repayment disclosures matter.

Recent behavioral research also suggests that the expectation of access to BNPL can change spending behavior, and that clearer risk disclosures improve understanding even when they do not fully change usage patterns. See the Central Bank of Ireland technical paper on BNPL behavioral mechanisms for details and measured effects: Behavioural Mechanisms of Buy Now Pay Later Products.

For marketing leaders, the takeaway is practical. BNPL is powerful, so the guardrails matter. If the buyer does not understand the terms, the short-term conversion win can create long-term trust damage.

What The Data Says About BNPL Adoption And Impact

BNPL is no longer a niche add-on. It is a mainstream behavior with increasing visibility from regulators, lenders, and credit scoring models.

The data is also uneven. Some sources are provider-reported. Others are survey-based. The most reliable view comes from public-sector reporting and well-described merchant experiments.

What Regulators Track In The BNPL Market

In December 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau published a BNPL market report based on data from large BNPL companies, tracking metrics like loan volume, users, frequency of use, average loan size, late fees, and charge-offs across recent years. The report is a strong baseline for market-level trends.

From a marketing standpoint, the more important point is not a single statistic. BNPL sits inside the consumer-credit ecosystem, but the federal treatment has shifted. The CFPB withdrew its 2024 BNPL interpretive rule on May 12, 2025, so teams should not describe that rule as a current BNPL-specific Regulation Z mandate. Other federal and state requirements can still apply depending on the product and provider, which makes current legal review important. See the CFPB’s current BNPL compliance resources.

What Merchant Experiments Suggest About Lift

Merchant-side experimentation is where the conversion story becomes concrete. In 2024, Stripe published results from A/B tests across 150,000+ checkout sessions, testing the presence of a single BNPL option among eligible payment methods. The reported outcomes included net-new sales, revenue lift, and higher conversion rates when BNPL was presented at checkout. See the methodology and results here.

These experiments are not universal truth and were conducted by a payments provider, but they are directionally useful because the test design compares eligible checkout sessions with and without a BNPL option.

What BNPL Does For Merchants: Conversion, AOV, And Net-New Revenue

The commercial case for BNPL typically includes three levers:

  1. Higher conversion
  2. Higher basket size
  3. Access to buyers who would otherwise abandon

This is why BNPL has become a standard topic in conversion reviews and growth planning. It often shows up in the same conversations as page speed, checkout friction, and offer clarity.

If you already run conversion rate optimization (CRO) programs, BNPL should be evaluated the same way. It is a testable lever with measurable tradeoffs.

The Cannibalization Question

A common concern is cannibalization. If buyers simply switch from card payments to BNPL, the brand may pay higher processing or BNPL fees for the same sale.

The Stripe experiment discussed above directly addresses this concern, reporting that more than two-thirds of BNPL volume in its tests came from net-new sales rather than substitution. The practical takeaway is not to assume that BNPL only changes payment mix, but also not to assume the same result for every merchant. Stripe’s BNPL experiment is a useful reference for how to test this question in your own environment.

Where Lift Usually Shows Up

BNPL lift tends to be clearer in a few scenarios:

  • Higher AOV products where sticker shock is real.
  • Categories with longer consideration cycles, where timing and budget uncertainty delay decisions.
  • New customer acquisition flows, where trust and commitment are lower.

The best teams also watch for second-order effects:

  • Changes in refund and return rates.
  • Changes in customer support volume tied to billing confusion.
  • Shifts in repeat purchase behavior.

This is why BNPL average order value (AOV) gains should never be treated as pure upside. AOV lift is only one line in a larger unit economics model.

Where BNPL Works Best In The Funnel

Most BNPL implementations focus on checkout. The stronger implementations focus on the full decision path.

This is the core BNPL checkout UX idea: show affordability early, confirm it at cart, and keep the payment step clean and readable.

The general rule is supported by merchant implementation guidance. Fiserv, for example, recommends informing consumers early in the purchase journey and shows BNPL information across multiple surfaces, not only at the last step: Best Practices for Implementing a Buy Now Pay Later Solution.

Product Page Placement

Product pages do most of the persuasion work. If you want BNPL to act as an affordability message, it needs to appear where the price is first evaluated.

Common patterns:

  • A single line under the primary price: “From $X per month” or “4 payments of $X.”
  • A short explainer tooltip that answers what happens next (approval, terms, fees).
  • A “Learn more” drawer that keeps users on-page, rather than sending them away.

This is also where design quality matters. When BNPL modules are visually inconsistent, they can feel bolted on rather than part of the product experience. Treat BNPL as part of the component system.

This is one reason BNPL often becomes a joint project between growth, product, and UI UX design. A UX audit can identify where affordability messaging, terms, and payment selection create friction across templates instead of treating each page as a one-off patch.

Cart And Checkout Placement

Cart is the second decision point. The buyer is now facing a subtotal, shipping, taxes, and tradeoffs. Cart is where BNPL can reduce abandonment tied to total cost clarity.

Context matters. Baymard’s 2025 aggregation puts the average documented cart abandonment rate at about 70%. That is a reminder that checkout friction is a structural problem, not an edge case. Source: Baymard cart abandonment rate statistics.

Practical placement guidance:

  • In cart: show installment pricing next to the subtotal, not buried below.
  • At checkout: include BNPL as a standard payment method with a short clarifying line. Avoid long paragraphs.

If checkout is slow or unstable, BNPL will not save it. Performance remains a conversion prerequisite. If you need a baseline for speed and stability work, revisit how website speed ROI ties directly to conversion and revenue.

Microcopy, Disclosures, And Accessibility

BNPL copy should be clear and restrained. It should answer basic questions without creating false certainty.

A practical microcopy checklist:

  • Clarify whether approval is required.
  • Clarify whether terms vary by buyer.
  • Link to full terms without hiding them.
  • Avoid implying everyone will qualify.

Accessibility is part of trust. BNPL modules should be keyboard navigable, screen-reader readable, and consistent in color contrast. The disclosure, tooltip, and payment-selection behavior are also an interaction design problem. If each campaign creates a new BNPL variant, governance breaks down and UX becomes uneven.

If your current UX has drifted, a structured mobile UX audit often surfaces where BNPL blocks add friction on smaller screens.

Brand Examples: How Companies Position BNPL Without Discounting

BNPL is visible across retail, marketplaces, and services. The most useful examples are not the brands themselves. It is the positioning pattern.

Retail And Marketplaces

Retailers often treat BNPL as a conversion tool for higher-ticket baskets, and as a way to reduce sticker shock when the buyer compares alternatives.

A current, concrete example is Walmart’s shift to installment loans offered through OnePay, powered by Klarna, reported in March 2025. It shows how large retailers integrate installment financing directly into checkout to support sales and flexibility. (Reuters)

On the surface, this is a payments partnership. In practice, it is a marketing and conversion decision. A retailer is choosing a financing narrative at the point of purchase.

Travel And Higher-Consideration Purchases

Travel and other higher-consideration categories often use BNPL to reduce the psychological barrier of a single large purchase. For teams working in travel and hospitality marketing, the payment message needs to remain secondary to the full price, cancellation terms, and the experience being purchased.

The UX pattern is consistent:

  • Present installment pricing at the point of browsing, not only at checkout.
  • Reinforce flexibility when the buyer compares options.
  • Keep disclosures clear because terms can vary.

This is where BNPL behaves like a product feature. The payment method is part of the offer.

What The Strongest Examples Have In Common

Strong BNPL implementations usually share a few traits:

  • BNPL messaging is consistent across product pages, cart, and checkout.
  • The brand does not oversell. It states terms and keeps the promise narrow.
  • Analytics are clean enough to separate approval issues from UX issues.
  • The cost model is understood before scaling BNPL promotion.

This is also where brand positioning matters. A premium brand can offer BNPL, but it must frame the message as flexibility and planning, not as desperation pricing. That is typically a concern for branding services as much as for payments teams.

A Simple BNPL ROI Model For Marketing And Finance Teams

BNPL decisions often stall because teams cannot align on profitability. Growth sees conversion potential. Finance sees fees and risk. Both are rational.

A workable model does not need to be complicated. It needs to be shared and testable.

Inputs To Gather Before You Launch

Collect these inputs first:

  • Baseline conversion rate and baseline AOV
  • Gross margin by product category
  • Return and refund rates, by category
  • The BNPL fee structure and how it compares to existing payment mix
  • Approval rate and failure points (where buyers drop)
  • Customer mix: new vs returning, and any LTV differences

Two of these items are commonly missed:

  • BNPL fees for merchants, including how fees vary by product type and terms
  • BNPL approval rate impact, which can create silent drop-offs if approvals are low or slow

A Quick Profitability Test

Use a simple incremental profit frame:

Incremental profit
= (Incremental orders × AOV × gross margin) − incremental BNPL costs and fees − incremental refunds and returns cost − incremental support and dispute cost

If you want a fast filter before a full rollout, set guardrails:

  • Require a minimum lift in completed orders, not just BNPL selection clicks.
  • Require stable refund rates in the first test cohort.
  • Require approval flow completion rates that do not create new friction.

In practice, this model becomes a weekly dashboard. Marketing owns the funnel. Finance owns the margin assumptions. Product owns the experience. When those three views align, BNPL becomes a controlled growth lever.

Risks And Trust: What To Get Right Before You Promote BNPL

BNPL can improve access and flexibility. It can also be used by financially vulnerable consumers at higher rates. That reality is now well documented and increasingly visible to regulators and lenders.

For brands, this is not only a compliance issue. It is a trust issue. BNPL is part of how buyers judge transparency.

Financial Vulnerability And Responsible Messaging

Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston highlights that BNPL use is higher among some financially vulnerable consumers and varies across demographics. It is a reminder to be cautious with messaging and to avoid framing BNPL as a default solution for everyone. (Boston Fed)

A responsible marketing stance looks like this:

  • Do not imply universal approval.
  • Do not hide fees, late policies, or term variations.
  • Do not push BNPL as a substitute for affordability. Present it as an option.

The Central Bank of Ireland research reinforces a related point: salient risk disclosures can improve understanding, which supports informed decisions. See: Behavioural Mechanisms of Buy Now Pay Later Products.

Credit Reporting And The Next Phase Of BNPL

BNPL is moving closer to the formal credit ecosystem. In June 2025, FICO launched FICO Score 10 BNPL and FICO Score 10 T BNPL, versions designed to incorporate reported BNPL data where available. That does not mean every BNPL loan is now automatically reflected in every consumer credit score. (FICO)

For brands, the practical implication is to avoid treating BNPL as invisible credit. Clear terms and restrained affordability messaging are more durable than promises that depend on consumers ignoring repayment consequences.

Implementation Checklist: UX, Analytics, And Governance

BNPL works best when it is implemented as a product surface, not as an afterthought. That requires clear ownership and a short checklist.

Provider Selection Criteria

Start with a structured comparison. At minimum, evaluate:

  • Payment types supported (pay-in-four vs longer installment loans)
  • Approval flow speed and completion rates
  • Fee structure and settlement timeline
  • Dispute handling, refunds, and customer support responsibilities
  • Reporting, analytics exports, and attribution support

This is where teams naturally ask about Affirm vs Klarna vs Afterpay for merchants. The right answer depends on your buyer profile, average basket size, and how approval rates behave in your traffic mix.

A practical warning: approval rates can become a hidden conversion sink. Even if BNPL selection rates look strong, BNPL approval rate impact can quietly reduce completed orders if the experience is slow, confusing, or inconsistent across devices.

Analytics Events And KPIs To Track

Treat BNPL like a measurable funnel inside your funnel.

Track at least these events:

  • BNPL impression on product page
  • BNPL click or expand (learn more)
  • BNPL selected at checkout
  • BNPL application started
  • BNPL approved
  • BNPL declined
  • Order completed with BNPL
  • Order completed with non-BNPL
  • Refunds and chargebacks by payment type

The KPIs that matter:

  • Overall conversion rate
  • BNPL conversion rate (orders completed with BNPL divided by sessions exposed to BNPL)
  • BNPL cart abandonment (abandonment rate among sessions that selected BNPL)
  • AOV by payment type, including BNPL average order value (AOV)
  • Approval rate and time-to-approval

If these metrics are not clean, debates become subjective. If they are clean, BNPL becomes a controllable lever.

For acquisition teams, align onsite messaging with your broader SEO strategy. If BNPL is a differentiator, make it visible on landing pages, product pages, and comparison content, not only at checkout.

Experiment Design And Rollout

Run BNPL like a staged release:

  1. Start with a holdout test, not a global launch.
  2. Test placement, not only the provider.
  3. Separate new vs returning cohorts.
  4. Monitor refunds and support tickets in parallel with conversion.

Use clear stop conditions:

  • If approval rates are low, do not scale promotion. Fix the flow first.
  • If refund rates rise materially, re-check product fit and messaging clarity.
  • If performance degrades, prioritize stability before optimizing copy.

Teams that treat BNPL as a component of web design and web development can build the module into a governed system instead of a one-off campaign artifact.

FAQs

Does BNPL Increase Conversion Rate?

It can, but the result depends on category, order value, eligibility, approval flow, and implementation. The best evidence comes from controlled merchant experiments and clean in-house testing. The most reliable approach is to measure conversion lift by exposing a segment of traffic to BNPL while keeping everything else constant.

Does BNPL Increase Average Order Value?

It can. BNPL can encourage buyers to choose higher-ticket items or add complementary products when the incremental payment feels smaller than the incremental total price. Measure BNPL average order value (AOV) against card and wallet AOV, and watch return rates so the lift is not offset downstream.

Does BNPL Increase Returns?

It depends on category, buyer intent, product fit, and how BNPL is messaged. Do not assume return rates will stay stable. Monitor refunds and exchanges by payment type from day one and include them in the profitability model.

Should Premium Brands Offer BNPL?

Premium brands can offer BNPL without eroding brand position, but the framing matters. Position BNPL as flexibility and planning. Keep the design minimal. Keep the disclosures clear. Avoid language that implies financial strain.

How Much Do BNPL Providers Charge Merchants?

BNPL fees for merchants vary by provider, product type, and term length. Treat the fee structure as one variable in an ROI model, not as a standalone decision. A slightly higher fee can still be profitable if it creates net-new orders or meaningfully improves conversion for higher-margin categories.

Key Takeaways And Next Steps

  • BNPL is a marketing tactic because it changes perceived affordability at the decision moment.
  • The strongest BNPL programs are designed across product pages, cart, and checkout, with consistent components and restrained copy.
  • Measure BNPL with an internal funnel: impressions, selections, approvals, completions, refunds.
  • Evaluate profitability with incremental gross profit, not with AOV alone.
  • Treat trust as a first-order KPI. Clear terms and accessible disclosures protect the brand.
  • Run BNPL as a controlled experiment, then scale only when the data supports it.

BuzzFeed’s marketing strategy helped define an era of internet media. Quizzes, listicles, highly shareable headlines, social distribution, and later video brands such as Tasty showed how content could be designed around the way people discovered and passed stories between one another online. The challenge has always been turning that attention into a durable business.

That challenge looks different in 2026. BuzzFeed Inc. still operates recognizable brands including BuzzFeed, HuffPost, and Tasty, but the company has gone through years of restructuring, asset sales, leadership changes, and new bets on AI and streaming. The useful marketing lesson is not simply how BuzzFeed became viral. It is how a media brand has had to keep changing its distribution, monetization, and brand development as the internet around it changed.

Virality Was Built Into the Product

BuzzFeed launched in 2006 and became known for formats that were easy to consume and easy to share. Listicles, quizzes, reaction posts, celebrity coverage, humour, and visual explainers reduced the effort required to understand or pass along a story. The content was often designed around a specific social behaviour: “Which one are you?”, “You need to see this,” or “Send this to a friend who…”

This made BuzzFeed an important entertainment marketing case study. The company did not wait for audiences to visit a homepage first. It learned how content travelled through Facebook, YouTube, search, and other platforms, then adjusted formats to suit those environments.

The strength of that model was reach. The weakness was dependence on platforms BuzzFeed did not control. When algorithms, referral traffic, audience habits, or advertising economics changed, the same distribution system that accelerated growth could also become a vulnerability.

BuzzFeed Built Distinct Content Brands for Different Audiences

BuzzFeed’s expansion into video showed another useful idea: one media company can contain several recognizable audience propositions. BuzzFeed Video, Tasty, BuzzFeed Celeb, As/Is, and other channels were not presented as identical feeds. They used different subjects, formats, and tones for different communities.

That is a form of brand strategy. The parent company could serve several interests without forcing every viewer to follow every subject. Tasty is the clearest surviving example: food content developed its own visual language, production conventions, and audience expectations while remaining part of the wider BuzzFeed portfolio.

Video also gave BuzzFeed formats that could travel beyond its own website. Short recipes, challenges, explainers, celebrity interviews, and serialized entertainment were suited to YouTube and social feeds. The broader lesson is similar to modern video marketing: the format has to work where the audience actually watches it, not only where the publisher would prefer them to arrive.

Platform Growth Did Not Automatically Create a Durable Business

BuzzFeed’s early model proved that a publisher could build massive attention on social platforms, but attention and monetization are different problems. Advertising rates, referral traffic, creator competition, and platform rules can all change without a publisher controlling them.

This is why a modern publisher needs a clear content strategy that distinguishes discovery from ownership. Social platforms may introduce a story to someone, but email, direct visits, apps, subscriptions, communities, or repeat search behaviour can create a more durable audience relationship.

BuzzFeed’s own 2026 reporting points in that direction. In its first-quarter update, the company said direct visits, internal referrals, and app pageviews represented a majority of traffic to owned-and-operated properties, with direct traffic surpassing both Facebook and Google referrals as one of BuzzFeed.com’s largest sources. That is materially different from the platform-first image many people still associate with the company.

The 2023 Closure of BuzzFeed News Marked a Business-Model Reset

BuzzFeed’s expansion into serious news created editorial credibility, including a Pulitzer Prize, but the standalone news operation became difficult to sustain financially. In April 2023, Jonah Peretti announced that BuzzFeed would begin closing BuzzFeed News while reducing the broader workforce by about 15%. The company’s SEC-filed memo said it could no longer continue funding BuzzFeed News as a standalone organization.

The closure should not be read as proof that digital news or interactive content failed as marketing formats. It is better understood as a reminder that audience engagement, editorial value, and sustainable economics have to work together. A publisher can create influential content and still struggle if the revenue model does not support the cost structure.

Asset Sales Narrowed the Portfolio

BuzzFeed continued to simplify the company after the news shutdown. In February 2024, it sold Complex Networks to NTWRK for $108.6 million in cash. Later that year, it sold First We Feast, the company behind Hot Ones, for $82.5 million.

Those transactions helped reduce debt and concentrated more attention on the remaining brands. From a marketing perspective, the shift is a form of rebranding and portfolio refocusing even without a wholesale change of name. A company can change what the parent brand represents by selling, closing, or separating businesses that no longer fit the operating model.

The lesson for other media companies is to distinguish audience value from portfolio complexity. Owning more brands does not automatically create a stronger business if teams, technology, sales systems, and distribution cannot support them efficiently.

BuzzFeed Entered a New Ownership and Leadership Era in 2026

In May 2026, Allen Family Digital, an affiliate of Byron Allen’s family office, completed a majority investment in BuzzFeed. Allen Family Digital acquired approximately 51% of the company’s outstanding shares. Byron Allen became chairman and chief executive officer, while founder Jonah Peretti moved into the role of President of BuzzFeed AI.

The announced strategy combines BuzzFeed’s digital brands with Allen’s distribution infrastructure. The company has described plans around free streaming video, audio, user-generated content, AI-assisted media, and direct-to-consumer experiences. That is a major change from the older model that depended heavily on social distribution and programmatic advertising.

The same change affects advertising sales. In August 2026, BuzzFeed said Allen Media Group would represent BuzzFeed advertising inventory, creating another route for brands and agencies to buy campaigns spanning digital media, streaming, television, and local broadcast.

The Current Financial Picture Is Still Challenging

BuzzFeed is not describing the 2026 reset as a completed turnaround. In its second-quarter results, the company reported total revenue of $36.3 million, down 22% year over year, and a net loss of $11.8 million. Cash and cash equivalents were $16.3 million at June 30, 2026. BuzzFeed’s Q2 2026 release also quoted Byron Allen saying that BuzzFeed, Tasty, and HuffPost had been carrying an unsustainable cost structure and that significant cost reductions were needed.

This is why BuzzFeed’s marketing challenge cannot be reduced to “make more viral content.” The company has to improve monetization while protecting the audience value of its brands. Advertising, content production, commerce, streaming, and product innovation need to contribute to a business model that can support the cost of creating and distributing the media.

That requires an integrated marketing and revenue strategy rather than treating content, advertising sales, product, and distribution as unrelated teams.

What BuzzFeed’s Marketing Strategy Still Gets Right

BuzzFeed’s history still offers several useful lessons. It learned early that formats should fit the channel, that audiences respond to recognizable content franchises, and that a publisher can build multiple brands around different interests. It also demonstrated how data and rapid experimentation can shape editorial packaging.

The harder lesson is that distribution strategy and business strategy cannot be separated. A publisher that rents most of its audience from another platform is exposed when that platform changes. A publisher that owns attention but cannot monetize it efficiently has a different problem. BuzzFeed has experienced both.

For a Los Angeles publisher choosing a Los Angeles branding partner, the useful application is to define how each content brand relates to the others, who each one serves, and what should stay consistent across the portfolio. A new visual identity alone cannot solve an unclear audience or revenue model.

The Bigger Marketing Lesson

BuzzFeed’s marketing strategy was never only about catchy headlines. Its real strength was understanding how content, platform behaviour, audience identity, and distribution fit together. The company’s current reset shows the other side of that equation: the distribution system, cost structure, and revenue model have to evolve too.
