Coca-Cola’s 2025 holiday campaign did not replace every film with generative AI. The company launched three new films, including “A Holiday Memory” and two AI-driven reimaginings of the 1995 “Holidays Are Coming” commercial. Those AI films kept the familiar red trucks and winter setting, while adding stylized animals and a production process built around generative video tools.

That distinction matters because the debate is larger than whether one commercial looks convincing. Coca-Cola is testing how far AI can enter a heritage-heavy brand system without weakening the emotional cues people already associate with Christmas.

At a glance

  • Coca-Cola returned to AI-driven holiday filmmaking in 2025 after criticism of its 2024 experiments. (People)
  • The 2025 campaign used two AI-driven “Holidays Are Coming” films alongside another new holiday film, so AI was an important part of the campaign but not the whole campaign.
  • Criticism focused on visual inconsistencies, synthetic motion, authenticity, and the effect of AI production on creative work.(Business Insider)
  • Coca-Cola says AI helps teams create versions more quickly and scale content across audiences and geographies while keeping human creative direction in control. (Coca-Cola Company)

The path from 1995 to the 2025 AI campaign

The creative benchmark is Coca-Cola’s 1995 “Holidays Are Coming” truck commercial, which the company itself still treats as a core holiday asset. Coca-Cola’s public generative-AI experimentation accelerated in 2023 with Create Real Magic, a platform built through its Bain and OpenAI alliance using GPT-4 and DALL-E. (Coca-Cola Company)

In 2024, Coca-Cola moved from AI-powered consumer experiences into AI-driven holiday films. Its own campaign materials described three production houses using generative tools to reimagine “Holidays Are Coming,” alongside other holiday creative and digital experiences. (Coca-Cola Company 2024)

By 2025, Coca-Cola had narrowed the approach to two AI-driven reimaginings created with Secret Level and Silverside AI, while repeatedly stressing that direction, creative ambition, and music remained human-led.

What the 2025 AI films look like

The AI-driven films preserve the caravan, snow, red trucks, and holiday animals, but they avoid making realistic human faces the center of the execution. Reporting on the campaign noted the shift toward animated creatures after the uncanny faces and motion criticized in 2024. (The Hollywood Reporter)

The result is more stylized, but it still shows some of the temporal-consistency problems associated with generative video. Business Insider highlighted trucks changing form between frames, while The Verge described the newer version as technically improved in some details but still visually inconsistent.

Why the campaign remains controversial

The criticism falls into three different categories that should not be collapsed into one. First is production quality: viewers can notice continuity mistakes and unstable movement. Second is authenticity: Coca-Cola holiday advertising carries decades of nostalgia, so a visibly synthetic execution can feel different even when it repeats familiar assets. Third is labor and craft: generative video raises a broader industry question about what happens to directors, animators, VFX artists, and production crews when more of the image-generation work moves into AI systems.

Those concerns are especially important for audience research. A campaign can attract attention and still create a trust problem with part of the audience. Brands need to measure both.

Why Coca-Cola keeps using AI

The business case is clearer than the creative consensus. Coca-Cola says generative tools make it easier to produce multiple versions for different audiences and geographies, while keeping humans in charge of direction and decision-making. Company materials describe the work as AI-powered brand storytelling, not autonomous creative production. (Coca-Cola Company)

The Verge, citing The Wall Street Journal, reported that Coca-Cola’s chief marketing officer said the newer process was cheaper and faster than traditional production, with work completed in roughly a month rather than starting a year in advance. That is a reported production advantage, not proof that AI improves the campaign itself.

For a global beverage brand, the appeal also relates to beverage branding at scale: the company wants recognizable assets to remain consistent while versions change across markets.

How the 2025 AI films were made

Reporting on the production describes a hybrid workflow rather than a one-prompt commercial. Around 100 people were involved, including five AI specialists who generated and refined more than 70,000 clips. Editors and other human creatives then selected, assembled, corrected, and finished the material. (Business Insider)

That scale explains why campaign graphic design and post-production judgment still matter. Generating more options does not remove the need to decide which frame, motion, composition, and brand cue actually belong in the final film.

Backlash is not the same as failure

The campaign illustrates why attention and effectiveness need separate measures. Business Insider reported that System1 gave the 2025 ad a strong emotional-response score while DAIVID found a small trust deficit. That combination is more useful than assuming negative discussion automatically creates brand value or that backlash automatically means the work failed.

This is also where brand strategy matters. Coca-Cola is balancing two goals that can conflict: protecting deeply familiar holiday memory structures while proving that its marketing organization can use emerging production technology at global scale.

The previously published version of this article attributed an unsourced quote to Arman Tale. A search for that wording only surfaced this article itself, so the quote has been removed rather than repeated without verifiable provenance.

What changed from 2024 to 2025

The clearest change is creative direction. The 2025 AI films lean more heavily on stylized animals and fantasy rather than realistic people. The trucks also receive more consistent treatment than in the 2024 films, although critics still point to shape changes and uneven motion. (The Wall Street Journal).

The larger shift is process maturity. Coca-Cola is not presenting AI as a one-off stunt anymore. It is incorporating AI into a broader marketing and design infrastructure, while the consumer-facing work is still being judged by ordinary standards of craft, warmth, and continuity.

What marketers can learn from Coca-Cola’s AI ads

Start with the story and the brand assets before choosing the production technology. Generative tools can expand options, but they also create more material that needs human judgment. For a heritage brand, visual identity consistency matters because small errors in familiar assets are easier for audiences to notice.

The second lesson is to build a world that can survive format changes. Coca-Cola keeps returning to trucks, snow, Santa, animals, red, and holiday generosity. Brand Vision’s guide to brand world-building explains why recurring codes can make experimentation safer when the audience still recognizes the underlying system. (Business Insider)

FAQ

Why did the Coca-Cola AI ads receive backlash?

Critics pointed to visible continuity problems, synthetic motion, questions about authenticity, and concerns about the effect of generative tools on creative jobs. 

Did Coca-Cola avoid realistic human characters on purpose?

The 2025 AI films place stylized animals at the center, which reporting described as a way to reduce the uncanny-human problems seen in the previous campaign. 

Why does Coca-Cola keep using generative AI?

The company emphasizes faster production, scalable versions, and human-led control. Independent reporting also describes meaningful time and cost savings compared with traditional production. 

Was the 2025 campaign a clear creative breakthrough?

No. Some technical details improved and one reported consumer test scored the work strongly, but major outlets still criticized visible AI artifacts and the synthetic feel. “Breakthrough” would overstate the evidence. 

What Coca-Cola’s 2025 AI holiday ads actually prove

The 2025 campaign proves that Coca-Cola is willing to keep testing generative production inside one of its most recognizable marketing traditions. It does not prove that audiences prefer AI-made advertising or that speed and cost automatically improve creative quality.

Brand Vision approaches emerging production tools as part of a wider brand system, not as a substitute for strategy or craft. If your team is experimenting with AI while protecting established brand cues, you can discuss brand storytelling with Brand Vision.

Coca-Cola and Pepsi have competed for attention for generations, but their marketing playbooks are not identical. Coca-Cola tends to protect a stable set of distinctive brand assets and build emotional continuity around them. Pepsi is more willing to refresh its identity, lean into pop culture, and use reinvention as part of the brand story. The contrast makes the rivalry a useful case study in brand strategy, especially for companies deciding how much of an established identity to preserve and how much to evolve.

PepsiCo's Marketing Strategy: Reinvention and Cultural Relevance

Pepsi has long positioned itself close to music, sports, entertainment, and youth culture. Celebrity partnerships with figures such as Britney Spears and Beyoncé helped the brand turn major campaigns into cultural events rather than simple product advertisements. This approach can generate attention quickly, but it also makes creative judgment especially important because the brand is borrowing context from public figures and social moments.

Celebrity Partnerships and Campaign Risk

Pepsi's use of celebrities gives campaigns built-in reach and cultural relevance. The trade-off is that highly visible partnerships can magnify mistakes. The backlash to the 2017 Kendall Jenner advertisement remains a useful reminder that brands need to test not only whether a concept is memorable, but also how its message may be interpreted outside the intended creative frame.

Portfolio Expansion Beyond Traditional Cola

PepsiCo's broader business gives the company more ways to respond when beverage preferences change. Its portfolio spans convenient foods and beverages, including Pepsi-Cola, Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Quaker, and SodaStream. PepsiCo agreed to acquire SodaStream in 2018 in a transaction valued at $3.2 billion, not 2015 as this article previously stated. The deal expanded PepsiCo's reach into at-home beverage systems rather than simply adding another packaged cola.

Design Reinvention as a Marketing Tool

Pepsi also uses visual change more actively than Coca-Cola. Its globe, typography, packaging, and supporting visual system have evolved repeatedly, giving the company a way to signal new eras of the brand. Pepsi's 2023 redesign brought the wordmark back inside the globe and introduced a bolder black-and-electric-blue system. Brand Vision's breakdown of the new Pepsi logo and visual identity looks at that redesign in more detail.

Coca-Cola's Marketing Strategy: Consistency and Emotional Memory

Coca-Cola's approach is more closely associated with long-term continuity. Its script wordmark, red palette, contour bottle, and recurring themes of sharing and refreshment create a stable visual and emotional foundation. The company still adapts campaigns to new channels, but it often does so without discarding the assets audiences already recognize.

Share a Coke and Participatory Marketing

The Share a Coke campaign, first launched in Australia in 2011, replaced the familiar Coca-Cola logo on packaging with popular names. The idea made the product itself part of the campaign and gave consumers a reason to search, share, photograph, and gift bottles. Its strength came from combining personalization with a simple social action rather than relying only on media spend.

Heritage Advertising and Repeated Brand Assets

Coca-Cola's holiday advertising provides another example of repetition building memory. The company had used Santa Claus in advertising before 1931, but illustrator Haddon Sundblom's warm, human portrayal became a recurring part of Coca-Cola's Christmas campaigns for decades. Coca-Cola's own archive notes that Santa had worn red before the campaign, so the useful lesson is not that Coca-Cola invented Santa's appearance. It is that consistent imagery can become more powerful when a brand gives it time to accumulate meaning.

A Broad Beverage Portfolio Without Abandoning the Core Brand

Coca-Cola also operates far beyond its flagship cola, with brands across sparkling drinks, water, sports drinks, coffee, tea, juice, dairy, and plant-based beverages. That portfolio gives the company room to respond to changing tastes while keeping Trademark Coca-Cola as one of the central assets in the business.

Branding and Recognition: Two Different Models

The contrast is clearest in how the two brands treat identity. Pepsi repeatedly uses redesigns to signal movement and cultural relevance. Coca-Cola relies more heavily on continuity, allowing long-standing brand assets to compound recognition over time. Neither approach is automatically better. The right choice depends on whether the existing identity still carries useful equity and whether change solves a real audience or business problem.

Pepsi: Refresh the System, Preserve the Recognizable Core

Even when Pepsi changes its wordmark, packaging, or globe treatment, the red, white, and blue color family and circular symbol provide continuity. The challenge is to modernize without making the brand feel unfamiliar. This is where disciplined branding matters: a refresh should clarify or strengthen the system rather than change assets simply to look new.

Coca-Cola: Let Distinctive Assets Accumulate

Coca-Cola demonstrates the opposite advantage. Its script and red-and-white system have been used consistently enough that the brand can change campaign concepts without rebuilding its identity each time. Research on cola preference also shows why brand cues matter. A 2004 neuroscience study found that brand information influenced expressed preferences and brain responses when participants compared Coke and Pepsi, illustrating that product choice can be shaped by more than taste alone. The article's existing blind taste test reference is preserved here for additional context.

Where the Rivalry Stands Today

Comparing Coca-Cola and PepsiCo requires care because the companies are structured differently. The Coca-Cola Company is primarily a beverage business, while PepsiCo combines beverages with a major convenient-food portfolio. PepsiCo's current portfolio includes brands such as Lay's, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, Mountain Dew, Quaker, and SodaStream. That diversification means a single cola market-share statistic does not describe the full competitive picture.

The previous version of this article cited a 2020 Pepsi market-share figure and then claimed Coca-Cola was worth about five times as much as PepsiCo. That comparison mixed different measures and is not reliable enough to support a useful conclusion, so it has been removed. For marketers, the more durable takeaway is that both companies use brand strength to support broad portfolios while responding differently to changing consumer demand.

Consumer interest in reduced-sugar and alternative beverage options has also pushed both companies to broaden their offerings. Coca-Cola sells low- and no-calorie variants across its portfolio, while PepsiCo continues to develop zero-sugar beverages and at-home options such as SodaStream. These moves show that product strategy and marketing strategy cannot be separated: a brand promise has to evolve alongside what the company actually sells.

Lessons for Marketers From Coca-Cola vs. Pepsi

  1. Build emotional meaning around a clear strategy. Coca-Cola often uses sharing, nostalgia, and familiarity, while Pepsi frequently uses culture, entertainment, and momentum. Emotional marketing works best when it reinforces a defined brand strategy rather than substituting for one.
  2. Know what should stay consistent. Coca-Cola shows the value of distinctive assets that compound over time. Pepsi shows that a brand can evolve repeatedly if recognizable cues survive the change.
  3. Use research before changing the identity. A redesign should respond to a real audience, positioning, or usability problem. Structured brand research can help teams distinguish between a system that needs refinement and one that needs a more substantial reset.
  4. Connect marketing to the category. Beverage brands compete through product, packaging, retail presence, sponsorship, culture, and digital media at the same time. A strong food and beverage marketing plan has to account for how those touchpoints reinforce one another.
  5. Make participation easy. Pepsi's entertainment partnerships and Coca-Cola's Share a Coke campaign work differently, but both give audiences a role beyond passively watching an advertisement.

Which Marketing Strategy Is Better?

There is no single winner because the two brands are solving different strategic problems. Coca-Cola's strength is continuity: it has built a system in which familiar visual assets and emotional themes reinforce one another over long periods. Pepsi's strength is active reinvention: it uses design, celebrity partnerships, and cultural moments to keep the brand feeling current.

For other companies, the useful question is not whether to copy Coke or Pepsi. It is whether the brand has distinctive assets worth protecting, whether the audience still recognizes and values them, and whether a change would improve the strategy rather than simply refresh the surface.

If your company is deciding between protecting an established identity and making a more substantial change, working with a branding agency can help connect the decision to positioning, research, and the wider brand system.

Collectibles have moved well beyond their traditional association with hobbyist activity. Rare whiskies, vintage watches, fine art, and premium equipment now occupy a recognized place in diversified investment portfolios — appealing to investors because they combine genuine passion with tangible asset value. But the collectibles market also functions as an unusually clear case study in the mechanics of brand trust. The principles that separate credible operators from fraudulent ones in this space map almost exactly onto the principles that determine whether a brand earns lasting customer loyalty or squanders it.

Understanding what protects investors in the collectibles market illuminates something broader: the same standards that sophisticated buyers apply to high-value asset purchases are the same standards consumers increasingly apply to every brand relationship. Transparency, verifiable reputation, fee clarity, and pressure-free engagement are not just due diligence checkboxes: they are brand signals that determine conversion and retention at every price point.

Verification Is the Foundation of Every Credible Brand Relationship

The first principle in collectibles investing is rigorous asset verification. Emotional connection to a category — which is precisely what draws many investors to collectibles — makes objective assessment harder. Alphie Valentine, Co-founder of Hackstons — established whisky specialists providing opportunities for both investment and consumption — captures this dynamic directly:

"Cask whisky is an exciting and unique asset, but as with everything, it's important to go with your eyes fully open."

The parallel for brand strategy is direct. Consumers make purchase decisions in categories they care about — and passion does not eliminate the need for verification. Brands that proactively provide verifiable proof of their claims, whether through certifications, third-party reviews, or transparent documentation, reduce the friction that causes buyers to hesitate. Research on consumer trust and purchase behavior consistently shows that verifiability is one of the strongest predictors of conversion, particularly for high-consideration purchases.

Guaranteed Outcomes Are a Red Flag in Any Market

In collectibles investing, any operator claiming guaranteed returns should be treated as a fraud signal. Values fluctuate based on dozens of interrelated factors: collector demographics, cultural trends, economic conditions, and supply dynamics — and no credible professional can predict future outcomes with certainty. The same logic applies to marketing. Agencies or platforms that guarantee specific results in search ranking, lead volume, or conversion rate are overpromising in ways that should raise questions about their methods and their honesty. As guidance from the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority notes, guaranteed return claims are among the most reliable indicators of misrepresentation in alternative investment categories — a pattern that has a direct analogue in the marketing services industry.

The brands and partners worth working with are those that speak in probabilities, benchmarks, and evidence, not certainties. That intellectual honesty is itself a trust signal.

Transparency About Operations Builds Confidence Before the Sale

In the collectibles market, a credible operator can explain exactly where and how an asset is stored, what the facility certifications are, and what the logistics look like at every stage of the investment journey. Slow responses, vague answers, and reluctance to discuss specific details are recognized red flags.

The brand strategy lesson is identical. Operational transparency — clear pricing, honest product descriptions, specific delivery timelines, accessible support — reduces buyer anxiety before the transaction is completed. Research on the relationship between transparency and customer loyalty shows that brands perceived as operationally open generate meaningfully higher repeat purchase rates than those that manage information asymmetry in their favor. Transparency is not just ethical: it is a conversion and retention strategy.

Third-Party Reputation Is More Persuasive Than Self-Promotion

Collectibles investors are advised to seek out operators with verified track records on independent review platforms, because feedback from a diverse range of past clients with different risk profiles and investment objectives is more credible than any marketing material an operator produces about itself. Reviewing a partner's history on platforms provides cross-sectional evidence of consistent performance that cannot be manufactured through advertising spend.

This is one of the most important and underutilized insights for brand marketing. Third-party validation — whether through verified review platforms, media coverage, industry recognition, or user-generated content — carries exponentially more persuasive weight than equivalent investment in owned channels. Brands that systematically cultivate third-party proof of their quality build a credibility asset that compounds over time and operates independently of their advertising budget.

Fee Clarity and Pressure-Free Engagement Are Non-Negotiable Brand Standards

Convoluted fee structures and high-pressure sales tactics are the two most reliable signals that a collectibles operator is not operating in the client's interest. Legitimate partners present complete, simple fee information upfront and allow investors the time they need to conduct due diligence without artificial urgency.

The marketing implication is clear. Brands that hide costs, use dark patterns to push conversions, or manufacture urgency through misleading scarcity tactics may see short-term conversion lift, but they systematically destroy the trust that drives customer lifetime value. Research on ethical marketing practices and customer retention consistently finds that transparent, pressure-free customer experiences produce higher long-term revenue per customer than high-pressure conversion optimization. The brands that build durable market positions are those that treat conversion as the beginning of a relationship, not the end of a transaction.

Conclusion

The collectibles investment market is an unusually instructive environment for brand marketers because the stakes are high enough that buyers scrutinize every element of the operator relationship — and the principles that emerge from that scrutiny are universal.

Verification, transparency, honest communication about risk and limitations, independent reputation signals, fee clarity, and respect for the buyer's decision-making process are not niche requirements of a specialist investment category. They are the foundations of every brand relationship that sustains itself beyond the first transaction. For a broader perspective on how these principles connect to long-term brand positioning, the Brand Vision Insights guide to brand trust and marketing strategy provides additional context on building credibility as a commercial asset.

Commodity vs. brand is not only a marketing distinction. It is an economic one. When buyers see an offer as interchangeable, price carries more weight and differentiation becomes harder to defend. When buyers can explain why they prefer one option, the business may gain more room to protect price, retain customers, and invest for the long term. That is why brand equity matters, and why a clear brand strategy should connect positioning to the evidence and experience buyers actually evaluate.

At a Glance

Most companies do not deliberately become commodities. The drift happens when differentiation becomes harder to see, proof is scattered, and promotions begin carrying more of the demand. In procurement-led categories, the offer can then be reduced to a line item unless the business makes its value and trade-offs easy to verify.

Key points to keep in view:

  • Commodity vs brand is an economic condition. It shows up in pricing power, demand elasticity, and margin stability.
  • Brand equity is more useful when it can be observed through preference, reduced substitutability, retention, or willingness to pay.
  • Digital experience is part of the engine. Speed, accessibility, UX, and governance affect conversion, retention, and trust.
  • Long-term growth becomes easier to plan when customer lifetime value, acquisition efficiency, and margin behavior are measured together.

The Economics of the Commodity Trap

In a commodity environment, buyers do what the system rewards. They compare fast, reduce risk, and justify decisions with clean spreadsheets. If your offering looks interchangeable, the only defensible choice becomes price. That is not irrational. It is what happens when the market makes comparison easy and differentiation hard to verify. Competition policy frameworks even define markets around substitution patterns and demand-side switching using tools like the SSNIP test, which reinforces how central substitutability is to economic outcomes (OECD).

The commodity trap is not only lower prices. It is the instability that follows. When pricing power fades, growth becomes dependent on discounts, urgency, and reactive promotions. That pulls resources away from product quality, customer experience, and proof. It also creates internal behavior you can feel: sales wants concessions, marketing wants volume, and operations tries to hit margin targets with fewer degrees of freedom.

Common signs you are being commoditized:

  • Sales calls begin with “what can you do on price” instead of “how do you solve this.”
  • Customers ask for side-by-side comparisons because differentiation is not clear.
  • Renewal conversations become negotiations, not continuation.
  • Marketing produces demand, but conversion remains fragile and CAC rises.

This is where brand equity becomes useful. The goal is not fame. It is to give buyers credible reasons to evaluate the offer on fit, risk, proof, and experience instead of defaulting to price alone.

Commodity vs Brand: Definitions That Matter in Board Meetings

The easiest way to make this topic useful is to define commodity vs brand in terms of buyer behavior. You do not need a philosophical definition. You need a diagnostic that explains why margins, retention, and growth feel the way they do.

The Commodity Baseline: Price, Parity, and Procurement Logic

A commodity is anything buyers treat as equivalent. Sometimes the products truly are similar. Often, the perception of parity is the bigger problem. If a buyer cannot quickly see the difference, they assume the difference is not worth paying for.

Commodity dynamics typically include:

  • High substitutability. Many credible alternatives.
  • Low switching friction. Moving feels easy or low risk.
  • Price as the sorting mechanism. Buyers anchor on cost, not outcomes.

Digital comparison accelerates this. When a category is searchable, scannable, and comparable, buyers can evaluate alternatives quickly. If the reasons to choose you are buried in vague language, scattered documents, or unsupported claims, structured brand research can help identify which differences customers actually notice and value.

The Brand Advantage: Preference, Trust, and Reduced Substitutability

A brand is the set of expectations that enters the room before the sales team does. It is built from consistency, proof, and experience. When those expectations create a meaningful preference, some alternatives become less acceptable even if they look similar on paper. That reduced substitutability can support a defensible brand premium.

Brand advantage often shows up as:

  • Shorter evaluation cycles because perceived risk is lower.
  • Stronger conversion from the same traffic because clarity is higher.
  • Better renewal stability because trust is already banked.
  • Less need to “explain” your value in every conversation.

Value also extends beyond features. Functional outcomes, risk reduction, ease of use, confidence, and emotional benefits can all influence how buyers judge alternatives. The useful question is which benefits matter enough to change a real decision.

The Unit Economics Lens: Where the Difference Shows Up

To move beyond opinions, look at unit economics over time. Brand strength should not be assumed from awareness or aesthetics alone. It is more credible when changes in preference are accompanied by healthier commercial signals.

Commercial signals worth testing include:

  • Gross margin stability.
  • Customer lifetime value relative to acquisition cost.
  • Win rates at intended pricing.
  • Retention and expansion behavior by cohort.

If those signals are not present, your “brand” may be confined to language and visuals. The economics change only when the delivery system changes.

Brand Premium and Pricing Power: The Margin You Can Defend

Pricing power is one of the clearest places where commodity vs. brand becomes measurable. If a business can increase price while conversion, retention, or demand remain resilient relative to comparable alternatives, that can indicate stronger pricing power. The test is behavioral, not rhetorical.

What a Brand Premium Really Is

A brand premium is the amount customers accept above the nearest credible substitute. It is granted by buyers, not claimed by marketing. It comes from perceived risk reduction and perceived value increase.

Brand premium usually comes from:

  • Reliability. You do what you say, consistently.
  • Proof. Outcomes are visible and verifiable.
  • Clarity. Buyers understand who you are for and why you win.
  • Experience. Buying and using the product feels controlled, not chaotic.

This is closely tied to willingness to pay. If you want a clear definition and practical way to think about it, HBS Online’s willingness-to-pay explainer is a useful reference point for how buyers set their internal ceiling price.

Pricing Power Without Wishful Thinking

Pricing power is not a claim on a pricing page. It is observed when price changes do not create disproportionate losses in demand, conversion, or retention. Negotiation behavior can be another signal, but the reason buyers accept a price may include product performance, switching costs, availability, service, and brand preference.

Signals that pricing power is real:

  • Modest price increases do not trigger disproportionate churn.
  • Discount requests decline over time in the segments you care about.
  • Win rates hold even when you are not the cheapest.
  • Sales cycles compress because the decision feels easier.

The profit impact of pricing is often underestimated inside organizations. McKinsey has long argued that small pricing improvements can materially lift operating profit (McKinsey pricing PDF).

When Promotions Become the Business Model

Discounting is not always wrong. It becomes risky when customers learn to delay purchases or when realized prices drift far below the intended position. Over time, the promotion pattern itself can become part of what buyers expect from the brand.

Symptoms of promotion dependency:

  • Revenue spikes followed by troughs that force new promotions.
  • A widening gap between list price and realized price.
  • Customers who buy only when a discount appears.
  • Internal teams that plan around urgency instead of value.

If this is the current state, the problem is broader than campaign execution. Exiting commodity pressure requires clearer differentiation, stronger proof, and a more consistent experience system. Broad branding services and focused brand strategy address different parts of that work, from the overall identity system to the positioning and decision rules behind it.

For consumer businesses, a B2C marketing program should also separate intentional promotional mechanics from discounting that weakens the intended position over time.

Demand Elasticity and Switching Costs: Why Some Customers Stay

Demand elasticity sounds academic, but it is practical. It describes how demand responds to a change in price. Categories with many close substitutes tend to be more price-sensitive, while differentiated offers may be less sensitive when buyers perceive fewer acceptable alternatives.

Demand Elasticity in Plain Language

Demand elasticity answers a simple question: if price changes, how much does demand change? Brand equity can contribute to lower sensitivity when it creates meaningful preference, but elasticity also depends on category structure, available substitutes, income, urgency, and other market conditions. BDC’s overview provides a practical definition (BDC price elasticity glossary).

Factors that lower demand elasticity:

  • Differentiation buyers can repeat to others without coaching.
  • Proof that makes outcomes feel predictable.
  • Integration into routines and workflows.
  • Reputation that reduces anxiety for decision makers.

If customers cannot explain why they chose you, a claimed brand premium is harder to defend. Clear reasons for preference are useful evidence, but willingness to pay still needs to be tested rather than assumed.

Switching Costs: Operational, Cognitive, and Social

Switching costs are the friction of changing providers. Some are obvious, like contract penalties. Many are hidden, like retraining a team or rebuilding internal alignment.

Three switching cost categories matter:

  • Operational switching costs: onboarding, integration, migration, compliance reviews.
  • Cognitive switching costs: learning a new interface, building new habits, new internal playbooks.
  • Social switching costs: justifying the switch to stakeholders, reputational risk if it fails.

Switching costs are a well-established topic in economics and competition, including how they shape loyalty, lock-in, and pricing strategy (Farrell and Klemperer working paper).

Trust as a Hidden Economic Input

Trust can influence economic behavior because it changes how buyers perceive risk. Higher trust may reduce the amount of reassurance required during evaluation or renewal, while inconsistent delivery can increase scrutiny and make alternatives easier to consider.

Trust is built through repeatable proof:

  • Specific claims supported by visible evidence.
  • Consistent delivery across every touchpoint.
  • Clear, calm communication when change happens.
  • Stable standards, not improvised experiences.

This is where brand strategy and UX meet. If the website, onboarding, or support experience contradicts the promise, perceived risk can rise and the intended differentiation becomes harder for buyers to believe.

Intangible Assets and Market Value: Why Brand Shows Up in Finance

Brand is one type of intangible asset, alongside assets such as software, data, intellectual property, and customer relationships. Ocean Tomo has documented the long-term rise of intangible assets as a share of S&P 500 market value, which is useful context for why leadership teams increasingly evaluate intangible value explicitly (Ocean Tomo). Brand should not be treated as the entire intangible-value story.

The Intangible Economy Problem

Accounting captures physical assets cleanly. It is less direct with intangibles like brand, software, data, and customer relationships. Yet market value increasingly reflects those assets. Brand Finance’s Global Intangible Finance Tracker is one of the more cited, structured attempts to quantify the scale of intangible value (Brand Finance GIFT 2025).

For leadership teams that want formal structure, ISO 10668:2010 remains the published international standard for monetary brand valuation, although ISO now lists it as scheduled for revision. Brand Finance also provides an accessible overview of how the framework has been applied in practice (ISO 10668 overview PDF).

How Brand Can Affect Cash Flow

Brand equity can influence cash flow through several mechanisms, but each one should be measured in the business rather than assumed:

  • A defendable premium can support gross margin.
  • Preference may reduce sensitivity to price in some segments.
  • Trust and fit can contribute to retention or expansion.
  • Recognition can make acquisition more efficient when it improves qualified demand.

Brand valuation frameworks connect brand strength to economic performance. Interbrand’s methodology explicitly connects brand value to factors like brand strength and the role of brand in purchase decisions (Interbrand Best Global Brands). Kantar BrandZ frames brands as financial assets and publishes brand value rankings annually (Kantar BrandZ Global Top 100).

You do not need to appear on a global ranking for these mechanisms to be relevant. Private companies can test the same questions through price realization, retention, referral behavior, and willingness to choose the brand when credible alternatives exist.

The Differentiation Stack: From Product to Experience to Meaning

Differentiation is rarely one thing. It can exist across product capability, experience, proof, and meaning. Relying on one easily copied feature makes the position more vulnerable; combining several defensible layers can make comparison less straightforward.

Level 1: Functional Differentiation

Functional differentiation is what you do and how well you do it. It matters. But in many categories, functional differences compress over time as competitors copy features and processes.

Functional differentiation that holds tends to be:

  • Built on a capability you can sustain, not a temporary feature.
  • Protected by operational standards and consistent delivery.
  • Tied to a customer job that is expensive to fail.

If your story relies only on features, you will end up in price comparisons, even if the product is excellent.

Level 2: Experience Differentiation

Experience differentiation is how it feels to evaluate, buy, use, and renew. This layer is often harder to copy because it is a system, not a component.

Experience differentiation often includes:

  • Clear onboarding and faster time to value.
  • Consistent UX patterns that reduce cognitive load.
  • Predictable support, policies, and communication.
  • Cohesive content and proof that reduces uncertainty.

If you want a practical primer on brand equity itself, HBS Online has a clear explanation of how it shapes willingness to pay and preference (HBS Online on brand equity).

Level 3: Narrative Differentiation

Narrative differentiation is the meaning behind choosing you. It works when it is earned, not declared. In practice, it is the alignment between what you claim, what you do, and how consistently you do it.

Narrative differentiation holds when:

  • Positioning is specific, not vague.
  • Proof points are concrete and visible.
  • The company is willing to say no to misaligned work.
  • The experience reinforces the promise every time.

This is why “brand” is not just language. A strong brand strategy creates standards that shape decisions, while a coherent visual identity makes those decisions recognizable across touchpoints. The goal is consistency without reducing the brand to a logo system.

‍

Digital Experience as Growth Infrastructure

In many markets, the digital experience is an early evaluation point. A slow, confusing, inaccessible, or inconsistent website can create friction before a buyer understands the differentiation, making it easier to fall back on simpler comparisons such as price.

Performance: Speed Is a Business Variable

Performance affects whether people can evaluate an offer efficiently. Faster, more stable pages remove avoidable friction, while slow or unstable pages can interrupt the path to proof, contact, or purchase.

Performance decisions that support long-term growth:

  • Keep pages lean and prioritize clarity over decoration.
  • Use reusable templates that stay fast as content grows.
  • Set performance budgets and enforce them as a standard.

Google’s Core Web Vitals documentation is the clearest reference for how performance is defined as real-world user experience, including LCP, INP, and CLS (Google Core Web Vitals). Search Console also reports Core Web Vitals status based on field data, which makes performance measurable at scale (Core Web Vitals report help).

Web design services should treat performance as part of the user journey and conversion system, not as a technical afterthought.

Accessibility: Reach, Risk, and Trust

Accessibility is about reach and trust, not only compliance. Accessible experiences reduce friction for everyone and expand the audience that can complete key actions.

How Accessibility Supports the Experience

  • Wider reach and fewer blocked conversions.
  • Better usability for mobile and edge cases.
  • Lower risk in regulated or public-facing environments.

WCAG is the web standard most teams use to define accessibility requirements. The canonical reference is WCAG 2.2 as a W3C Recommendation (WCAG 2.2 specification) with supporting guidance from the WAI overview pages (WCAG overview).

Accessibility can also reinforce trust by making important journeys usable by more people. It should be treated as a product and experience standard, not as proof by itself that customers will pay more.

UX and Information Architecture: Fewer Dead Ends, More Conversions

UX is decision support. Clear information architecture, readable proof, and predictable interaction patterns help buyers evaluate the offer with less unnecessary effort. UX research can help identify where users hesitate, what evidence they look for, and which parts of the journey create avoidable uncertainty.

High-performing UX patterns include:

  • Task-based navigation aligned to top buyer questions.
  • Proof near decision points, not buried in hard-to-scan pages.
  • Shorter forms and clearer paths to next steps.

UI/UX design can improve these journeys by organizing the experience around what buyers need to understand and decide, rather than around the company’s internal structure.

Governance: Consistency at Scale

Brand inconsistency is often a governance problem. Teams add pages, campaigns, and offers without shared standards, which can make the promise harder to recognize across touchpoints and increase perceived risk during evaluation.

Governance that protects brand equity:

  • A content and design system with clear standards.
  • Defined ownership for key journeys and conversion pages.
  • Regular audits of performance, accessibility, and messaging drift.

For long-term growth, governance is the mechanism that keeps positioning, experience, and proof from drifting as more teams and channels contribute to the brand.

A Measurement System for Long-Term Growth

Long-term growth is hard to measure because short-term metrics are noisy. The solution is not to ignore short-term performance. It is to pair it with brand equity signals that indicate whether pricing power is strengthening.

Leading Indicators That May Signal Pricing Power

Leading indicators can show whether preference is strengthening before the full financial effect is visible. They are directional signals, not proof on their own.

Useful leading indicators:

  • Win rate without discounts in target segments.
  • Sales cycle reduction for the accounts you want most.
  • Higher conversion on key pages after UX and performance changes.
  • Growth in direct traffic and branded search behavior over time.

If you track customer advocacy, NPS is one widely used mechanism. Bain outlines the Net Promoter framework and how it is calculated (Bain NPS system, how NPS is measured).

Lagging Indicators That Help Confirm Brand Equity

Lagging indicators help show whether the business is actually becoming harder to substitute and whether that preference is reaching commercial outcomes.

Lagging indicators to watch:

  • Gross margin stability across multiple quarters.
  • Retention and expansion by cohort.
  • Customer lifetime value relative to acquisition cost.
  • Price realization, meaning how close deals land to intended pricing.

If these stay flat, review whether differentiation is unclear, proof is weak, experience is inconsistent, or other commercial factors are offsetting the brand work.

A Simple Dashboard for Executive Teams

A dashboard should support action, not debate. Keep it simple, review it monthly, and connect it to decisions.

A practical executive dashboard:

  • Pricing power: discount rate, price realization, win rate at target price.
  • Demand elasticity: churn sensitivity after price changes, conversion sensitivity to pricing shifts.
  • Brand equity: direct traffic, repeat purchase rate, referral share.
  • Digital experience: performance benchmarks, accessibility checks, key journey conversion.

If you want help aligning measurement to strategy and execution, a marketing consultation and audit can help connect the metrics to pricing power, brand equity, and long-term growth rather than isolated channel performance.

FAQ

What is the fastest way to tell if you are received as a commodity or a brand?

If buyers lead with price, ask for side-by-side comparisons, and switch easily, you’re being treated like a commodity. If they choose you for trust, consistency, and clear preference, brand equity is working.

Does brand strategy matter in B2B procurement-driven buying?

Yes. In B2B marketing, procurement makes comparison more structured, but it does not remove risk. Clear positioning and visible proof can help buyers understand why one option deserves preference beyond the line-item price.

How long does it take to build brand equity that changes economics?

Some effects can show quickly through clearer messaging or a stronger digital experience, while durable preference takes longer to prove. The timeline varies by category, buying cycle, evidence, competitive response, and how consistently the business delivers the promise.

Can we have pricing power without being “premium”?

Yes. Pricing power comes from reduced substitutability and credibility, not luxury cues. Reliability, clarity, and proof can earn willingness to pay.

What role does the website play in commodity vs brand?

It is a credibility test. Speed, accessibility, and UX can reduce friction and make proof easier to evaluate, supporting the broader brand promise rather than replacing it.

Where Brand Vision Fits When You Want to Build the System

The practical challenge is building a system where brand strategy, proof, experience, accessibility, performance, and governance reinforce the same differentiation. For a company evaluating outside support in the Bay Area, a San Francisco branding agency can provide regional coordination without changing the core strategic problem the business needs to solve.

Brand Vision’s branding, web, and UI/UX services address different parts of that system: define the differentiation, express it consistently, and make the digital experience easier to evaluate. The goal is not to promise pricing power from design alone, but to make the business’s real advantages clearer and more consistent.

If you want a plan that connects brand strategy to execution and measurable outcomes, start a conversation with Brand Vision and review what a stronger system could look like across brand identity, web design, and UX work.

We generally associate the hospital with getting better, not with being a place where you suffer harm. Unfortunately, many people do suffer harm there, and the fact that you are reading this guide could mean that either you or a loved one has suffered harm when seeking medical help. 

Medical malpractice is the legal term used to describe harm suffered due to the negligence of health providers. These providers can be an institution, surgeons, doctors, nurses, pharmacists, or anyone else in that field. This guide looks into the different types of medical malpractice and can help you understand what types of medical malpractice you may be dealing with. 

‍

Misdiagnosis

Doctors do not always get the diagnosis correct. Still, a failure to get the diagnosis right doesn’t always mean there was malpractice. It only becomes a case of malpractice if the reason for failing to diagnose was a deviation from the standards of practice. Speaking to attorney Russell Berkowitz of Berkowitz Hanna Malpractice & Injury Lawyers can prove to be useful during this time. 

For example, a patient can present headaches and dizziness, which can be symptoms of many ailments, including stroke. The doctor runs tests for every other condition, but not for a stroke. They then go ahead to treat the patient for something completely different when the issue is a stroke. 

Suppose the patient's condition deteriorates as a result, and the patient suffers permanent damage. The failure to test for stroke indicates a deviation from the expected standard based on the symptom, creating grounds for a valid medical malpractice claim. 

Surgical Errors

Surgical errors are also pretty common and can take many forms. They can involve operating on the wrong part of the body or conducting unnecessary surgery. They could also involve operating on the right part of the body, a necessary surgery, but following poor protocol, leading to something like having an instrument left in the patient's body. 

There have also been reported cases of doctors operating on the wrong patients due to poor communication or identification problems. All these point to one thing: negligence, making such situations cases of medical malpractice. 

Medication Errors

Medication errors, which occur when patients receive the incorrect medication or dosage, also fall into the category of medical malpractice. Often, these mistakes spring from miscommunication, illegible handwriting on prescriptions, confusion between drugs with similar names, or simply overlooking a patient's drug allergies or existing medications, which could lead to severe interactions. 

The impact can range from minor discomfort to more critical, sometimes life-threatening conditions. These errors reflect a lapse in the care that healthcare providers are entrusted to deliver, highlighting the need for rigorous checks within pharmaceutical protocols.

Birth Injuries

During childbirth, any harm that comes to a baby or mother due to medical negligence fits into the birth injuries category of malpractice. These injuries can occur from improper handling or monitoring during delivery, failure to anticipate birth complications, not effectively addressing distress signals on fetal monitors, or errors in using tools like forceps or vacuums. 

Such incidents might lead to conditions ranging from nerve damage and fractures in infants to severe postpartum bleeding in mothers. Often, these traumatic outcomes stem from poor decision-making or inadequate skill, casting a shadow on what is supposed to be a joyous occasion.

Navigating the Complexities of Medical Malpractice Cases

Tackling a medical malpractice case is not for the faint-hearted, given its intricate nature involving detailed medical knowledge and legal nuances. This complexity means partnering with a skilled lawyer is essential. 

To choose the right attorney, look for someone with a robust track record in medical malpractice, clear communication skills, and an understanding approach to your situation. Consider also their availability to handle your case personally rather than passing it off to less experienced associates. 

A specialist in this sector can comprehend medical language, negotiate paperwork mazes, and aggressively argue for you—an vital ally in these trying times.

‍

Conclusion

Suffering harm while seeking medical care can feel deeply unfair. Whether it’s a misdiagnosis, surgical mistake, medication error, or birth injury, these experiences are often life-changing. Understanding the most common types of medical malpractice is the first step in recognising whether your situation may involve negligence. From there, the right legal support can make all the difference. If you or someone you care about has been affected, don’t stay in the dark—get answers, get support, and take action.

Computers are an indispensable part of any office. But it is not always possible to use large spaces to accommodate standard PCs. Today, mini PCs confidently take their place in the modern approach to organizing office space.

Despite their compact size, they are characterized by high performance, space saving, and a minimalistic appearance. Therefore, for many companies, mini PCs are an ideal choice. If you are looking to optimize work processes and the work environment, you should pay attention to such devices.

‍

Compactness and Great Possibilities

Interest in mini computers has been growing rapidly over the past few years. It is important to understand that when choosing such solutions, you get a full-fledged PC, which is placed in a compact case. Usually, the size does not exceed the size of a book. If you buy a GEEKOM mini PC, you will get compactness combined with excellent features:

  • modern processor;
  • large amount of RAM;
  • fast SSD drive, etc.

The technical characteristics of mini PCs allow you to easily cope with basic office tasks:

  • working with documents;
  • data analysis;
  • video conferencing;
  • graphic design, etc.

The key advantage here is compactness. The PC can be placed behind the monitor, put under the table, or mounted on the wall. This will free up the workspace, making it more convenient and practical.

Ergonomics and Space Saving

In offices, regular PCs take up a lot of space. In fact, due to massive system units, you have to take up a significant part of the desktop. Mini PCs allow you to quickly and easily solve this problem. You will be able to free up space for other, more important tasks. For example, place a tablet, install a second monitor, or just get space for comfortable work.

In addition to compactness, mini PCs have a positive effect on ergonomics. Fewer wires, the ability to quickly connect and disconnect them, the use of concealed mounting systems, etc. As a result, the workplace looks neater, and you get more free space.

Corporate Image and Modern Design

When producing cases for modern mini PCs, a laconic, minimalistic design is used. This allows such devices to fit organically into any interior. For many companies, the visual component is of particular importance. Therefore, if you want to create and adhere to a corporate image, mini PCs will be an excellent solution.

Performance and Efficiency

You should not be misled by the compact size that mini PCs are characterized by. Inside the case are quite powerful processors capable of supporting up to 64 GB of RAM. Some models can be equipped with several high-speed SSD drives.

Therefore, such computer devices easily cope with office tasks, are multitasking, and are capable of working with large amounts of information, tables, and presentations. Even photo and video editing on such a PC will not be a problem.

In some cases, you can use the installation of an additional video card via a special port. This is relevant for those employees who need high graphics performance while maintaining the compact size of the PC.

Cost Reduction and Energy Efficiency

Another important advantage of mini PCs is lower power consumption compared to traditional computers. This allows you to reduce electricity costs, reduce heat generation, which affects the microclimate in the office and the comfort of employees.

‍

Installation Flexibility

Compactness is not only an opportunity to save space. It also provides additional options for placing mini PCs:

  • behind the monitor;
  • on the walls using VESA mounts;
  • cabinet racks;
  • table niches;
  • under the tabletop;
  • in video conference rooms (PC as a media center).

Therefore, mini PCs are universal solutions that can be used even in the smallest rooms.

Final Thoughts

Businesses find mini PCs to be an extremely versatile, all-purpose solution. They assist in space utilization, make them productive, and at the same time make the office more modernized and trendy. The devices are small, elegant, and yet strong enough to perform a majority of tasks.

A familiar label on a grocery, personal-care, or household product does not always tell you which company sits behind it. Large consumer-goods groups often manage many distinct brands at once, using different names, packaging, audiences, and positioning across the same corporate portfolio. That structure is a practical example of brand architecture: the parent company can stay relatively quiet while individual brands build their own recognition.

This September 2026 snapshot looks at ten companies behind familiar household brands. Ownership changes over time, so the list separates current portfolios from brands that have been sold, spun off, or moved into new companies. Historical revenue figures already present in the article are kept where they still describe the same parent company, but they are not intended as a current ranking.

1. General Mills

Founded: 1928‍

Revenue (2022): $20.09  billion‍

Major Brands: Betty Crocker, Bisquick, Gold Medal, Cheerios, Chex, Yoplait, Pillsbury, Nature Valley

General Mills is a clear example of a parent company whose corporate name is less visible than many of its products. Families can move from Cheerios at breakfast and Betty Crocker cake mixes for birthdays to Pillsbury doughs and Nature Valley snacks without changing parent companies.

The portfolio spans cereal, baking, refrigerated dough, snacks, meals, and pet food. That breadth gives General Mills multiple consumer occasions while allowing each brand to keep a distinct identity rather than forcing everything under one consumer-facing name. It also shows why parent-company awareness and consumer-brand awareness can be very different even when the products share distribution, investment, and corporate ownership.

2. Nestlé

Founded: 1867‍

Revenue (2024, CAD): Approximately $145.37  billion‍

Major Brands: Nescafé, KitKat, Gerber, Stouffer’s, Nesquik, Maggi, Toll House

Nestlé remains one of the world’s largest food and beverage companies, with brands spanning coffee (Nescafé) and confections (KitKat) to baby nutrition (Gerber) and prepared meals (Stouffer’s). Founded in 1867, the company has built a portfolio that reaches many different eating occasions and markets.

For teams working in food and beverage marketing, Nestlé is a useful example of how one parent can manage brands with very different audiences, price points, and category expectations while keeping the corporate structure mostly in the background.

3. Unilever

Founded: 1929‍

Revenue (2024): Approximately $60 billion‍

Major Brands in the current Unilever portfolio: Dove, Axe, Hellmann’s, Knorr, Vaseline, Sunsilk

Unilever still spans personal care, beauty, foods, and home-care categories, but two familiar names in the older version of this article have moved out of the portfolio. An earlier portfolio view linked here grouped Dove (personal care), Lipton (tea), and Ben & Jerry’s (ice cream). That no longer reflects current ownership.

Unilever sold its global tea business, including Lipton in most markets, in 2022. LIPTON Teas and Infusions now states that CVC completed the acquisition of the business. Unilever then completed the demerger of its ice-cream business in December 2025. Ben & Jerry’s is now part of The Magnum Ice Cream Company, while Unilever retained a minority stake in that newly independent company after the demerger.

4. PepsiCo

Founded: 1898 (as Pepsi-Cola Company; merged with Frito-Lay in 1965)‍

Revenue (2024): $91.854  billion‍

Major Brands: Pepsi, Lay’s, Doritos, Gatorade, Quaker, Cheetos, SodaStream

PepsiCo’s portfolio reaches well beyond cola. Pepsi and other beverages sit alongside large snack and food brands such as Lay’s and Doritos. Notably, Gatorade and Quaker Oats expand its range into sports hydration and breakfast staples. The combination makes PepsiCo one of the clearest examples of a consumer company operating across both beverage and convenient-food categories.

Tropicana should no longer be listed as a PepsiCo-controlled brand. PepsiCo sold Tropicana, Naked, and other selected juice brands to a joint venture led by PAI Partners, retaining a 39% non-controlling interest. For a broader comparison of parent companies and individual drink labels, see Brand Vision’s guide to major beverage brands.

5. Kraft Heinz Company

Founded: 2015 (merger of Kraft Foods and Heinz; legacy brands date back further)‍

Revenue (2024): $25.85 billion‍

Major Brands: Heinz Ketchup, Kraft Mac & Cheese, Jell-O, Philadelphia, Oscar Mayer, Velveeta

Kraft Heinz is a relatively recent corporate combination built from much older consumer brands. Heinz ketchup and Kraft Mac & Cheese bring decades of recognition, while Philadelphia, Jell-O, Oscar Mayer, and Velveeta extend the portfolio across several grocery categories.

With recognized staples like Oscar Mayer hot dogs and Velveeta cheese, the company shows how a parent can combine established household products without erasing each brand’s separate brand identity. That separation can preserve different audiences, histories, and shelf positions inside one corporate portfolio.

6. The Coca‑Cola Company

Founded: 1892‍

Revenue (2024): $47.1 billion‍

Major Brands: Coca‑Cola, Diet Coke, Sprite, Fanta, Minute Maid, Dasani

The Coca‑Cola Company is best known for its namesake soda, but the portfolio extends across sparkling drinks, juices, water, coffee, sports drinks, and other beverage categories. A shopper who skips cola might still buy Dasani water or Minute Maid juice from the same overarching brand family.

That structure lets Coca‑Cola serve different tastes and occasions while keeping each consumer brand recognizable. Behind that storied identity is a portfolio strategy in which the parent company can invest across multiple labels instead of relying on a single product name. It also lets the company position products differently by market, category, and consumption occasion while still benefiting from shared distribution and corporate resources.

7. Procter & Gamble (P&G)

Founded: 1837‍

Revenue (2024): $84  billion‍

Major Brands: Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest, Oral‑B, Olay, Downy

P&G has spent nearly two centuries building and reshaping a house of consumer brands across laundry, baby care, grooming, oral care, skincare, and home care. Tide leads in laundry; Pampers, in diapers; and Gillette reigns in shaving. Many households use several P&G products without treating P&G itself as the primary consumer brand.

The company can update formulas, positioning, and branded packaging at the individual-brand level while managing the larger portfolio centrally. That is one reason P&G remains a frequently used example of a house-of-brands model.

8. Mars, Inc.

Founded: 1911‍

Confectionery sales estimate (2024): ~$22  billion (est.)‍

Major Brands: M&M’s, Snickers, Pedigree, Ben’s Original, Orbit, Pringles, Cheez-It, Pop-Tarts

Mars is a privately held business spanning snacking, food, pet care, and veterinary services. Its long-standing portfolio includes Snickers, M&M’s) and Pedigree dog food, among many other brands.

The portfolio became significantly larger in December 2025 when Mars completed its acquisition of Kellanova. That transaction brought Pringles, Cheez-It, Pop-Tarts, Rice Krispies Treats, RXBAR, and Kellogg’s international cereal brands into Mars. Mars described the combined company as a family-owned business with more than $65 billion in annual sales.

9. Ferrero Group

Founded: 1946‍

Major Brands: Nutella, Kinder, Ferrero Rocher, Tic Tac, plus WK Kellogg cereal brands including Frosted Flakes, Froot Loops, Rice Krispies, and Special K

Ferrero is best known for confectionery brands such as Nutella, Kinder, Ferrero Rocher, and Tic Tac, but its North American portfolio expanded materially in 2026. On February 12, 2026, Ferrero completed its acquisition of WK Kellogg Co, making the cereal company a wholly owned subsidiary.

That means familiar North American cereals such as Frosted Flakes, Froot Loops, Rice Krispies, Special K, and other Kellogg’s cereal brands now sit within the wider Ferrero group. The change is easy to miss because the Kellogg’s name remains on the boxes even though the ultimate parent company changed. It is also separate from Kellanova, whose Pringles, Cheez-It, Pop-Tarts, and international Kellogg’s cereal portfolio moved to Mars in December 2025.

10. Kenvue (Formerly J&J Consumer Health)

Created: 2022; fully independent from Johnson & Johnson since 2023‍

2025 net sales: $15.1 billion‍

Major Brands: Aveeno, Band-Aid, Tylenol, Neutrogena, Listerine, Johnson’s Baby

These consumer-health brands were long associated with Johnson & Johnson. Older ownership summaries commonly grouped Band-Aid, Tylenol, or Listerine under J&J, but that is no longer the current corporate structure.

Johnson & Johnson completed the separation of its consumer-health business in 2023. Kenvue is now the independent company behind Aveeno, Band-Aid, Johnson’s, Listerine, Neutrogena, and Tylenol, while Johnson & Johnson focuses on medicines and medical technology. As of September 29, 2026, Kenvue remains independent, although a pending acquisition by Kimberly-Clark is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to the remaining transaction conditions. This pending deal is another reason ownership guides need a clear date.

The Parent Companies Behind Familiar Brands

These ten examples show why the logo on the front of a package tells only part of the ownership story. Some parent companies operate a classic house of brands, while others have sold or spun off major businesses and reshaped their portfolios. The changes at Unilever, PepsiCo, Kellogg, Mars, and Johnson & Johnson also show that parent-company maps can become outdated quickly.

For consumers, checking the parent company is one way to understand how brands connect. For businesses managing several products or acquired brands, the same exercise is part of brand research: ownership, audience overlap, positioning, and portfolio relationships all influence how a brand should be presented. A parent-company change does not automatically require a consumer-facing rebrand, but it can affect governance, investment priorities, distribution, naming rights, and the relationship between individual brands. If you are working through a similar portfolio question, you can contact Brand Vision for a focused discussion of the brand structure and next steps.

When people ask which companies have the most employees, the answer depends on more than one headline number. Large employers report headcount on different fiscal calendars and may use different definitions for employees, associates, trainees, joint-venture staff, or other workers. Using company filings, annual reports, investor disclosures, and dated Fortune data, the list below compares ten major employers using the most relevant 2024 or 2025 headcount figures available for each.

The pattern is striking. Retail, ecommerce, utilities, manufacturing, professional services, postal networks, automotive groups, IT services, and logistics all appear because each business model needs scale in a different way. Walmart and Amazon rely on enormous retail and fulfilment networks, while BYD and Volkswagen show how manufacturing depth can translate into hundreds of thousands of employees.

Methodology: How This 2025 Employer Ranking Works

This is a sourced 2025 reference ranking of ten large employers, ordered by the headcount figures used here. It is not a synchronized census of every employer worldwide because companies do not all report on the same date or with the same workforce definition. Where a dated filing or 2025 ranking provides a clearer reference point than an undated profile, the dated figure is used. Franchise workers and independent contractors are excluded unless the cited organization explicitly includes them.

It is also important not to confuse workforce size with revenue rank. Fortune’s Global 500, for example, ranks companies by revenue, while this article compares employee counts. Readers looking at revenue-based corporate rankings can also see Brand Vision’s guide to Canadian company rankings.

1. Walmart: About 2.1 Million Associates

Walmart reported approximately 2.1 million associates worldwide as of January 31, 2025, including about 1.6 million in the United States. That scale supports stores, ecommerce, fulfilment, merchandising, and one of the world’s largest retail supply chains. Among private-sector companies with the most employees, Walmart remains a defining example of how physical distribution and digital commerce can operate together at enormous scale. Walmart Inc.

2. Amazon: Approximately 1.556 Million Employees

Amazon reported approximately 1,556,000 full-time and part-time employees as of December 31, 2024. Its filing separately notes that the company also uses independent contractors and temporary personnel, so those workers are not part of this employee figure. The scale reflects Amazon’s reach across ecommerce, logistics, cloud computing, devices, advertising, and other services. SEC

3. State Grid Corporation of China: About 1.354 Million in 2025 Fortune Data

State Grid is one of the world’s largest utilities. Fortune’s 2025 Global 500 data lists 1,354,310 employees, while the World Economic Forum’s organization profile describes a larger 1.72 million workforce and a service footprint reaching 1.1 billion people across 26 provincial-level regions. Because the WEF profile does not provide the same reporting date, this ranking uses Fortune’s dated 2025 employee figure while retaining the World Economic Forum profile as useful organizational context. Fortune Global 500

4. China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC): 985,155 Employees

CNPC, the parent of PetroChina, is listed with 985,155 employees in Fortune’s 2025 company data. The workforce reflects the scale of an integrated energy business spanning exploration, production, refining, pipelines, engineering, and oilfield services. That operating breadth makes CNPC one of the largest state-linked industrial employers in this group. Fortune

5. BYD Company: 968,872 Employees

BYD’s 2024 annual disclosures report 968,872 employees at year-end. The figure illustrates how quickly the company expanded the workforce behind electric vehicles, batteries, electronics, engineering, and vertically integrated manufacturing. BYD is a useful example of how a rapidly scaling industrial platform can approach the employment footprint of much older global corporations. HKEX News+1

6. Accenture: Approximately 774,000 Employees

Accenture reported approximately 774,000 employees as of August 31, 2024. Unlike retail or manufacturing employers, its scale comes from a global professional-services model covering strategy, consulting, technology, and operations. The company serves clients in more than 120 countries, making its headcount especially notable among knowledge-intensive service businesses. Accenture

7. China Post Group: 723,227 Employees

Fortune’s 2025 data lists China Post Group with 723,227 employees. Its workforce supports postal services, express delivery, logistics, banking, insurance, and other financial services across a vast national network. That mix explains why large public-service organizations can sit alongside retailers and manufacturers when companies with the most employees are compared. Fortune

8. Volkswagen Group: 679,472 in Total Workforce

Volkswagen reported a total workforce of 679,472 people as of December 31, 2024 when equity-accounted companies in China are included. Excluding those Chinese joint ventures, the group reported 614,082 employees. The distinction matters because workforce definitions can materially change a ranking, and Volkswagen is one of the clearest examples of why the reporting basis needs to be stated rather than reduced to a single unexplained number. Volkswagen Group Annual Report 2024+1

9. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS): 607,979 Employees

TCS ended fiscal 2025 with 607,979 employees and reported a workforce spanning 152 nationalities. That makes the company one of the largest employers in global IT services. Its scale reflects the labour intensity of enterprise technology delivery, consulting, managed services, and long-running client relationships across large organizations. TCS

10. DHL Group: 591,172 Employees in Its 2025 Half-Year Reporting

DHL Group reported 591,172 employees at the end of the relevant 2025 reporting quarter, including trainees. The group’s parcel, express, freight, supply-chain, and ecommerce operations make logistics one of the most people-intensive parts of global commerce. DHL’s headcount also shows why the reporting date matters: a mid-year figure can differ from a prior year-end total. DHL Group

What the Largest Employers Have in Common

The companies in this ranking operate in very different sectors, but their workforces point to a common operational reality: scale requires coordination. Retailers need stores and fulfilment networks, manufacturers need production and engineering capacity, service companies need large specialist teams, and logistics businesses need people distributed across complex physical networks.

For business readers, workforce scale is also a reminder that enterprise buying is rarely a one-person decision. Companies marketing to large B2B organizations often need to communicate across procurement, operations, finance, technical teams, and executive stakeholders. At the same time, employers at this scale rely on internal platforms and custom software development to coordinate workflows, while ERP software can connect finance, procurement, inventory, and other operating functions.

Headcount rankings will continue to move as companies automate work, expand into new markets, restructure operations, and change what they report. The most useful comparison is therefore not just who has the biggest number, but what that number includes and the date to which it applies.

FAQ

Which company has the most employees in this 2025 ranking?

Walmart is first in this ranking with approximately 2.1 million associates worldwide as of January 31, 2025. Amazon follows with approximately 1.556 million employees as of December 31, 2024.

Why does State Grid have different employee figures across sources?

Workforce figures can differ because sources use different reporting dates and definitions. Fortune’s 2025 Global 500 data lists 1,354,310 employees for State Grid, while the World Economic Forum profile lists 1.72 million without an equivalent dated reporting basis. This article uses the dated Fortune figure for ranking order.

Are contractors and franchise workers included?

Not by default. The article uses the workforce definition reported by each organization or source. Amazon, for example, explicitly separates independent contractors and temporary personnel from its employee count. Other companies may define their workforce differently, which is why the methodology matters.

What dates do these employee counts reflect?
