Season 34 showed how Dancing with the Stars could refresh a 20-year-old franchise without discarding the ballroom format that made it recognizable. The 2025 season combined live television, streaming, creator-led casting, social clips, and audience participation, making the show a useful example of brand development through access and experience rather than reinvention. (Northeastern University)

  • Dancing with the Stars 2025 reframes a legacy show as a live social media and streaming event.
  • The Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy combines casting, distribution, and fandom into one system.
  • The format did not radically change; the way it is marketed and experienced did.

At a Glance

  • Northeastern reported that Season 34 became the first fall show in decades to increase its audience for five consecutive weeks after the premiere. (Northeastern University) 
  • Contemporary coverage also tracked a sharp year-over-year increase in opening-night voting, an early sign that participation was growing alongside attention. (King Street Chronicle) 
  • By the end of the season, ABC said Season 34 averaged 10 million total viewers over 35 days of multiplatform viewing, drew 72 million votes in the finale, and generated nearly half a billion votes across the season. (ABC)
  • The show now streams live on ABC and Disney+, with full episodes available the next day on Hulu, which Disney Advertising highlights as “shining” across all three platforms. (Accio) (Disney Advertising) 

Multi-Platform Distribution As A Core Growth Engine

One of the biggest shifts in the Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy was the move from a single-network show to a multi-platform live event. Season 34 aired live on ABC and Disney+, with next-day streaming on Hulu and additional clips across social and video platforms. (Accio) The practical brand strategy lesson is consistency: the format can appear in different viewing contexts without changing what the audience recognizes as the core product.

  • ABC delivers classic prime-time “appointment viewing” at 8 p.m. ET.
  • Disney+ captures younger, streaming-first viewers, including Gen Z fans.
  • Hulu provides a next-day window for busy viewers, creating a second wave of engagement.
  • Clips and extras on the official YouTube channel and social feeds fill in the gaps between episodes.

Casting As Marketing: “Casting The Audience”

Casting became a central distribution mechanism in Season 34. The lineup combined nostalgic actors, Olympians, reality-TV personalities, and social media creators such as Alix Earle, Robert Irwin, Jen Affleck, and Whitney Leavitt, each arriving with a different audience. (Northeastern University) Deena Katz has described the logic as “casting the audience,” where the ensemble creates multiple entry points into the same show. (Evie Magazine) Other brands can apply the principle more carefully through audience research, testing which communities actually overlap instead of assuming a celebrity following will transfer automatically.

  • Influencers and reality stars arrive with built-in social media fandoms.
  • Nostalgia picks, such as Elaine Hendrix from “The Parent Trap,” attract older viewers.
  • Athletes and creators bring sports and TikTok audiences who might not watch ballroom otherwise.
  • The Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy leverages these fanbases to create cross-generational reach.

Social Media As A Second Stage

Dancing with the Stars treated TikTok and Instagram as a second stage, not only as promotional outlets. Northeastern notes that Season 34 included TikTok Night, featured viral songs, and distributed weekly dances across social platforms so viewers could keep following the show between broadcasts. (Northeastern University) Nativa also describes rehearsals, bloopers, and day-in-the-life material designed for vertical feeds. (Nativa) That is an integrated marketing lesson: the live program creates the event, while social content extends the relationship between episodes.

  • TikTok-themed nights are built to generate shareable short-form dances.
  • Weekly routines are posted quickly to TikTok and Instagram for rewatching and remixing.
  • Behind-the-scenes content turns the learning process into daily entertainment.
  • Social content keeps Dancing with the Stars 2025 in feeds all week, not just on Tuesday nights.

Creators And Pros As Built-In Influencers

The Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy has shifted attention from just the celebrities to the professional dancers and younger cast members who behave like creators. Pros such as Rylee Arnold document rehearsals, food runs, and goofy moments on TikTok, and showrunner Conrad Green has said that social media-savvy pros help other contestants reach fans where they already are. (Evie Magazine) The Nativa analysis highlights that younger pros and contestants, especially those active on TikTok, have become key conduits for Gen Z engagement. (Nativa)

  • Professional dancers behave like recurring creator characters, not just background partners.
  • Contestants with large followings act as amplifiers for the Dancing with the Stars brand.
  • Parasocial relationships with pros and influencers keep fans invested across seasons.
  • This creator-first approach is a pillar of how the Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy reaches Gen Z.

Fandom, Voting And A Return To Shared Pop Culture

Dancing with the Stars 2025 has become an unlikely symbol of “shared pop culture” in a fragmented streaming world. Evie Magazine argues that the show brings TikTok kids, nostalgia lovers and grandparents back to watching the same thing at the same time, reviving the weekly ritual of live TV plus next-day arguments. (Evie Magazine) King Street Chronicle reports that audience engagement has deepened, with votes surging from 8 million in the Season 33 premiere to 21 million on the opening night of Season 34. (King Street Chronicle)

  • Live voting turns viewers into participants, not passive watchers.
  • Weekly episodes build anticipation and shared conversation across age groups.
  • Fan communities on TikTok and other platforms extend debates and support between episodes.
  • High vote counts show that participation is part of the product experience, although votes should not be treated as equivalent to viewers, impressions, or sales.

Demographic Targeting: From Boomers To Gen Z

The King Street Chronicle describes the show’s revival through demographic targeting, nostalgia, and digital virality, while Northeastern points to creator casting as an important route to younger viewers. (King Street Chronicle) (Northeastern University) The balance matters: nostalgia marketing can make a legacy property feel familiar, while creator casting gives new audiences a current reason to enter.

  • Nostalgia casting appeals to older viewers who remember earlier TV eras.
  • Influencers and Olympians attract younger audiences used to creator culture.
  • Younger pros like Rylee Arnold make ballroom dancing feel current and accessible.
  • The Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy carefully balances tradition with internet-era energy.

Disney Ecosystem And Advertiser Positioning

From a corporate perspective, Dancing with the Stars is a showcase franchise inside Disney’s portfolio. Disney Advertising’s Road to the Upfront messaging highlights that “Dancing with the Stars is shining on ABC, Disney+, and next-day on Hulu,” presenting it alongside live sports and other tentpole events as a driver of fandom and cross-platform reach. (Disney Advertising) Upfront coverage in trade press notes that Disney’s 2024 to 25 ad sales grew about 5 percent, with live, fandom-driven shows and streaming inventory as central pillars. (Variety)

  • The franchise fits perfectly into Disney’s story about live, shared experiences in a streaming world.
  • Multi-platform distribution gives advertisers flexible reach by age and viewing habits.
  • Dancing with the Stars 2025 is packaged as both nostalgia and innovation in Disney’s pitch.
  • For advertisers, the show combines live reach with visible fan participation, but voting totals should be evaluated separately from advertising impressions and campaign outcomes.

Retail And Cross-Industry Effects

Accio reported an 82 percent spike in searches for dance-related products during the Season 34 premiere week, including sequined apparel, dance shoes, and fitness gear. (Accio) That correlation is useful as a directional retail signal, but it does not establish that the show directly caused the demand. The more durable lesson is timing: cultural events can create short windows when related products and creative themes become more relevant.

  • Premiere-week search interest suggests an opportunity for timely retail activation, not proof of direct sales impact.
  • Retailers use DWTS airing patterns to plan promotions and limited drops.
  • Brands increasingly align capsule collections and campaigns with theme nights.
  • The Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy has become part of a broader live entertainment commerce trend.

Brand Experience: Spectacle, Sets, And Story

A large part of the show’s brand experience is visual. Architectural Digest’s 2025 feature explains how each dance gets its own miniature world, with sets built and swapped quickly to support the story of the routine. (Architectural Digest) Northeastern adds that social footage exposes more of the learning process behind the finished performance. (Northeastern University) For another brand, the transferable principle is a consistent visual identity with enough flexibility to create distinct moments without losing recognition.

  • Carefully crafted sets and lighting make each routine feel like a music video moment.
  • Behind-the-scenes footage on social builds emotional investment in those moments.
  • The show balances TikTok-friendly spectacle with traditional ballroom discipline.
  • This integrated brand experience is a core part of why Dancing with the Stars 2025 feels fresh rather than dated.

Lessons From the Dancing With the Stars Marketing Strategy

The strongest lesson from Season 34 is not that every legacy brand needs creators or TikTok. It is that distribution, casting, participation, and presentation all reinforced the same recognizable entertainment product. For audience-driven businesses, entertainment marketing works best when those pieces support one clear promise rather than operate as separate tactics.

For an entertainment or creator business building in Southern California, a branding agency in Los Angeles can help translate that audience strategy into positioning, identity, digital experience, and campaign execution without copying the show’s specific playbook.

  • Modernise where and how people can watch before you throw out the format.
  • Cast people your target audience already loves, not only traditional celebrities.
  • Design episodes from the ground up with shareable moments and fan interaction.
  • Use social and streaming to keep the brand alive between live broadcasts.

FAQ

What is the core Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy right now?

The core Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy is to pair a classic ballroom competition with modern distribution, creator-heavy casting and constant social content so that each season, especially Dancing with the Stars 2025, functions as both live event television and an ongoing social media phenomenon.

How did Dancing with the Stars 2025 grow its audience?

Dancing with the Stars 2025 grew its audience by simulcasting on ABC and Disney+, streaming episodes on Hulu, casting influencers and nostalgia stars, and using TikTok, Instagram and behind-the-scenes content to keep viewers engaged between live shows. 

Why is social media so important to the Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy?
 Social media is critical because it turns each routine into a short, shareable clip and allows pros and contestants to document the process, which pulls in Gen Z viewers and turns voting and fandom into a continuous loop rather than a once-a-week event. 

How does distribution contribute to the Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy?

Distribution is central, since airing live on ABC and Disney+ with next-day streaming on Hulu lets Dancing with the Stars reach traditional TV audiences, streaming-first viewers and on-demand watchers, which maximises fandom and advertiser appeal across demographics. 

What can other brands learn from the Dancing with the Stars marketing strategy?

Other brands can learn to modernise access without abandoning their core product, treat casting and partnerships as marketing inputs, design content for the channels where audiences actually participate, and build interaction into the experience. A branding agency can help connect those choices back to one coherent brand rather than a collection of tactics.

Harley-Davidson sells motorcycles, but its marketing system is built around something broader: identity, participation, and long-term ownership. The company combines a century-plus story with owner communities, dealership experiences, customization, events, apparel, and multiple ways into the product range. That is why its brand strategy works as more than a campaign. Harley turns the motorcycle, the rider network, and the ownership journey into connected touchpoints, while its broader branding keeps the experience recognizable across product, retail, events, and media.

At a Glance: How Harley-Davidson Builds Demand

  • A heritage story built around freedom, craft, and the open road.

  • Community building at global scale via H.O.G.

  • Distinctive design and sound cues, plus customization that supports self-expression.

  • Dealers, learn-to-ride pathways, and demos that help prospects move toward ownership.

  • A lifestyle ecosystem of gear, membership, and events that keeps the brand present between rides.

1) Brand Story: Freedom, Craft, and the Open Road

William S. Harley and Arthur Davidson began experimenting with motorized bicycles around 1901. They sold their first motorcycle in Milwaukee in 1903; Walter Davidson joined the effort that year, and William A. Davidson joined the company by 1907. Harley-Davidson has since turned that origin into a durable narrative about freedom, craft, and the open road. The story is reinforced through the museum, historical content, the Bar & Shield, motorcycle design, and rider culture rather than relying on advertising copy alone (Harley-Davidson).

  • Positioning: independence and belonging (two ideas that sound opposite, but meet on the open road).

  • Creative cue: let bike silhouette, textures, and road narrative lead; specs support the feeling.

2) The Revival: Quality, Independence, and Collectibility

Harley-Davidson’s history includes expansion, periods of pressure, and a pivotal return to independent management. In 1981, 13 senior executives led by Vaughn Beals bought the company back from AMF; Harley-Davidson’s archives say the new management team focused on improving quality and manufacturing efficiency (Harley-Davidson, Harley-Davidson Archives). Later anniversary collections and limited editions added collectibility and storytelling around milestones. The 120th Anniversary collection, for example, used serialized models and commemorative design, but that is evidence of a limited-edition product strategy, not proof that scarcity automatically guarantees margins or resale value (120th Anniversary).

  • Brand lesson: improve the product and ownership experience before treating exclusivity as a marketing device.

  • Launch lesson: limited editions work best when the product, occasion, and story genuinely justify the distinction.

3) Segmentation by Riding Style and Use Case

Harley-Davidson organizes its range around different riding needs rather than one generic motorcycle buyer. Its current lineup spans Grand American Touring, Cruiser, Trike, Adventure Touring, and Sport, which gives the company distinct product stories without abandoning the parent brand (Motorcycle Families; 2026 lineup). This is a useful B2C marketing lesson: segmentation can widen relevance when each offer still carries recognizable brand cues.

  • On-ramps: Riding Academy + urban-friendly models + financing lower first-bike friction.

  • Retention: parts, service, and upgrades turn first owners into lifelong builders (Genuine P&A).

4) Product Range and Customization: Make the Bike Yours

Harley’s motorcycles, parts, and accessories give riders room to personalize fit, comfort, appearance, touring capability, and performance. That makes customization part of the ownership experience rather than an afterthought. Dealers can connect motorcycle selection, fitment, parts, and service in one journey, creating more reasons for riders to return without assuming that every upgrade produces the same financial result (Harley-Davidson Accessories).

  • Merchandising lesson: group accessories around clear rider needs such as touring, comfort, performance, or style.

  • Experience lesson: connect motorcycle selection, fitment, parts, service, and community instead of treating them as isolated transactions.

5) Community Building: H.O.G. as the Heartbeat

The Harley Owners Group makes belonging operational. Harley-Davidson says there are more than 1,400 official H.O.G. chapters worldwide, each sponsored by an authorized dealership, with chapter activity built around rides, events, community, and shared interests (H.O.G.; H.O.G. Chapters). That network keeps the brand active between purchase occasions and gives local groups a structured way to participate. For national brands, it also illustrates a challenge familiar to a US marketing agency: local communities need room to feel local without losing the core identity.

  • Always-on touchpoints: chapter nights, dealership rides, charity events, touring challenges.

  • Identity loop: recognition through badges, milestones, and exclusive moments.

6) Dealerships as Brand and Community Touchpoints

Harley-Davidson’s dealer network connects product discovery with test rides, parts, service, events, and local rider activity. That gives retail a larger role than a one-time motorcycle transaction. Dealers can help prospects experience the product, understand customization options, and connect with local events or chapters. Useful measurements include demo bookings, event registrations, service engagement, and accessory attachment, depending on the dealer’s goals (Harley-Davidson Event Calendar).

  • Layout: stage touring, heritage, and sport with matching accessory vignettes.

  • Metrics: prioritize demo-to-deposit and P&A attachment, not raw footfall.

7) Signature Design and Sound as Distinctive Brand Cues

Harley-Davidson’s silhouettes, finishes, Bar & Shield, engine sound, materials, and riding imagery operate as distinctive brand cues. They are part of the broader visual identity and sensory system that helps people recognize the brand before a long explanation is needed. That is different from claiming every sound or design feature is legally protected as a trademark. The marketing lesson is consistency: new products can evolve while recognizable cues continue to connect the experience to Harley-Davidson.

  • Content rule: win the first five seconds with look and sound; copy follows.

  • Product rule: modernize propulsion and tech, protect silhouette and stance.

8) Lifestyle Ecosystem: Apparel, Licensing, and Media

Harley extends its identity beyond motorcycles through apparel, helmets, licensed products, collaborations, and heritage merchandise. These products give riders and fans another way to participate in the brand even when they are not on a motorcycle. Official content, museum storytelling, and rider stories extend the same identity system across media and merchandise without requiring every audience member to be at the same stage of ownership (Harley-Davidson Apparel & Gear).

  • Collab filter: durability, craft, Americana. Partners who reinforce the myth.

  • Calendar: capsules tied to rallies, anniversaries, and key model launches.

9) Events and Rallies: Turning Ownership Into Participation

Rallies, touring events, dealer rides, and Harley-Davidson Homecoming give riders reasons to participate together rather than experience the brand only through ownership. Events can support demos, merchandise, content, dealer relationships, and community storytelling, while factory and museum experiences make the company’s heritage tangible (Harley-Davidson Event Calendar). They also intersect with travel and hospitality marketing because major rider events create trips, stays, dining, and destination activity around host communities.

  • Measurement: track demos, qualified dealer follow-up, event participation, merchandise, and post-event engagement according to the program’s goals.

  • Content: capture owner miles and stories on-site; publish recap reels per chapter.

10) Digital Ownership Touchpoints: Extend the Relationship

Harley-Davidson’s digital ecosystem extends the relationship between visits, rides, service moments, events, and membership. H.O.G. now includes digital community features and event discovery, while dealership and ownership touchpoints can keep riders connected after the sale (H.O.G.). The strategic lesson is not that every interaction must become an automated sales message. It is that product, service, membership, events, and content should feel like parts of the same ownership journey.

  • Journey: connect learn-to-ride, test rides, purchase, service, customization, events, and membership without assuming one fixed path for every rider.

  • Measurement: track the repeat interactions that matter to the program, such as service engagement, event participation, membership, and accessory activity.

11) Limited Editions and Milestone Storytelling

Limited editions and anniversary motorcycles give Harley-Davidson a way to connect product design with company milestones. The 2023 120th Anniversary collection included six limited-edition, serialized models, turning the anniversary into both a product story and a reason for owners to pay attention (Harley-Davidson 120th Anniversary). That supports a collectibility and occasion strategy. It should not be stretched into an unsupported claim that limited supply automatically protects resale values or margins.

  • Launch lesson: connect limited editions to a clear milestone, design story, and owner experience.

  • Ownership lesson: parts, service, pre-owned programs, and events can extend the relationship beyond the initial purchase.

FAQ

What is the core marketing strategy of Harley-Davidson?

Harley-Davidson combines heritage, distinctive product design, community, dealerships, customization, events, merchandise, and ownership programs. The motorcycle remains central, but the surrounding system gives riders more ways to participate in the brand.

How does community building of Harley-Davidson drive sales?

H.O.G. chapters, rides, rallies, and dealer-sponsored activity create recurring opportunities for owners to meet and participate. That can support loyalty and advocacy, but the article does not assume a direct sales effect from every community interaction.

What makes the Harley-Davidson brand story effective?

The story is reinforced across company history, the museum, product design, the Bar & Shield, events, dealerships, and rider culture, so the same themes appear across multiple touchpoints rather than only in advertising.

What fueled the Harley-Davidson rise after its slump?

The 1981 management buyback was followed by a documented focus on quality and manufacturing efficiency. Later community programs, model development, events, and anniversary products became additional parts of the brand system.

How does Harley balance heritage with innovation?

Harley can modernize motorcycles, technology, and the ownership experience while carrying forward distinctive design cues, the riding culture, and the community structures that make the brand recognizable.

What Harley-Davidson’s Marketing Strategy Teaches

The marketing strategy of Harley-Davidson works because the product is surrounded by a coherent system: heritage, distinctive design cues, customization, dealer experiences, H.O.G. chapters, events, merchandise, and ongoing ownership touchpoints. The broader lesson for consumer brands is to build participation around a clear identity rather than relying on campaign reach alone.

Hermès has built one of luxury's clearest examples of marketing through restraint. The house does advertise, publish, collaborate, sell online, and expand its store network, but the experience is organized around craftsmanship, selective distribution, controlled availability, and a brand language that changes slowly.

That strategy now operates at substantial scale. Hermès reported €16.0 billion in 2025 revenue, €6.569 billion in recurring operating income, and €4.524 billion in net income attributable to owners of the parent in its current financial key figures. In the first half of 2026, revenue reached €8.163 billion and the workforce reached 27,107 people. The business has grown without abandoning the central idea that desirable objects should remain tied to craft and controlled distribution.

The previous full-year comparison still shows the trajectory: 2024 revenue was €15.2 billion, recurring operating income €6.2 billion, and net profit €4.6 billion (GlobeNewswire). A January 5, 2026 market snapshot also estimated Hermès' market capitalization at €220.58 billion (StockAnalysis).

Craftsmanship Is the Center of the Hermès Brand

Hermès began in 1837 as a harness workshop, and the company's current financial materials still describe the group as an independent house guided by craftsmanship, authenticity, responsibility, and a long-term approach. That history matters because the strongest part of the Hermès marketing strategy is not a slogan. It is the consistency between what the brand says and how the products are made.

For a premium brand, brand strategy works best when the positioning is supported by something operationally difficult to copy. Hermès can point to skilled labor, materials, production time, repairability, and long product life. Those facts make the idea of craft more credible than a campaign alone could.

  • Craft limits how quickly supply can expand.
  • Stable brand codes reduce the need to reinvent the identity every season.
  • The making process creates storytelling material without requiring constant promotional claims.
  • A disciplined visual identity helps the house carry the same tone across leather, silk, watches, home, fashion, and digital content.

That is the kind of system a broad branding agency should aim to build: the market position, product experience, and brand expression support the same promise.

Hermès by the Numbers: Scale Without Mass Positioning

Hermès' 2025 results show that a controlled luxury model can still grow. Revenue reached €16.002 billion, recurring operating income reached €6.569 billion, and the 2025 recurring operating margin was 41%. The group's 2025 presentation also listed 294 stores in 45 countries and 26,494 employees. Those figures are materially above the 2024 baseline reported earlier (GlobeNewswire).

The operating model explains why the scale does not automatically translate into mass positioning. Hermès' 2025 presentation said 55% of objects were made in in-house and exclusive workshops and highlighted continued investment in French production capacity. The point is not that every Hermès object is scarce in the same way. It is that the company keeps a large share of production, training, materials expertise, and distribution close to the house. That makes growth dependent on adding real capacity and know-how rather than only increasing media spend.

Communication spending also exists at meaningful scale. The 2025 Universal Registration Document reported €620 million in communication expenses. Hermès is therefore not a brand that “does not market.” It markets selectively within a broader branding system where product, store environment, editorial content, events, and advertising are expected to reinforce the same position.

The old 2024 snapshot remains useful for comparison:

  • 2024 revenue was €15.2 billion (GlobeNewswire).
  • 2024 recurring operating income was €6.2 billion (GlobeNewswire).
  • 2024 net profit was €4.6 billion (GlobeNewswire).
  • The 2024 communication described a workforce of almost 25,000 people (GlobeNewswire).
  • It also cited 54 production sites in France (GlobeNewswire).

Hermès previously described a retail network of 293 stores across 45 countries (Hermès). The 2025 full-year presentation updates that network to 294 stores, showing how selective the physical footprint remains relative to global demand.

The Birkin's secondary-market reputation is often used as evidence of scarcity and cultural signaling. The existing reference summarizes examples above $200,000.  Those auction outcomes should not be treated as a guaranteed investment return, but they help explain why availability itself has become part of the product story.

Scarcity, Pricing, and Distribution Work as One System

Hermès does not need artificial countdowns to create scarcity. Production capacity, specialist labor, materials, boutique allocation, and product-specific demand create real constraints. The marketing effect comes from how those constraints interact with price and distribution.

This is where brand research can matter for another premium company. Scarcity only strengthens a brand if buyers already value the product enough to accept limited availability. Research can test which attributes customers consider distinctive, which parts of the experience create confidence, and whether a premium position has real evidence behind it.

  • Supply is controlled rather than expanded simply to satisfy every short-term spike in demand.
  • Pricing remains part of the positioning, not a lever that changes with constant promotions.
  • The boutique experience adds service, context, and discovery to the transaction.
  • Distribution itself signals that the brand is not designed for universal availability.

That coherence is why Hermès is a useful example in luxury brand marketing. Exclusivity is not just copy. It is reflected in operations.

Local store purchasing freedom adds another layer. Hermès' own description of its model emphasizes a rich offer and the purchasing freedom of stores. That means assortment can vary by market without forcing the master brand to change. Customers experience uncertainty about what may be available at a specific boutique, while the house preserves global standards for product, presentation, and service. This is more durable than manufactured scarcity because the variation comes from a real distribution model.

For another company, the useful principle is to separate genuine constraints from promotional theater. If a service has limited capacity because senior specialists do the work, say so. If a product requires small-batch production or scarce materials, explain that process. If supply is actually unlimited, using scarcity language too aggressively can weaken trust instead of strengthening demand.

The Birkin Shows How Product History Becomes Brand Memory

Hermès' own Birkin history says the bag was created in 1984 after Jane Birkin met Jean-Louis Dumas on a Paris-to-London flight and described the kind of bag she needed. The story is still part of the current Birkin product world.

The association with Jane Birkin gives the object a human story beyond leather and construction.  More importantly, the bag has retained a recognizable shape, name, and set of cultural associations for decades. That continuity creates brand memory in a way a short-lived campaign cannot.

For other companies, the lesson is not to manufacture mythology. It is to document real origins, design decisions, and customer stories when they genuinely explain why a product exists.

Selective Collaborations Protect the Core Brand

Hermès collaborates, but the strongest partnerships make sense in terms of design values rather than audience size alone. Apple Watch Hermès remains the clearest example. In 2015, Hermès x Apple joined Apple's technology platform with Hermès craftsmanship and design. Apple described the original collaboration as a meeting of product innovation, heritage, iconography, and craftsmanship.

The partnership has lasted because the roles remain legible. Apple contributes the watch platform and technology, while Hermès contributes materials, bands, watch faces, color, and luxury context. The current Apple x Hermès collection shows that the collaboration is still active rather than functioning as a one-season licensing exercise.

Hermès has also worked with designers and artists in categories where creative interpretation fits the house. The existing (Vogue) reference documents Rei Kawakubo's silk-scarf collaboration. These projects work because the outside voice is brought into an existing Hermès system rather than replacing it.

Digital Strategy Extends the Brand Without Replacing the Boutique

Hermès has an ecommerce business and active digital publishing, but online access does not make every product equally available. The website is useful for discovery, education, product browsing, editorial content, and many direct purchases, while some of the highest-demand leather goods remain closely tied to store relationships and allocation.

The official site still plays an important storytelling role, including product context around icons like the Birkin (Hermès). A premium digital experience therefore has two jobs: make information and transactions usable while preserving the cues that support the brand's position.

That is where thoughtful web design and UI UX design matter for other premium businesses. The goal is not to make the interface difficult in the name of luxury. It is to make the experience clear, deliberate, and consistent with the product.

A premium site still has to answer ordinary customer questions: what is available, how products differ, where stores are located, how care or repair works, and what happens after purchase. Removing useful information does not create prestige. The stronger approach is to control pacing, imagery, copy, interaction, and merchandising while keeping the journey understandable. Digital restraint should feel intentional rather than incomplete.

The same applies to data. A luxury brand can measure search behavior, product interest, appointment demand, store visits, repeat purchase, and content engagement without letting dashboards dictate the creative identity. Measurement should explain where the experience is working or breaking, not turn every page into a direct-response landing page.

Quiet Luxury Is a Result, Not the Whole Strategy

Hermès is frequently associated with “quiet luxury” and old money aesthetics because many of its products communicate status through materials, construction, recognizable forms, and subtle codes rather than large logos. But that description only captures the surface.

The deeper strategy is a combination of product quality, pricing integrity, controlled access, service, heritage, and cultural recognition. The brand can be visually restrained because the objects and distribution system already carry meaning. Restraint without those foundations would simply be minimalism.

Hermès also benefits from social proof. Owners, collectors, fashion media, auction coverage, and celebrity sightings keep products culturally visible without requiring the company to treat every appearance as an official endorsement. That distinction helps the house maintain distance from the constant paid-creator cycle common elsewhere in consumer marketing.

What the Hermès Marketing Strategy Can Teach Other Businesses

The strongest lesson is coherence. Product, pricing, distribution, service, creative direction, and communication reinforce one another. A company does not need Hermès scarcity or luxury pricing to apply the same principle.

  • Make one defensible advantage unmistakable. Hermès has craftsmanship. Another company might compete through speed, specialization, reliability, or a proprietary process.
  • Use scarcity only when it reflects a real constraint such as capacity, quality control, customization, or selectivity.
  • Protect pricing integrity when the business model supports it. Constant discounting can make the published price feel temporary rather than meaningful.
  • Turn process into proof. Show the work, standards, quality checks, expertise, or decisions that make the outcome different.
  • Create an experience people want to return to. Service, follow-up, packaging, onboarding, and support can reinforce the same position as the product.
  • Choose collaborators for fit. Reach is useful only when the partnership strengthens the meaning customers already associate with the brand.
  • Use B2C marketing channels to distribute the story without changing the core promise every time a platform or trend changes.

Hermès' 2024 results already showed how powerful that model had become (GlobeNewswire), and the 2025 and first-half 2026 figures show that the system continued to grow.

For a smaller business, this can be tested with a simple audit. Compare the promise on the homepage with the actual offer, price structure, sales process, fulfillment experience, and customer support. Look for places where the brand claims selectivity but the experience feels generic, or claims craftsmanship without showing evidence. The most useful improvement is often not another campaign. It is making the proof and the promise agree.

From Brand Vision's perspective, the point is not to copy Hermès aesthetics. It is to make sure the business model and the brand story support each other. If those pieces are disconnected, a focused marketing consultation can help identify which part of the system needs attention first.

IKEA's marketing strategy is built around a promise that is easy to understand and difficult to imitate: well-designed home furnishings at prices intended to be accessible to many people. That promise shapes product development, flat-pack logistics, self-service retail, store design, ecommerce, loyalty, and communication. Marketing works because the operating model gives the message something concrete to prove.

For marketers, IKEA is useful as a case study in how a brand system that scales can stay recognizable while adapting to local markets. In 2026, affordability remains especially important as IKEA continues to invest in lower prices, smaller store formats, digital shopping, and localized campaigns.

At a Glance

  • IKEA treats affordability as an operating decision, not a temporary promotion.
  • The store and digital journey turn room inspiration into product discovery and purchase.
  • Swedish brand codes stay consistent while products, campaigns, and formats adapt by market.
  • The latest published full-year retail results are FY25, while September 2026 announcements show affordability remains a current strategic priority.

Affordable Design and Quality: Price Is Built In, Not Discounted

IKEA's affordability story begins before advertising. Products are developed against target prices, while flat-pack design, high-volume production, self-service elements, and material choices help control the costs of manufacturing, storage, and distribution. That is a different proposition from a retailer that depends mainly on short promotional cycles.

The result is a value message customers can encounter repeatedly: in product design, packaging, pricing, logistics, and the store experience. Affordability is more credible when the business model supports it.

  • Flat-pack construction reduces transport and storage volume.
  • Self-assembly and self-service are part of the value exchange, not hidden compromises.
  • Product design balances function, materials, manufacturing, and target price.

Staying True to Scandinavian Roots: Consistency as a Growth Lever

IKEA does not need to redesign its identity every season. Functional Scandinavian design, blue and yellow, Swedish language cues, simple typography, and a direct tone create continuity across decades. IKEA's Time Capsule 1984 archive is a useful reminder of how long those design ideas have been present.

Consistency reduces the amount of explanation each campaign needs. The same principle applies to logo design and visual assets more broadly: distinctive cues become more valuable as they are repeated coherently rather than reinvented.

Store Layout and Customer Experience: The Store Is Part of the Campaign

IKEA's physical stores translate the brand promise into a guided experience. Room sets provide context before customers reach individual product bins, while the market hall, self-service warehouse, food areas, and checkout complete a journey that mixes inspiration with practical purchase steps.

The store therefore acts as both retail infrastructure and media. Customers can see scale, combinations, materials, storage ideas, and complete rooms before deciding what belongs in their own home. Brand Vision's guide to retail marketing and branding explores the same challenge of keeping in-store and digital experiences aligned.

  • Room sets show products in use rather than in isolation.
  • The guided path exposes customers to multiple categories without requiring a separate campaign for each one.
  • Food and family-oriented services make the visit part of the broader IKEA experience.

Simple, Consistent Branding: Brand Codes That Do the Heavy Lifting

IKEA's blue and yellow palette, wordmark, Swedish product names, and plain-spoken tone make the brand easy to recognize. The system is simple enough to scale but distinctive enough to remain identifiable across packaging, stores, catalogues, apps, social content, and signage.

The Swedish product names are especially useful because they reinforce origin while giving thousands of products a consistent naming logic. A deliberate brand naming system can play a similar role for companies with large product portfolios: it makes expansion feel organized rather than improvised.

Localized Marketing Strategies: Global Story, Local Proof

IKEA's promise is global, but the proof changes by market. Product emphasis, room sizes, seasonal moments, media choices, and store formats can reflect local living conditions without changing the basic ideas of affordability, function, and Scandinavian design. That is a core principle of international marketing: protect what makes the brand recognizable while adapting the evidence around it.

Canada provides a current example. In September 2026, IKEA Canada launched “You Give It Meaning” for its 50th anniversary, using familiar Swedish product names as a starting point for stories about what those products came to mean in Canadian homes. (IKEA Canada) The campaign localizes the cultural story without abandoning IKEA's global brand codes.

For businesses translating a broader brand system into Canadian market realities, Brand Vision also works with companies across Canada. The useful lesson is to localize context and proof without turning the brand into a different company in every market.

IKEA Marketing Strategy 2026: Affordability as a Business Decision

IKEA's latest published full-year retail results remain FY25. The company reported EUR 44.6 billion in retail sales, with sales volumes and customer counts each increasing 3% after two years of price investments averaging 10% lower prices. Online sales represented 28% of IKEA turnover, and store visitation reached 915 million. (IKEA Global)

The latest full-year source also notes IKEA's ongoing strategy of launching new products at lower recommended retail prices than existing ones. (IKEA Global)

The affordability strategy is still active in September 2026. IKEA announced a combined EUR 1.2 billion investment in lower prices across Europe, with selected products receiving reductions of up to 25%. (IKEA Global) That is useful marketing evidence because the promise is being funded operationally rather than communicated only through advertising.

  • FY25 retail sales were EUR 44.6 billion. (IKEA Global)
  • Online sales represented 28% of total IKEA sales in FY25. (IKEA Global)
  • The FY26 commercial focus was kitchen and dining, supported by lower-price ranges such as KNOXHULT. (IKEA Global)

Digital Marketing and E-Commerce: Confidence, Not Just Convenience

Furniture ecommerce has an uncertainty problem. Shoppers need to judge dimensions, fit, combinations, delivery, assembly, and whether the product will work in a real room. IKEA's digital tools, planning content, product information, and visualization features are designed to make those decisions easier.

For a large B2C marketing operation, digital experience is part of the value proposition. Better UX research can reveal where shoppers hesitate, while strong web design turns those findings into clearer navigation, comparison, product detail, and checkout flows.

  • Planning and visualization tools make size and configuration easier to evaluate.
  • Instructional content can answer objections before they become abandoned sessions.
  • Customer examples and room inspiration connect products to real-life use cases.

Sustainability as a Core Value: Circularity That Supports Value

IKEA's sustainability message is strongest when it connects environmental goals with everyday value. The company's current strategy sets 2030 objectives across healthy and sustainable living, climate, nature and circularity, and fair and equal practices. Its sustainability strategy also emphasizes making sustainable choices affordable and accessible.

That makes sustainability less dependent on broad claims. Product longevity, renewable and recycled materials, energy use, repair, reuse, and circular services can all become tangible proof points when they are tied to what customers actually do.

  • Product design can reduce material use while preserving function and price.
  • Circular services extend the usable life of products and materials.
  • Specific goals and progress reporting make sustainability messaging easier to evaluate.

Emotional Storytelling: Everyday Life Beats Product Features

IKEA often frames products through the moments they support: a first apartment, a family dinner, a shared bedroom, a crowded kitchen, or the relief of finally organizing a small space. That makes everyday life the story and furniture the tool.

The approach works because the emotional layer does not replace function. It makes function relevant. A storage system matters because of the room it improves; a table matters because of the people who gather around it.

  • Everyday scenarios make practical products easier to imagine in context.
  • Humour can keep the tone human without weakening the value message.
  • Lifestyle storytelling gives a broad product range one shared purpose.

Loyalty Programs and Customer Engagement: Retention Built Into the Model

IKEA Family gives the retailer a direct relationship with customers beyond individual purchases. Member pricing, benefits, communications, and store experiences support repeat visits in a category where customers may return across moves, renovations, new family stages, and changing rooms.

The loyalty lesson is broader than discounts. Membership works best when it consistently makes the brand easier or more useful to choose, reinforcing the same affordability and accessibility promise customers encounter elsewhere.

What You Can Apply to Your Own Brand

  • Make price and value legible. Buyers should understand what they receive and why it costs what it does.
  • Turn the customer experience into a sequence. Each step should make the next decision easier.
  • Protect a small set of distinctive brand codes instead of redesigning the system constantly.
  • Localize proof and examples while keeping the underlying position recognizable.
  • Use digital tools and content to reduce uncertainty before asking for conversion.
  • Treat sustainability as operations and evidence, not adjectives.
  • Design retention early so the customer relationship continues after the first transaction.

How Business Owners Can Apply IKEA's Affordability Strategy in 2026

IKEA's advantage is alignment. Product decisions, operations, store experience, digital tools, and communication all make the affordability promise more believable. The same principle applies at a smaller scale: positioning should be visible in what the customer experiences, not only in campaign language.

A clear branding foundation can keep the promise consistent, while an SEO agency strategy can make durable demand easier to capture when customers begin actively researching the category. The goal is not more channels for their own sake. It is a system in which brand, experience, and discoverability reinforce the same reason to choose you.

Red Bull marketing has never been about selling an energy drink louder than everyone else. It is about building a world people want to join, then distributing that world with the discipline of a media company. That is why Red Bull's campaigns still set the pace in 2026, in a market crowded with creators, sponsorships, and short-form everything.

At Brand Vision, we read campaigns like these less as ads and more as systems. The mechanics travel across categories. Attention is only worth something when it lands on a clear brand story and a website that makes the next step obvious. Get that right and marketing stops being a run of launches and starts behaving like an engine.

At a Glance

  • Red Bull's biggest marketing campaigns work because the story leads and the product follows.
  • Each campaign is built as a long-term content asset, not a one-day event.
  • Owned media and recurring platforms make every new campaign cheaper to scale than the last.
  • The transferable lesson for 2026 is systems over stunts: one promise, repeatable proof, a clear next step.

The Scale Behind the Strategy (and Why It Matters)

Red Bull's consistency makes more sense once you see the size of the operation. As of 2025 the company reports selling 13.969 billion cans worldwide, with group turnover up to EUR 12.196 billion (Red Bull company profile). That scale funds what most brands cannot sustain: premium production, recurring events, and year-round storytelling that does not disappear when a campaign ends.

Scale is not the strategy, though. The strategy is how Red Bull turns that spend into compounding demand. Big moments are treated as long-term assets rather than one-day wins. Content is planned as a library from the start, the highlight, the behind-the-scenes, the follow-up. And distribution is designed in at the beginning, not bolted on at the end.

The Red Bull Marketing Strategy Blueprint (Built Like a Flywheel)

Red Bull's marketing strategy is best read as a flywheel with four connected parts: positioning that stays stable, proof that feels real, publishing that never stops, and platforms that generate repeatable stories. Each part feeds the next, which is why the campaigns compound instead of resetting every quarter.

Red Bull formalized the publishing side through Red Bull Media House, which runs as a multi-platform media company built around sports, culture, and lifestyle. That structure is the quiet advantage behind the loud campaigns.

From a Brand Vision lens, this is the line between running marketing and building a marketing system. A good partner does not just make posts. It protects the positioning, engineers the proof, and connects every campaign to a website journey that converts.

Stratos: Turning a Single Moment Into a Global Broadcast

Stratos worked because it was built as a story people wanted to watch live and then rewatch for years. Training, risk, tension, the jump, the aftermath. The arc was clear before anyone switched on a camera.

The distribution proof is public. YouTube's own newsroom put the livestream peak at more than 8 million concurrent viewers (YouTube newsroom), the most concurrent views the platform had ever seen at the time. Red Bull still keeps the project alive through its dedicated Stratos hub, which is the tell: the brand treats a campaign as an ongoing media asset, not an expiring ad.

Why it worked

  • A simple narrative anyone could retell in a sentence.
  • Built-in replay value and real demand for the behind-the-scenes.
  • A brand promise delivered through proof, not copy.

The transferable move is to design one flagship moment that can feed a whole content library and to build the place you are sending people to before you spend on the attention.

F1: Sponsorship as a Platform, Not a Placement

For Red Bull, Formula 1 is not a logo on a car. It is a platform that manufactures storylines every season, with weekly moments and year-round content. The team lays out its history and structure on the Oracle Red Bull Racing pages, and Formula 1's year-by-year record reinforces the continuity that makes the sponsorship read as identity rather than advertising.

That is why Red Bull stays present without feeling repetitive. The platform writes new episodes on its own.

Why it worked

  • Ongoing proof through performance and consistency.
  • A built-in content cadence: races, rivalries, engineering stories, fan culture.
  • An identity that never needs reinventing.

The lesson is to choose platforms that generate repeatable stories instead of one-time exposure, and to treat partnerships as content infrastructure. The same platform thinking shows up in Nike's marketing strategy and how it builds presence across recurring cultural moments.

Flugtag: Experiential Marketing Engineered for Sharing

Flugtag is participation disguised as entertainment, and the format is the distribution. Teams build human-powered flying machines, launch them off a pier, and the spectacular failures become content people share without being asked. Red Bull runs the Flugtag event series across cities worldwide, so local events roll up into one global identity.

This still matters in 2026, because community-made content travels further than polished brand content when the mechanic is right.

Why it worked

  • Participation produces the content automatically.
  • The tone is approachable, not exclusive.
  • Recognition, not a discount, is the reward.

For a smaller brand, the move is the same at a smaller scale: build a simple mechanic customers can join in minutes, and make being featured the prize.

The Art of Flight: Premium Content as Brand Equity

The Art of Flight shows the strategy at its most patient. Rather than borrow culture, Red Bull funded it. The brand treated a feature-length snowboarding film like premium entertainment and kept it inside its own media library, which turns one production into an asset with a long shelf life.

For a marketing partner that is the useful part: one premium piece can fuel months of cutdowns, highlights, clips, and social hooks. Build a content hub that keeps a visitor moving to the next story, the way our own Insights hub is meant to. Even luxury brands run this play; the patient, equity-first approach in Louis Vuitton's marketing strategy rewards the same restraint.

Why it worked

  • Quality high enough to earn attention rather than demand it.
  • Cultural credibility bought with real investment.
  • Repurposing potential that lasts for years.

"Red Bull Gives You Wings": The Message That Holds Everything Together

Plenty of brands confuse activity with strategy. Red Bull does not. The tagline is a promise that stays fixed across wildly different executions, which is how Red Bull's campaigns can move from extreme sports to culture to everyday social rituals and still feel instantly like the same brand.

This is the hardest part for most businesses to hold, and it is not creativity. It is discipline. The job is to write one promise and protect it, then use branding to turn that value into language people repeat. A stable line is also why McDonald's has stretched "I'm Lovin' It" across two decades; the discipline behind McDonald's marketing strategy is the same one at work here.

Why it worked

  • A promise flexible enough to stretch across categories.
  • Consistency that builds memory and recall.

Social-First Campaigns: Broadening Relevance Without Diluting Identity

Not every Red Bull campaign needs a stunt. The brand also wins by turning everyday identity into a shareable ritual, tying itself to belonging and social energy. That matters in 2026, when not everyone wants to watch a man jump from the edge of space, but almost everyone wants to feel part of something.

The mechanic is the same promise in a quieter setting: build something simple that invites participation, start small, and expand what works. For a contrast case, Duolingo's TikTok strategy shows how a brand builds cultural presence through repeatable social mechanics rather than budget.

Why it worked

  • A simple mechanic that encourages sharing on its own.
  • Everyday relevance that raises how often the brand shows up.

What You Can Apply to Your Own Brand

Red Bull's campaigns look intimidating because the outputs are enormous. The transferable part is the structure, and it is smaller than it looks. This is the playbook we adapt most often when we act as a long-term marketing partner, and none of it needs a Stratos budget.

1. Write a promise that can survive a hundred campaigns

If the core idea keeps changing, your audience never builds memory. Write one sentence that says what you do and why it matters, specific enough to mean something and broad enough to scale, then keep the message and the visual cues locked together across your site, social, and campaigns.

2. Build proof that people can see, not claims they have to trust

Red Bull earns belief through real-world proof. Yours can be smaller, but it has to repeat. Turn your expertise into something visible, a challenge, a demo, a transformation series, and publish the outcomes and the lessons on a schedule rather than when you remember to.

3. Design participation into the campaign

Flugtag works because the audience becomes the content. Pick a mechanic a customer can join in minutes, then build a recognition loop that spotlights people, features submissions, and celebrates results. Make the sharing feel natural by anchoring it in identity, not discounts.

4. Treat content like a product line

The Red Bull engine never stops, and random posting builds no recall. Choose two or three formats you can sustain for a full year, a weekly insight, a monthly story, a quarterly hero asset, and run them on a real process with clear owners and approvals. In food and beverage marketing, that repetition matters because recognition is built through consistent category presence.

5. Make your website the closer, not the brochure

Attention is only worth something if the landing experience converts, and this is where most campaigns leak. Map each campaign to one primary action, whether that is an inquiry, a booking, or a subscription, and build dedicated pages that answer the decision questions quickly with as little friction as possible.

6. Build partnerships that work as credibility infrastructure

Red Bull does not chase random sponsorships. Its partnerships line up with the promise and produce proof. Choose partners who validate your message in public, structure the relationship to create stories rather than logos, and let that content live on your own site so it keeps earning attention. Our deeper look at Red Bull's extreme sports sponsorships shows how that model compounds over time.

7. Create internal pathways so your marketing compounds

The best brands never let a reader hit a dead end. Link campaign content to its supporting proof, then to the relevant service, so each page strengthens the next instead of standing alone.

8. Measure the metrics that compound

Views are not value. Track the marketing metrics tied to memory and conversion, repeat visits, branded search interest, sign-ups, and conversion rate by content type, and give the system a full cycle before you judge it. Keep what compounds and cut what spikes without payoff.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Red Bull's most famous marketing campaigns?

Red Bull's best-known campaigns are Stratos (Felix Baumgartner's jump from the edge of space), the Flugtag flying-machine events, the snowboarding film The Art of Flight, its Formula 1 team Oracle Red Bull Racing, and the long-running "Red Bull Gives You Wings" platform. Each was built to keep producing content long after the moment itself passed.

What is Red Bull's marketing strategy?

Red Bull's marketing strategy runs like a flywheel: stable positioning, real-world proof, nonstop publishing through Red Bull Media House, and platforms such as Formula 1 that generate repeatable stories. The product follows the story rather than leading it.

Why is Red Bull's marketing so effective?

It works because Red Bull treats every campaign as a long-term media asset, not a one-off ad. One stable promise carries across formats, owned media keeps the content alive, and the scale of the business, 13.969 billion cans sold in 2025, funds production most brands cannot match.

Can a small business copy Red Bull's campaign strategy?

Yes, but copy the structure, not the budget. The transferable part is one protected promise, a proof format you can repeat, and a website that turns attention into action. We see that smaller version working far more often than the stunt-led one.

Red Bull's campaigns look expensive to copy and easy to misread. The budget is not the lesson. The discipline is: one promise, proof you can rerun, and a clear place to send the attention. If that last piece is where your campaigns leak, conversion-focused web design is the part we would fix first.

Build the system and the math changes. Your marketing stops being a run of separate campaigns and starts being one engine that compounds.

Slow approvals delay launches and raise costs. The fix is a clear marketing workflow that sets decision rights, limits review cycles, and leaves an audit trail legal can trust. Findings from the B2B Content Marketing Trends research point to the same root issues: unclear goals, thin resourcing, and ad-hoc processes. A simple path—clean intake, defined owners, and contained rounds—solves most of it.

Why approvals stall

Delays usually start with three things: unclear decision rights, too many reviewers, and late edits that change scope. When roles aren’t defined, feedback arrives out of order and conflicts. That creates rework and additional rounds. A lightweight change-control mindset helps: decide what can change after creative lock, who can approve it, and the time limit for that decision.

How a marketing workflow drives faster campaign approvals

Give every asset a single owner who is accountable for moving it forward. Name approvers and contributors. Keep reviewers limited to those who must weigh in. Set one-sentence criteria for each round (for example, “message and compliance” for round one, “visual polish” for round two). End each round with a clear go/no-go. The goal is fewer cycles, not faster spinning.

Standardize intake to prevent rework

Use one brief for all assets on a campaign. Capture the objective, single CTA, audience, support for any claims, channel specs, and due date. Freeze the brief at kick-off; treat new ideas after that as new requests. For examples of tight objectives and crisp execution, see our rundowns of best marketing campaigns in 2025, McDonald’s marketing strategy, and the Share a Coke campaign analysis.

Version control and file standards keep reviews clear

Keep assets in one place. Name files with project, channel, size, and version (Q2_Promo-IG_1080x1350_v03). Drafts stay editable. Review copies export to PDF/MP4. Finals are read-only. That prevents duplicates and accidental edits.

Reviews that end on time

Centralize comments on the asset itself so feedback is specific and visible to everyone. Avoid side threads in email or chat. Real-time annotation helps teams avoid duplicate or conflicting notes and speeds resolution. Tools that support live markups for teams let brand, creative, and legal comment in one place, assign owners, and close threads before the next cut.

Fast without risk: change control and audit trails

Speed and governance can work together. Treat each approval as a small change-control step: record what changed, why, and who approved it. Keep a system log that ties comments to versions and users. Structured approvals reduce slippage and rework, as outlined in the PMI guidance on change control.

Tools that support the process without adding complexity

Use your project system for intake, owners, dates, and status. Use your asset store for versioned files. Use one annotation layer for comments and signoff so feedback isn’t scattered. Consolidation is what saves time; adding more tools without a clear role usually slows teams down.

SLAs that work for US marketing teams

Set response times that match asset risk. A practical baseline is one business day for brief approval, 24 hours for first-cut reviews on low-risk assets, and 48 hours for higher-risk or claims-bearing work. Make weekend and holiday rules explicit. If someone misses an SLA, the owner escalates once and then proceeds with a documented decision.

Metrics that show the workflow is working

Track four numbers: time to first response, total time in review, average number of rounds by channel, and hit rate (approved on the planned round). Add these to campaign retros alongside performance results. Over a few cycles, the trend lines will show where to adjust staffing, SLAs, or round goals.

A one-week rollout you can start now

Pick one live campaign and apply the workflow. Kick off with a frozen brief. Assign a single owner per asset and name approvers. Collect all feedback as annotated comments in one system. Resolve every thread before moving to the next round. Lock finals and keep the audit log. Review the four metrics at the end of the week and fine-tune the SLAs.

Conclusion: make your marketing workflow your 2025 advantage

A clear marketing workflow is the fastest path to faster campaign approvals. Standardize intake, set decision rights, keep comments in one place with live markups for teams, and use simple change control to keep risk low. Do it once, measure it, and keep it as your default for the rest of 2025.

Rhode’s marketing strategy combines founder visibility, a tightly controlled product assortment, recognizable creative direction, social distribution, and an ecommerce experience built around product desire. Hailey Bieber’s audience helped the brand attract attention at launch, but celebrity alone does not explain the business Rhode became. The stronger story is how the product, visual system, campaigns, and customer journey reinforced one another.

Rhode launched in June 2022 and quickly became a useful consumer marketing case study. It started with a small group of skincare essentials rather than a large catalogue, built a highly recognizable “glazed” aesthetic around them, and used social content to turn product textures, packaging, routines, and limited releases into repeatable creative material. This breakdown is shaped by the real brand, web, and growth work we do at Brand Vision, with the focus on what other founders can actually learn from Rhode’s system.

From a Focused Launch to a $1 Billion Acquisition Deal

Rhode’s early growth is easier to understand through disclosed figures than through the revenue estimates that circulated after launch. Forbes reported in late 2022 that the brand had built a waitlist of about 700,000 people across its initial products, while Bieber said revenue was on track to reach eight figures but did not provide a specific number. That is more reliable than the earlier chart in this article that estimated $10 million in 2022, $50 million in 2023, and $100 million in 2024.

The most useful later figure came from e.l.f. Beauty. When it announced an agreement to acquire Rhode in May 2025, the company disclosed that Rhode generated $212 million in net sales for the 12 months ended March 31, 2025. The transaction closed in August 2025 for $800 million at closing, with up to another $200 million tied to future performance. The deal therefore carried potential consideration of up to $1 billion rather than proving that Rhode had generated $1 billion in sales.

That growth gives the marketing discussion a stronger foundation. Rhode was not simply creating viral beauty content. It was building a direct-to-consumer business with enough demand, repeatable brand equity, and category expansion potential to become attractive to a larger beauty company.

A Small Product Line Made the Brand Easier to Understand

Rhode launched around a small set of core products, including Peptide Glazing Fluid, Barrier Restore Cream, and Peptide Lip Treatment. A narrow assortment helped customers understand the routine and gave the brand a few hero products to repeat across founder content, creator posts, product photography, and press coverage.

This restraint supported Rhode’s brand strategy. The company did not need to explain dozens of products at once. Instead, it could build memory around a few textures, package shapes, product names, and routines. The “glazed” language attached the skincare outcome to a visual idea that was easy to reproduce in photography and short-form video.

For founders, the lesson is not that every business should launch with three products. It is that a product line should be easy to understand. A smaller range can make positioning, content production, inventory planning, and customer education more focused when the offer is still being established.

Founder Visibility Became a Distribution Channel

Hailey Bieber’s personal audience gave Rhode an immediate advantage, but the brand used that reach in a way that was closely tied to product usage. Get Ready With Me videos, routine demonstrations, close-up texture shots, launch posts, and founder appearances made the products part of an existing content behaviour rather than a separate stream of conventional advertisements.

That founder-led approach also works because Rhode has a visual system that can survive without Bieber appearing in every frame. Its visual identity relies on restrained packaging, product close-ups, glossy skin, food references, muted neutrals, and occasional bursts of colour. Those elements give creators and customers recognizable material to work with while keeping the brand coherent.

The practical lesson is to make founder content repeatable. A founder can create trust and attention, but the company still needs visual rules, product stories, and content formats that employees, creators, and customers can use without requiring the founder in every post.

Food, Texture, and Product Naming Created Shareable Campaign Ideas

Rhode’s marketing repeatedly turns product benefits into sensory language. Words such as “glaze,” “toast,” “raspberry jelly,” and “espresso” make texture and shade easier to imagine. That approach became especially visible around Peptide Lip Treatment and Peptide Lip Tint, where food-inspired creative gave the campaigns an immediate visual hook.

The Strawberry Glaze collaboration with Krispy Kreme is a clear example. The product name, colour, food association, and founder’s existing “glazed” language all supported the same concept. The campaign felt larger than a standard limited edition because each part of the creative system reinforced the same memory cue.

This is also where packaging design and art direction become commercial tools. The package does not need to be complicated to be distinctive. It needs enough recognizability that a close-up image, unboxing video, or product held in someone’s hand still reads as the brand.

The Ecommerce Experience Carried the Same Brand World

Rhode’s website extends the product styling rather than treating ecommerce as a separate utility layer. Product photography, typography, whitespace, copy, and mobile layouts support the same minimal, glossy aesthetic customers see on social. That makes website design part of the marketing system rather than simply the place where transactions happen.

Shopify’s partner directory states that VAAN worked with Rhode to build its Shopify site and continues to support development, design, and strategy. That makes Rhode a relevant example of Shopify storefront design: the commerce platform handles the transaction infrastructure, while the brand layer has to preserve product storytelling and make the path to purchase clear.

As the assortment grows, the digital challenge becomes harder. Customers need to distinguish skincare from hybrid makeup, compare shades, understand routines, and move between inspiration and checkout. A strong UI/UX design system helps the site scale without losing the simplicity that made the early brand easy to navigate.

Retail Expansion Changed Rhode From DTC-Only to Omnichannel

For its first years, Rhode built the business largely through its own ecommerce channel. That gave the company direct control over product presentation, customer data, launch timing, waitlists, and the relationship between social attention and checkout.

The next stage changed the distribution model. After e.l.f. Beauty completed the acquisition, Rhode launched at Sephora in North America and expanded to the U.K. in 2025. In 2026, e.l.f. announced a wider Sephora rollout across European markets. Rhode’s own current FAQ also lists Sephora in the U.S., Canada, and U.K., alongside MECCA availability in Australia and New Zealand.

This expansion is important because retail is not only a sales channel. It changes how people discover, test, compare, and purchase products. Rhode now has to maintain the same brand clarity across its own storefront, retail shelves, retailer product pages, testers, merchandising, and in-store customer experience.

The Trademark Dispute Ended Through Settlement, Not a Court Win

Rhode’s naming history also needs careful wording. A fashion company called RHODE sued the skincare business in June 2022, alleging trademark infringement. The court denied the fashion company’s request for a preliminary injunction, which allowed Bieber’s brand to keep operating while the case continued.

The case was later dismissed in September 2023 after the parties told the court they had reached agreement on the core terms of a settlement. That is different from saying the court ruled that Rhode had won the trademark dispute. For founders, the practical lesson is to conduct brand naming and trademark review early, because a name that works creatively can still create legal and operational risk.

What Business Owners Can Learn From Rhode in 2026

Rhode’s marketing strategy is useful because the system is consistent. Product assortment, founder content, naming, packaging, photography, ecommerce, retail expansion, and campaign concepts all reinforce a recognizable point of view. The transferable lesson is not to copy glazed skin or food-inspired launches. It is to make each part of the customer experience feel like it came from the same brand.

  • Build the brand world before scaling media. Clear branding gives content, packaging, web design, and campaigns a common set of rules.
  • Keep hero products easy to understand. A sharp product story gives creators and customers something specific to repeat.
  • Design for sharing without making every asset look like a social post. Packaging, texture, naming, and photography can create natural moments people want to capture.
  • Use scarcity carefully. Waitlists and limited releases can concentrate attention, but they should not become a substitute for reliable supply and customer trust.
  • Make the path from content to purchase simple. Social interest should lead to a product page, shade choice, routine, or checkout without unnecessary friction.
  • Build a brand that can outgrow the founder. Celebrity or founder visibility can open the door, but the identity has to remain recognizable when someone else is telling the story.
