Search interest around the most expensive marketing campaigns of 2025 mixes several different kinds of spending: media prices, full campaign budgets, and large campaigns whose totals were never disclosed. This article separates those categories instead of pretending they form one precise ranking. The clearest reported costs came from Super Bowl LIX media and Friend’s New York subway buy, while campaigns from Anthropic, Fanta, Nike, and Coca-Cola were described at scale without comparable public budgets. For a branding agency or marketing agency, the useful lesson is how each investment matched the audience, brand strategy, and moment, not which brand spent the most.

For additional 2025 campaign examples, our fall marketing campaign roundup focuses on creative format and timing rather than spend.

At a glance

  • Super Bowl LIX media averaged close to $8 million for a 30-second spot. That is an airtime benchmark, not a complete campaign budget. (CBS MoneyWatch)

  • The Verge reported that OpenAI spent about $14 million on its 60-second Super Bowl debut. The article supports the media figure, not a full all-in campaign total that includes every production and extension cost. (The Verge)

  • Axios described Anthropic’s “Keep thinking” launch as a multimillion-dollar campaign across film, streaming, print, out-of-home, influencers, and podcasts. It did not publish an exact total. (Axios)

  • Friend’s New York subway campaign had a reported spend of more than $1 million. Fanta’s global Halloween campaign was large in scope, but its total budget was not disclosed in the reporting used here. (Business Insider)

1) OpenAI’s Super Bowl Debut: About $14M in Reported Media Spend

OpenAI’s first Super Bowl commercial is the clearest single 2025 example in this list with a reported eight-figure media figure. The Verge reported about $14 million for the 60-second Super Bowl LIX spot. The creative used a pointillist animation to place ChatGPT inside a broader history of human tools and inventions. That $14 million figure should be read as the reported Super Bowl advertising cost, not as a verified all-in budget for production, PR, and every follow-on asset. (The Verge)

  • The reported media figure was about $14 million for 60 seconds.

  • Production and downstream campaign costs were not separately disclosed in the cited report.

  • The strategic lesson is to use expensive reach for a message that can be understood in one viewing.

2) Super Bowl LIX: Close to $8M per 30 Seconds as a Media Benchmark

Super Bowl LIX is better treated as a media-price benchmark than as one campaign. CBS MoneyWatch reported an average close to $8 million for a 30-second spot. Advertisers then had to fund creative, talent, production, PR, digital extensions, and other activation costs on top of that airtime. The number shows why Super Bowl advertising sits at the top end of U.S. mass-reach media, but it does not establish which advertiser had the largest total campaign budget. (CBS MoneyWatch)

  • The roughly $8 million figure refers to a 30-second media unit, not the complete campaign.

  • Advertisers often added production, talent, teasers, social cutdowns, retail, and PR around the broadcast buy.

  • A high-cost media moment is useful only when the brand has a plan to extend the asset beyond the game.

3) Anthropic’s “Keep thinking”: Multimillion-Dollar Campaign, Exact Total Undisclosed

Axios described Anthropic’s first major Claude brand campaign as a multimillion-dollar effort. The 90-second hero film was only one part of the buy: the campaign also ran across sports, Netflix, Hulu, print, out-of-home in a dozen cities, influencers, and podcasts. That makes it a useful example for B2B marketing because a company known for enterprise AI invested in broad consumer awareness. The exact campaign total was not published. (Axios)

  • The source supports “multimillion-dollar campaign,” not a specific budget.

  • The 90-second film anchored a larger international media system rather than representing the whole spend.

  • The campaign used one positioning line across enterprise and consumer-facing channels.

4) Fanta Halloween 2025: Large Global Activation, Budget Undisclosed

Fanta’s 2025 Halloween campaign was large in scope, but there is no disclosed budget in the source used here. Coca-Cola partnered with Universal Pictures and Blumhouse on horror-character packaging, cinema and retail activations, influencer content, limited products, and the Haunted Fanta Factory in New York. The company later said Fanta Halloween activated in roughly 50 markets. That makes it a useful example of entertainment marketing and food and beverage marketing, but not a campaign that can be ranked by total cost from public evidence. (Business Insider)

  • Confirmed scope included licensed horror IP, limited packaging, retail and cinema activations, digital content, and a New York experience.

  • The source does not disclose a total spend, so this article does not assign one.

  • The strategic lesson is to use one seasonal platform across packaging, retail, media, and physical experience.

5) Nike’s “So Win”: Super Bowl Brand Anthem, Budget Undisclosed

Nike introduced “So Win” during Super Bowl LIX with a 60-second anthem centered on women athletes including Jordan Chiles, Caitlin Clark, Sabrina Ionescu, Sha’Carri Richardson, A’ja Wilson, and Sophia Wilson. The campaign included athlete extensions, still photography, and social content. Its total budget was not disclosed in the cited source, so it should not be called one of the most expensive campaigns as a verified fact. It is included because the campaign shows how a branding platform can extend one message across athlete stories and multiple formats. (Marketing Dive)

  • The campaign launched during the Super Bowl and expanded into athlete, photography, and social assets.

  • The budget was not disclosed in the cited reporting.

  • The useful lesson is message consistency across a large roster of recognizable athletes.

6) Coca-Cola’s Gen Z Global Platform: Budget Undisclosed

Coca-Cola’s “Enjoy the moment” platform launched in North America and then expanded to key global markets with films, talent including Tyla and Lamine Yamal, packaging and retail support, and U.S. sweepstakes activity. Coca-Cola described it as a global campaign, but did not disclose a total budget in the source. The example is relevant to visual identity because one recognizable brand system had to work across markets. For companies planning large U.S. rollouts, U.S. branding and marketing support is most useful when national consistency and local execution are planned together. (Coca-Cola Company)

  • The campaign was global in scope, but the source does not provide a comparable all-in spend.

  • Its creative system carried the same idea across films, talent, retail, packaging, and regional execution.

  • Global scale should not be converted into an invented budget estimate.

7) Friend’s NYC Subway Campaign: More Than $1M in Reported OOH Spend

Friend spent more than $1 million on a New York subway campaign with over 11,000 car ads, 1,000 platform posters, and 130 urban panels, according to Business Insider. The campaign drew significant criticism and widespread defacement. Friend’s CEO said traffic and sales increased, but those are company claims rather than independently audited ROI figures. This is a good reason to separate reported spend from marketing performance metrics. (Business Insider)

  • The reported out-of-home spend exceeded $1 million.

  • The scale of the subway inventory is documented; the campaign’s total all-in cost is not.

  • Controversy created attention, but attention and independently verified return on investment are not the same measure.

FAQ

Why does Super Bowl LIX appear in a list about expensive 2025 campaigns?

Because CBS MoneyWatch reported an average close to $8 million for a 30-second spot. That figure is a media-price benchmark, not a full campaign budget for every advertiser.

Was Anthropic’s 90-second film itself a disclosed multimillion-dollar production?

The cited Axios report describes the overall “Keep thinking” campaign as multimillion-dollar. It does not say the film alone cost that amount, so this article treats the figure as a campaign-level descriptor.

Can Fanta, Nike, or Coca-Cola be ranked precisely by 2025 campaign spend?

Not from the sources used here. Their campaigns were large in scope, but comparable total budgets were not disclosed, so they are examples of high-scale campaigns rather than verified positions in a cost ranking.

What should a smaller brand take from these campaigns?

Choose a moment, audience, and measurement plan that fit the business. A single-market activation, creator program, or repeatable video format can be more useful than buying scale the team cannot support.

Does a larger budget make a campaign more valuable?

No. Cost and value are different questions. Reach, brand lift, qualified demand, sales, and long-term reuse need to be measured separately against the campaign’s objective.

The ROI lens

The reliable conclusion is narrower than the original ranking implied. Super Bowl media prices, OpenAI’s reported 60-second buy, Anthropic’s multimillion-dollar campaign descriptor, and Friend’s subway spend give us some real cost anchors. The other examples show scale without comparable disclosed totals. Before approving a large campaign, define the outcome, separate media from production and activation costs, and decide how the work will be measured. A focused marketing consultation can help build that measurement plan before the spend is committed.

The phrase “most expensive rebrands of 2025” suggests a cost ranking public evidence does not support. None of the seven examples below has a comparable, disclosed total budget. What the sources do show is rollout scope. This article therefore treats them as high-scope 2025 brand changes, not a ranking. For a branding agency, that distinction matters because a rebrand is an operating program as much as a design project.

At a glance

  • No comparable total budget is publicly disclosed for these seven examples.

  • Lay’s and Domino’s documented broad packaging and brand-system changes across large consumer footprints.

  • TIC Solutions was a post-merger corporate rename; Long John Silver’s and Colgate-Palmolive described brand or corporate identity refreshes.

  • Dropbox’s current guidelines show a developed brand system but do not establish a 2025 rebrand date or cost.

The data behind the picks

Where cost is undisclosed, this article does not turn company size or location count into a dollar estimate. A rebranding program can involve strategy, naming, identity, packaging, digital products, signage, training, and rollout management.

Use brand research to decide what actually needs to change before estimating implementation scope. Our guide to the most expensive marketing campaigns in 2025 uses the same disclosed-spend distinction.

Lay’s: global packaging and identity overhaul

Lay’s described its October 2025 work as the largest brand redesign in its nearly 100-year history. The global identity updated the logo, color system, photography, and packaging while the U.S. product line also changed ingredients. That is a substantial food and beverage marketing program, but neither source publishes a total rebrand cost. (Fast Company; PepsiCo)

  • The documented scope includes a global visual identity and packaging redesign.

  • The rollout is substantial, but no public total budget supports a cost ranking.

Domino’s: first brand refresh in 13 years

Domino’s called its October 2025 work its first brand refresh in 13 years. It included brighter packaging, a new font, digital and print materials, in-store graphics, team-member gear, and the “Dommmino’s” jingle. Domino’s said the look would roll out across the U.S. and multiple international markets. Its system had more than 21,500 stores, but the company did not say every store would receive every element at once or disclose a total budget. (CNN; Domino’s)

  • Confirmed touchpoints include boxes, web and app, print, in-store graphics, advertising, and team-member gear.

  • The public sources do not provide a comparable total cost.

Cracker Barrel: rebrand rollout, backlash, and reversal

Cracker Barrel introduced a simplified logo during a broader 2025 brand-evolution program, then reversed the logo after backlash and later paused remodels. The episode involved design, communications, and operational change, but the sources do not publish a standalone rebrand budget. (Associated Press; brand statement: Cracker Barrel)

  • The logo was introduced and reversed; restaurant remodel plans were later paused.

  • A reversal can create additional work, but its total cost was not disclosed.

Long John Silver’s: identity shift to “CHICKEN + SEAFOOD”

Long John Silver’s introduced a refreshed logo that replaced the fish illustration with a stylized chicken and added a “CHICKEN + SEAFOOD” lock-up. The company said the design was rolling out across digital platforms and highlighted it with a NASCAR vehicle wrap. That supports calling it a 2025 brand refresh, not a documented chain-wide physical rebrand with a known budget. (PR Newswire)

  • Confirmed scope includes the logo, lock-up, digital rollout, and motorsport activation.

  • The source does not disclose a total spend or full physical-system rollout.

Acuren → TIC Solutions: post-merger corporate rename

Acuren announced that the combined Acuren and NV5 enterprise would rebrand as TIC Solutions, effective October 10, 2025. The announcement described more than 11,000 employees and 250+ locations, while Acuren, NV5, and other legacy brands would remain customer-facing. The stock continued under ticker TIC. This is a large corporate naming and architecture exercise, but no seven- or eight-figure rebrand budget was disclosed. (Acuren IR)

Keeping legacy customer-facing brands also makes this a useful brand architecture example.

  • Confirmed scope includes a corporate rename, post-merger identity, investor communications, and enterprise governance.

  • The public announcement supports complexity, not a specific rebrand cost.

Dropbox: current brand system, but 2025 rebrand evidence is incomplete

Dropbox’s current brand-guidelines site documents a broad identity toolkit across logos, icons, illustration, language, and other assets, making it a useful technology brand system example. However, the page does not by itself establish a company-wide 2025 rebrand or its cost. (Dropbox Brand)

  • The source documents Dropbox’s present identity system and governance materials.

  • It does not independently establish a 2025 rebrand date or budget.

Colgate-Palmolive: refreshed corporate brand identity

Colgate-Palmolive introduced a refreshed corporate identity in August 2025 with a brighter blue, revised CP logo, “Make More Smiles” tagline, and digital-first graphic system. It launched on the U.S. corporate website and global corporate social channels, with other corporate-brand touchpoints phasing in over time. This was a corporate identity refresh, not evidence that every consumer brand was rebranded at once. (Colgate-Palmolive)

  • Confirmed scope includes the corporate logo, palette, graphic system, website, social channels, and phased corporate touchpoints.

  • The source does not disclose a total budget.

FAQ

Why focus on scope instead of hard dollar amounts?

Because these companies did not publish comparable total budgets. Scope can show implementation complexity, but it cannot prove which rebrand cost the most.

What makes a QSR rebrand especially pricey?

Restaurant systems can require updates across packaging, digital channels, uniforms, signage, training, and franchise materials. Cost depends on which assets change, rollout speed, and who bears the expense.

Do reversals still count as “expensive”?

A reversal can still create design, production, communication, and change-management costs. Without disclosed figures, those costs should not be estimated as a total.

Which brands that invested in a rebrand in 2025 had the widest consumer reach?

The sources do not support a precise reach ranking. Lay’s and Domino’s operate at large consumer scale, while TIC Solutions is primarily a corporate and B2B identity change.

What’s the common thread across these overhauls?

The common thread is operational scope across packaging, digital products, physical environments, partner materials, and communications. Scope is important, but it is not a substitute for disclosed cost data.

The 2025 rebrand takeaway

What the evidence shows is a set of consequential 2025 brand changes, not a defensible cost ranking. For organizations planning U.S. branding support across many touchpoints, the budget should come from the actual rollout plan rather than a headline estimate. A focused marketing consultation can connect the brand change to launch, communications, and measurement before implementation begins.

Sephora has built one of beauty retail's most recognizable marketing systems by combining product curation, loyalty, stores and digital experiences rather than treating them as separate channels. Sephora describes itself as the world's leading global prestige beauty retail brand, with more than 3,400 stores across 37 markets and close to 500 curated brands alongside Sephora Collection. That scale makes its marketing strategy especially useful for understanding how a retailer can keep discovery, personalization and service consistent across physical and digital touchpoints. Sephora Newsroom provides the current global figures.

The strategy can still be understood through the 4 Ps of marketing: Product, Price, Place and Promotion. What makes Sephora distinctive is how those four elements connect. The assortment creates discovery, loyalty changes the value equation, stores and ecommerce reinforce one another, and promotion turns education and community into recurring reasons to return.

Product: Curation, Private Label and Beauty Discovery

Sephora's product strategy is built on curation rather than simply carrying as many items as possible. The retailer spans makeup, skincare, fragrance, haircare and tools while serving different routines, skin types and budgets. That breadth gives Sephora multiple discovery paths, but the assortment still has to feel edited enough that customers can navigate it.

This is where brand research and customer insight matter. Retailers have to understand which categories, trends and emerging brands deserve space without making the store or website feel unstructured. Sephora's current global media kit says its assortment is close to 500 brands, giving the retailer breadth while preserving a curated prestige positioning.

A key component is the retailer's own Sephora Collection. The private label gives Sephora more control over price points, product development and exclusivity while strengthening its own brand identity inside a store filled with third-party brands.

Sephora also uses partnerships and exclusive launches to keep the assortment current. In 2026, the retailer began rolling out an OLIVE YOUNG-curated K-beauty assortment, starting with 19 brands in more than 500 U.S. stores and online. That move shows how Sephora can use outside expertise to accelerate category discovery while keeping the experience under the Sephora umbrella. For broader context on the category itself, Brand Vision's analysis of Korean skincare marketing explains why K-beauty has become so influential. Sephora Newsroom documents the 2026 launch.

The mix spans long-established names such as Lancôme and Clinique as well as newer brands such as Rare Beauty. That mix lets Sephora serve familiar demand while still giving shoppers a reason to browse for what is new.

Product curation therefore acts as marketing. Each new brand, exclusive launch and category edit can create a discovery moment without requiring Sephora to reinvent its core retail identity.

Price: Value Comes From Choice and Loyalty

Sephora serves a wide range of price points within prestige beauty, from relatively accessible products and Sephora Collection to luxury fragrances, skincare and makeup. That range gives customers room to trade up or down while staying inside the same retailer.

Beauty Insider changes the value equation because price is not only about a shelf tag. Members earn points and can access rewards, events, offers and other benefits across stores and digital channels. Sephora said the free program reached more than 45 million members in North America in 2025, making loyalty a major retention and first-party relationship layer. Sephora Newsroom reported that membership figure.

That structure helps Sephora compete on more than discounting. Customers can compare brands and prices, but the rewards program, samples, services and exclusives can make the overall relationship more valuable than a single transaction.

Place: Sephora's Omnichannel Retail Model

Sephora's distribution model integrates stores, ecommerce and mobile into one retail system. The company now reports more than 3,400 stores across 37 markets, alongside ecommerce and digital platforms. That global footprint gives the brand physical discovery spaces while its digital channels extend assortment, education and convenience beyond the store.

Stores remain important because beauty is tactile. Testers, services, advisors and events let customers compare shades, textures and routines in person. Those experiences also create reasons to visit that go beyond simply picking a product off a shelf.

Sephora's website and app extend that discovery process with reviews, product detail, recommendations, wishlists, tutorials and virtual tools. Thoughtful interaction design matters here because shade exploration, virtual try-on, filtering and saved products all depend on clear feedback and low-friction choices. Product and category architecture also create an ecommerce SEO opportunity when shoppers search for specific brands, routines and product types.

Convenience connects the channels. Sephora Canada currently offers buy online, pick up in store, fast delivery, same-day options and free standard shipping for Beauty Insider members, depending on the service and location. These options let customers choose speed and channel without leaving the Sephora ecosystem.

The result is a connected customer journey rather than separate "online" and "offline" businesses. A user experience can start with social discovery, continue through search or the app, move into a store consultation and end with pickup or delivery.

Promotion: Education, Creators and Community

Sephora's promotion works because advertising is only one part of the system. Social content, creator partnerships, product education, loyalty benefits, events and exclusive launches all create reasons for customers to engage between major campaigns.

Digital content is particularly important in beauty because tutorials, reviews and demonstrations can show shade, texture, technique and results more clearly than a static product claim. Sephora uses platforms such as Instagram, YouTube and TikTok alongside brand and creator partnerships, giving products multiple paths into the customer's consideration set.

In-store events and beauty services add another layer. Workshops, consultations, product sampling and brand events make the store an education and community space, not only a checkout point. That can deepen trust while giving customers practical help with routines and product selection.

Exclusive launches and collaborations reinforce the same pattern: discovery feels more valuable when the customer believes Sephora can introduce something worth paying attention to. The promotional engine is therefore tied directly to the assortment and experience rather than operating as a separate communications layer.

Sephora's marketing success comes from making the 4 Ps work together. Product curation creates discovery, loyalty adds value beyond price, omnichannel retail makes the brand easier to use, and promotion turns education and community into repeat engagement. For consumer brands trying to connect those pieces more deliberately, a focused marketing consultation can help identify where positioning, channel experience or conversion is breaking down.

The Share a Coke marketing campaign began in Australia in 2011 and turned Coca-Cola packaging into a personal invitation: find a familiar name, give the drink to that person, and share the moment. The idea connected personalization with a simple social action, rather than asking people to circulate an ordinary advertisement.

For founders, marketers, and students, the useful question is not just why names attracted attention. It is how packaging, brand recognition, retail availability, and participation worked together. This Brand Vision case study examines the campaign's origins, documented results, and practical lessons without treating every later promotion as part of the original launch.

Where Share a Coke Started and Who It Targeted

Coca-Cola South Pacific called the initiative Project Connect, with the aim of strengthening its relationship with young adults. Its initial packaging featured 150 popular first names. Coca-Cola's retrospective on the marketing strategy identifies Ogilvy as the agency selected to develop the idea.

The business problem was familiarity without a compelling new reason to choose the product. A name created a different shopping question: not only whether to buy Coke, but who a particular bottle could be for. The campaign changed the invitation around the drink rather than its underlying flavour.

That distinction matters when studying Coca-Cola's broader marketing strategy. Share a Coke was a specific campaign within an established brand, not a replacement for its positioning, distribution, or entire identity.

Why the Personalization Worked

Recognition Did Not Require a Unique Product

Calling the idea deep personalization can obscure how straightforward the original experience was. Many shoppers could buy the same name. The connection came from what that name meant to the person choosing the bottle, not from a unique drink manufactured for each individual.

This is mass personalization: a shared product offers a choice that feels personally relevant. It is different from predicting an individual's preferences through their purchase history. The named packs let the shopper make the match, so the basic experience did not depend on identifying that person online.

A useful comparison is Spotify Wrapped's approach to personalization, which turns a listener's own activity into shareable content. Coke's name-based packaging and a personalized listening recap use different inputs. The planning question is which input your audience would actually value, not how much data you can collect.

The Name Suggested Someone to Share With

The lasting lesson is that personalization can feel social, not just segmented. A familiar name gives the buyer a possible recipient. The phrase "Share a Coke" then supplies an action, connecting recognition with a small gesture rather than leaving the personalized detail as decoration.

Consider a hypothetical shopper who notices a friend's name while buying lunch. Giving that bottle to the friend supplies its own context; there is no elaborate campaign explanation to repeat. Taking a photo becomes an optional extension of the moment, not the only way to participate.

For a B2C marketing strategy, this is a useful distinction. A promotion can give customers a reason to involve someone else without requiring them to become public advocates or write a testimonial.

The Brand Still Had to Be Recognizable

Names changed the focal point of the pack, but the idea still relied on people recognizing it as Coke. The design lesson is not to remove branding indiscriminately. It is to decide which elements can vary while the product remains identifiable.

That is a visual identity decision. Colour, typography, layout, and packaging shape need to work together so that a personalized element does not erase the brand. A less familiar business should test recognition before making the customer's name more prominent than its own.

How Packaging, Social Media, and Activations Worked Together

Coca-Cola's June 2014 U.S. launch announcement described 250 names on 20-ounce bottles across Coke, Diet Coke, and Coke Zero. It also outlined television and cinema advertising, digital billboards, virtual bottles, and a travelling customization tour. The #ShareaCoke hashtag connected customer photos with an online gallery and potential billboard exposure.

These channels had different jobs. Packaging made the idea visible at the point of purchase. Advertising explained the invitation. Customization events offered another way to participate, while social platforms let a personal interaction reach people beyond the original exchange.

Seen as a customer journey, the campaign connected four actions:

  1. Notice a name or message on a familiar product.
  2. Choose a bottle for yourself or someone you know.
  3. Give it to that person or enjoy the drink together.
  4. Optionally photograph, post, or share the experience online.

This helps explain the role of user-generated content (UGC). The brand provided a prompt, but the customer's relationship supplied the story. It is also why the campaign should not be described as social media alone: the offline action had value even when nobody posted it.

Share a Coke Campaign Results: What the Evidence Shows

The results are more useful when the market, period, and measurement are kept separate. A total number of promotional packs sold is not the same as additional sales caused by the promotion. Nor is dollar-sales growth interchangeable with growth in the amount of drink sold.

Australia's First Summer

In its September 2014 retrospective, Coca-Cola reported selling more than 250 million named bottles and cans during the first Australian summer. That establishes the scale of the named-pack rollout. It does not mean 250 million additional purchases, 250 million different buyers, or a measured return on advertising spend.

U.S. Retail Performance in 2014

BevNET's September 9, 2014 reporting described a Wells Fargo Securities analysis of Nielsen retail data. For the four weeks ending August 30, Coca-Cola's carbonated soft-drink products grew 3.7% in dollar sales and 2.4% in volume compared with the same period a year earlier. The report attributed the analyst's positive assessment partly to Share a Coke.

Those figures concern the company's carbonated soft-drink products in the measured retail data, not named bottles alone or worldwide revenue. They show growth during the promotion, but do not isolate what would have happened without it. Pricing, distribution, other advertising, and the mix of products sold also matter when interpreting commercial results.

Why One Market Cannot Stand for Every Market

The picture was not uniformly positive. Marketing Week reported in August 2014 that UK Coca-Cola retail sales value fell 2.1% and volume fell 6.2% in IRI's 52-week period ending July 19, 2014. The same report noted growth in single-pack sales and a strong prior-year comparison. That annual window is not comparable with the short U.S. window and includes time outside the summer campaign.

The contrast is a warning against a universal success percentage, not proof that the campaign caused the UK decline. Evaluating Share a Coke requires separating a strong creative idea from its effect in a particular market. The evidence above also does not establish campaign profit or long-term customer retention.

How the Campaign Adapted Across Markets and Years

Localizing popular names & phrases is more than translation. A campaign team needs to consider spellings, naming conventions, language, and who is left out of the available choices. A familiar invitation can travel, but its details still need local judgment.

Later executions added new ways to enter the experience. In Australia, a January 2020 Alexa promotion let people start with a voice request. They then received a text message directing them to the Share a Coke website. This was a voice-to-web handoff, not an entirely voice-based ordering process.

Coca-Cola's March 2025 relaunch announcement described on-pack QR codes and an app leading to a digital hub, additional name customization, and a Memory Maker for personalized videos. These were later extensions of the sharing idea, not features of the 2011 launch.

The useful lesson is to let the physical and digital experiences reinforce each other. A new channel earns its place when it helps someone discover, personalize, receive, or share the product. Adding technology without improving that journey makes the campaign more complicated, not necessarily more meaningful.

What Other Brands Should Be Careful About Copying

A name is not automatically a benefit. The product, occasion, and relationship still need to make sense. Personalization that asks for effort without providing something worth receiving can become an obstacle rather than an attraction.

There are practical trade-offs to resolve before launch:

  • A limited name list can make some customers feel excluded. Decide what useful alternative exists when a name is missing.
  • More packaging variants create production and stock-planning questions. Test whether personalization is worth the extra handling, waste, and complexity.
  • Custom text needs clear limits and a review process. Do not assume every submission will be appropriate to print or display.
  • A novelty purchase does not establish loyalty. Measure whether customers return once the personalized pack is no longer new.

These are particularly relevant to food and beverage marketing, where packaging must work on a shelf and through a real supply chain. A smaller brand might test a gift sleeve or message card before committing to a large run of variable packaging.

How to Apply the Principles Without Copying the Bottles

Start With a Customer Occasion

Choose a real moment your product can support: thanking someone, marking a milestone, sharing a break, or celebrating a shared interest. Explore the emotional aspects of your product through what customers already do, rather than inventing a sentimental story around an unrelated offer.

Use brand research to test whether the occasion and proposed choice make sense to the intended audience. Ask what people would select, who they would share it with, and what might stop them. Treat an appealing concept as a hypothesis until people can use it.

Design for Sharing on Purpose

Define the action you want someone to take immediately after encountering the campaign. Giving a product, sending a message, inviting a friend, and publishing a photo are different behaviours. Choose the one that supports your brand strategy, and make it clear without a long set of instructions.

For example, a hypothetical coffee company could test a small range of thank-you sleeves for customers buying a drink for a colleague. That tests the social gesture without copying Coca-Cola's name list or assuming a digital tool is necessary.

Make Participation Easy to Understand

Build a personalization option that is easy to spot and explain. In a digital experience, UI/UX design should make the available choices, preview, and next action clear. Test missing-name cases, long entries, and the experience on a phone, not just the ideal desktop journey.

The campaign's website also needs to explain what is available, how to participate, and what happens after submission. Consistent web design helps the landing page continue the promise made on the pack or advertisement, rather than introducing a different message and visual language.

Build a Repeatable Campaign, Not a One-Off Stunt

Decide which parts can change between releases and which must remain recognizable. The occasion, names, or format might vary while the core invitation stays stable. Consistent branding gives those variations a common identity.

Operational leadership matters here: someone needs to own the handoffs between creative, production, retail, customer support, and measurement. Before launch, agree who approves personalized content and who resolves problems when the promised experience cannot be delivered.

Measure Participation and Business Outcomes Separately

Choose a comparison period or test group before launching. Track completed personalizations, shares, purchases, repeat purchases, and fulfilment costs as distinct measures. Where possible, compare similar stores or audiences exposed and unexposed to the promotion, noting differences in price and availability.

A campaign with many photos but little additional purchasing presents a different decision from one that sells well but costs too much to fulfil. Keep the measure tied to the original objective, then refine the participation experience rather than simply increasing advertising.

Share a Coke's enduring lesson is not that every brand needs names on packaging. It is that a clear invitation can connect a familiar product to a meaningful action between people. The execution still needs an appropriate audience, recognizable design, workable operations, and evidence of what changed.

Shipping infrastructure has evolved from a back-office fulfillment task into a strategic system that influences profitability, customer trust, and a company’s ability to scale.

At a glance

  • Shipping impacts conversion, margins, and retention, not just delivery times.
  • Fragmented tools create hidden costs, errors, and slower fulfillment.
  • Strong shipping systems centralize workflows and make cost visibility measurable.
  • Leaders track per-order economics and operational friction, not just total spend.
  • In 2026, shipping capability is a competitive differentiator for ecommerce brands.

Shipping is now a growth lever

Shipping is no longer a neutral operational expense. It shapes growth outcomes across the customer journey.

Modern businesses increasingly see shipping influence performance in three areas:

Checkout conversion
Unclear or inconsistent shipping rates remain a common cause of checkout abandonment. When customers cannot predict delivery cost or speed, they hesitate or exit.

Margin protection
Carrier fees, label inefficiencies, and manual errors quietly erode margins. Without per-order visibility, teams struggle to understand the true cost of fulfilling different products, regions, and service levels.

Customer experience
Delivery speed, tracking accuracy, and communication directly impact trust. Late deliveries or missing tracking updates reduce repeat purchase rates, even when the product itself performs well.

In this environment, shipping becomes a lever that affects revenue, retention, and reputation.

How Shipping Infrastructure Affects Conversion Rate and LTV

Shipping is one of the fastest ways to lose a customer before they ever buy. Unclear rates, slow delivery estimates, or surprise fees create hesitation at checkout, which directly lowers conversion rate. On the flip side, a predictable shipping experience with accurate ETAs and clean tracking reduces drop-off because customers feel confident clicking “buy.” After purchase, shipping continues to shape loyalty. Fast fulfillment, fewer errors, and proactive updates reduce refunds and support tickets, which protects margins and improves the chance of a repeat order. Over time, that reliability compounds into higher retention and stronger lifetime value (LTV), because customers come back to brands that feel consistent and easy to buy from.

What “shipping infrastructure” actually means

Shipping infrastructure is not a single tool. It is a system.

In 2026, the term refers to the combined logic, software, and hardware that governs how orders move from checkout to delivery. At a minimum, modern shipping infrastructure includes:

  • Rate logic and label automation that reduce manual steps
  • Multi-carrier flexibility to avoid dependency on one provider
  • Per-order cost visibility to understand unit economics
  • Hardware integration (for example, faster label printing) as part of the ops stack
  • Cross-platform access across desktop and mobile for distributed teams

The difference between basic fulfillment and strategic shipping is how integrated and automated these components are.

The metrics leaders track when shipping becomes strategic

When shipping becomes strategic, the metrics change.

High-performing teams do not track shipping only as a monthly total. They track indicators that reveal efficiency, scalability, and friction.

Common leadership-level metrics include:

  • Cost per fulfilled order (not just average shipping spend)
  • Label creation time (a signal of operational friction)
  • Error rates (mislabels, returns, re-shipments)
  • Delivery promise accuracy (whether expectations match reality)

These metrics connect shipping directly to profitability and customer satisfaction.

The hidden bottleneck: tool fragmentation

One of the most common barriers to scalable shipping is fragmentation.

Many organizations rely on disconnected tools:

  • One system for orders
  • Another for carrier rates
  • Separate hardware workflows or manual printing
  • Standalone tracking or notification tools

Each handoff introduces delay, inconsistency, and risk. As order volume grows, fragmentation compounds inefficiencies instead of absorbing scale.

Fragmented stacks also make adaptation harder. Adding a new carrier, entering a new market, or supporting mobile workflows often requires new tools instead of simple configuration.

How modern teams operationalize shipping

High-performing teams treat shipping as infrastructure, not a collection of apps.

In practice, this means centralizing shipping into one automation-ready system that supports multiple carriers, faster label workflows, and standardized fulfillment logic. The goal is to scale output without scaling headcount at the same rate.

Centralization improves accountability as well. When shipping data lives in one place, leaders can trace cost, performance, and outcomes back to individual orders and decisions.

What infrastructure-first shipping looks like in practice

Infrastructure-first shipping models typically combine multi-carrier workflows, automated label generation, and optional hardware acceleration in one environment.

For teams evaluating tools that support that model, Rollo Ship is one example that’s often used for centralized workflows across common ecommerce channels. The strategic takeaway is not the tool itself. It is the model: centralized, flexible, and automation-ready shipping infrastructure.

What changes when shipping becomes infrastructure

When shipping is treated as a system rather than a task, it expands what the business can execute competitively.

At a strategic level, infrastructure-first shipping enables:

  • Faster market expansion through repeatable workflows and carrier flexibility
  • Stronger unit economics through per-order cost visibility
  • Lower dependence on operational headcount as volume grows

This shifts shipping from a limiting function into a scalable growth mechanism.

Decision framework: Is shipping a strategy or a liability?

Shipping remains an operational liability when systems cannot:

  • Support multiple carriers within a unified interface
  • Surface real-time shipping costs at the order level
  • Function consistently across mobile and desktop environments
  • Integrate automation as volume increases
  • Provide clear visibility into per-order economics

When these capabilities are absent, shipping behaves like a reactive cost center rather than a strategic enabler.

Final perspective

Shipping infrastructure has moved from the margins of operations into the core of business strategy. The brands that outperform are not necessarily those with the cheapest rates. They are the ones with systems that provide clarity, flexibility, and control at scale. Treating shipping as infrastructure aligns fulfillment with growth, profitability, and long-term competitiveness.

FAQ

How should a business evaluate shipping software integrations?
Start with the systems you rely on most (your ecommerce platform, marketplaces, inventory tools, and customer communications). A strong shipping platform should reduce manual entry, keep order data consistent, and support your carrier and workflow needs without workarounds.

What does “centralized shipping” actually improve?
Centralization reduces handoffs, speeds up label creation, lowers error rates, and makes per-order shipping costs visible. That visibility helps teams improve unit economics and make better decisions about service levels, pricing, and shipping policies.

Useful UX metrics answer a question that sessions, clicks, and scroll depth cannot answer alone: is the experience helping people complete their task and choose the brand with confidence? A dashboard becomes more useful when it connects activity to a clear user outcome.

The right UX metrics reduce ambiguity. A clear scorecard helps marketing explain performance, gives product teams evidence for prioritizing fixes, and shows leaders which parts of the journey need closer investigation. It should support decisions, not just add another layer of reporting.

This guide focuses on three measures for a practical UX scorecard: task success rate, lead quality, and user confidence. Task success measures usability directly. Lead quality connects the experience to business outcomes, while confidence captures how users feel about a decision. Together, they help teams investigate performance without treating every change as proof of UX impact.

Why UX Scorecards Need to Measure Outcomes

Acquiring more traffic does not resolve a confusing experience. When people cannot find the right information or complete a form, additional acquisition spend can send more visitors into the same problem. A scorecard helps separate traffic volume from the site’s ability to support a useful outcome.

Trust deserves attention alongside completion. Visitors may need clearer pricing, evidence, or next-step expectations before they act. Measuring those questions is more useful than assuming that a longer session or another page view means the experience is working.

A modern UX scorecard helps brands do three things consistently. It shows where users succeed, what kind of leads the experience produces, and whether people feel confident enough to continue.

At a Glance: Three Measures for Your UX Scorecard

Task success rate
A direct measure of whether users can complete critical actions. It is a straightforward starting point for a usability scorecard. (NNGroup)

Lead quality
A measure of whether enquiries meet agreed criteria for fit and intent. It reflects acquisition, messaging, UX, and sales follow-up, so it is a shared business outcome rather than a pure usability measure.

User confidence
A reported measure of how sure users feel about a choice. Read it alongside task outcomes and user feedback rather than assuming that confidence guarantees a conversion or a return visit.

How We Define “Good” UX Metrics

Good UX metrics are decision tools. If a metric cannot inform a clear next step, it becomes noise. Use consistent definitions, measurement methods, and context. Focused UX research helps establish which tasks matter to users before a team decides what to track.

A practical UX scorecard also recognizes that “more” is not always better. Time on page can mean confusion. Scroll depth can mean hunting. Higher engagement can be a symptom of friction, depending on the task. (NNGroup)

Use three principles when building the scorecard:

  • Measure outcomes on real tasks, not only page-level activity.
  • Pair behavioral signals with one simple attitudinal signal.
  • Track trends and deltas after changes, not isolated numbers.

Task Success Rate: The Metric That Cuts Through Opinions

If users cannot complete a core task, even clear brand messaging may not be enough to move them forward. Task success rate tells you whether the experience works for the job the user came to do. It is a useful starting point, not a complete assessment of experience quality.

Task success rate also gives teams a shared question to investigate. Instead of debating only what looks better, they can compare whether users complete the same task. Keep the definition stable when channels change, while checking whether a different audience affects the result.

Frame task success as “Did the user reach the defined outcome?” Record help, confusion, and backtracking separately: a user can complete a task while still finding it difficult. A falling success rate warrants investigation, but it does not establish that revenue or lead quality will fall next.

What To Measure For Task Success Rate

Start with three to five tasks that represent the highest-value actions on the site. For a brand site, that might be pricing evaluation, product comparison, locating a feature, booking a demo, or submitting a lead form. For ecommerce, it’s often add to cart, checkout, and account sign-in.

Define success before testing, then calculate task success rate as successful attempts divided by all valid attempts at that task, multiplied by 100. For example, 8 successful attempts out of 10 is 80%, not a precise estimate for every visitor. Record the sample size, audience, and device. Keep assisted and partial completions separate from unassisted success. (NNGroup)

For usability testing for lead generation, use realistic tasks such as finding the right service and submitting a test enquiry. Keep tasks and success criteria consistent between rounds so changes are interpretable.

Common supporting measures for task success rate:

  • Time on task to spot hesitation and friction
  • Error rate to identify where people get stuck
  • A one-question ease rating after the task

How Brands Improve Task Success Rate Without Guesswork

Task success rate improves when brands design for clarity, not cleverness. The fastest gains often come from removing uncertainty, simplifying choices, and aligning labels with how people search.

Practical improvements tend to focus on three areas: simpler navigation and page hierarchy, less form friction, and clearer interface states. Broken states, unclear errors, and inconsistent patterns are useful starting points for investigation.

Practical fixes that often lift task success rate:

  • Replace vague menu labels with customer language
  • Reduce steps in high-intent flows
  • Make errors explicit and recoverable, not generic

If task success rate is consistently weak, it is often an information architecture problem or a UI consistency problem. That’s when working with a UI UX design agency can help teams rebuild the system, not just patch pages.

Lead Quality: Connecting UX to Qualified Enquiries

A higher conversion rate is not enough if the resulting enquiries are a poor fit. Lead quality belongs beside usability measures because it checks whether the journey supports qualified interest, rather than simply producing more form submissions.

Lead quality is not only a sales concern. It is a marketing efficiency concern. Poor-fit enquiries consume follow-up time and can increase the cost of winning customers. Before changing the interface, check whether the audience, offer, and qualification process also need attention.

A strong UX scorecard tracks lead quality alongside task success rate. The goal is not to make forms harder as a filter. It is to reduce unnecessary effort while explaining who the offer is for and what happens after submission.

Lead Quality Signals You Can Measure

Define qualification with the team that follows up. A practical quality rate is the number of valid enquiries reaching an agreed qualified stage divided by all valid enquiries in the same intake cohort. Use a consistent follow-up window, report spam and duplicate exclusions separately, and do not compare new leads with older cohorts that have had longer to qualify.

For B2B marketing, qualification might reflect company fit, a relevant use case, and a genuine buying need. Marketing and sales should agree on those criteria before judging whether a form or landing-page change brought better opportunities.

High-quality lead signals often include:

  • Meaningful form completion with low rework
  • Completion of a key “evaluation” step before submitting
  • Fewer spam patterns, fewer empty fields, fewer throwaway emails
  • Higher rate of booked calls, qualified stages, or accepted demos

Connect form events to CRM outcomes so you can compare lead volume with later qualification. Simple tagging can reveal associations worth investigating, although it does not isolate the effect of a UX change. This is also where a marketing consultation and audit can help teams align measurement across marketing, UX, and sales.

UX Changes That Improve Lead Quality

Lead quality improves when the experience makes intent visible. Brands can do that by setting expectations, clarifying fit, and guiding users into the right path based on their situation.

Useful changes to test include better contact form UX, clearer qualification copy, and structured paths for different audiences. Review the content around the form too. When the page promises one outcome and the form implies another, visitors may misunderstand the next step.

UX adjustments that often lift lead quality:

  • Add one fit question that clarifies need, timeline, or use case
  • Use confirmation states that set next-step expectations
  • Route high-intent users to booking instead of long forms

Lead quality also depends on brand positioning. If the brand promise is vague, the funnel invites everyone. If the promise is specific, the funnel attracts fit. That’s why lead quality metrics belong in brand work as much as UX work. A focused brand strategy makes lead quality easier to earn.

User Confidence: Understanding Hesitation Before Conversion

User confidence can help explain hesitation that completion data alone misses. People may be unsure about the product, the price, the process, the credibility, or the risk. Asking about that uncertainty is more reliable than inferring it from an abandoned form alone.

Repeated visits, backtracking, and delayed decisions can indicate uncertainty, but they can also reflect comparison shopping or a complex task. Treat those behaviors as prompts for research. Do not interpret faster completion or higher-intent leads as direct proof of increased confidence.

User confidence is also where brand and UX meet. A polished interface is not enough if the promise, evidence, and experience disagree. Coordinated branding services can help align messaging and visual identity, while UX work checks whether people understand and trust the result.

How To Measure User Confidence

Ask about confidence at a defined moment, such as after a pricing evaluation, a demo request, or a checkout step. Choose the timing to match the decision being studied, and keep it consistent between measurement rounds.

One practical question is “How confident do you feel that you chose the right option?” For a custom scorecard, use a consistent scale, such as 1 for not at all confident and 5 for very confident. Keep the question, timing, and audience stable; report the response count and distribution. An ease rating can complement it, but ease and confidence are different measures.

Behavioral signals to investigate alongside confidence responses:

  • Rage clicks and repeated toggles in key flows
  • High backtracking between pricing, features, and trust content
  • Drop-offs after trust moments like payment, login, or form submit

Confidence Killers Brands Overlook

Brands can invest in visuals while leaving uncertainty unresolved. Review feedback and error recovery as part of interaction design: users should know whether an action succeeded, what went wrong, and how to continue without losing their work.

Potential confidence gaps include inconsistent information, unclear pricing, vague policies, missing proof, and forms that feel risky. In ecommerce, Baymard’s abandonment research provides context for checkout friction, but also separates it from people who are simply browsing or not ready to buy. An abandonment rate alone does not diagnose a trust problem. (Baymard)

Confidence killers to audit for:

  • Ambiguous pricing and hidden fees
  • Weak error messages that imply the user made a mistake
  • Generic claims with no proof, examples, or detail

Accessibility and performance are part of the experience too. A slow, unstable, or difficult mobile flow can make a task harder to complete. That’s where disciplined web design services and performance maintenance support usability and brand credibility.

A Practical UX Metrics Framework For Marketing Strategy

Brands need a framework that connects UX metrics that matter to marketing and growth decisions. Otherwise, UX metrics become a separate reporting lane that leadership ignores.

A useful model is to read the scorecard as a ladder of questions. Task success rate asks whether the experience works. Lead quality asks whether enquiries fit the business. User confidence asks how people feel about their choice. Each adds context; none proves the cause of changes in the others.

The Metrics Ladder

Start with task success rate, then review lead quality and user confidence together. This is a suggested reporting sequence, not a universal hierarchy. High confidence with low task success, for example, is a reason to inspect the task definition and user feedback rather than declare the experience successful.

A simple ladder for teams:

  • Task success rate answers “Can users complete the job?”
  • Lead quality answers “Are we attracting the right prospects?”
  • User confidence answers “Do users feel sure enough to proceed?”

The Weekly Scorecard

A weekly review should create focus rather than demand new research data every week. Use a small scorecard, show when each measure was collected, and avoid treating fluctuations in a small sample as a trend. Refresh study-based measures after meaningful changes or on an agreed research schedule.

A practical weekly UX scorecard:

  • Task success rate for three core tasks
  • Lead quality rate based on CRM or proxy signals
  • User confidence score at one key moment
  • One friction indicator, like error rate or drop-off step

This scorecard works best when owned jointly by marketing and product. Marketing owns the promise and acquisition. Product owns the experience and system. Both are accountable for outcomes.

For organic acquisition, connect this view to SEO reporting KPIs. Track the path from search visits to valid enquiries and qualified outcomes, while keeping attribution limits visible.

How To Instrument UX Metrics Without Breaking Your Analytics

Instrumentation should answer the questions in the scorecard. Choose events that capture meaningful steps and outcomes, then test whether they fire correctly. Collecting more activity does not help when the same event means different things on different pages.

A scoped UX audit can review critical journeys and identify missing or unreliable evidence before the scorecard is interpreted. Define what confirms a completed action, not just which button was clicked.

A clean event model makes UX metrics that matter reliable. It also prevents measurement arguments later, because each event has a definition that stays consistent.

Event Design Principles

Design events around moments of intent. For example, “pricing view,” “feature comparison click,” “form start,” “form submit,” “demo booking,” “error displayed.” These are closer to decisions than raw page views.

Principles that keep instrumentation usable:

  • Track intent and completion, not every interaction
  • Use consistent naming across the funnel
  • Log errors and validation failures as first-class events

Common Measurement Mistakes

Most measurement errors come from ambiguity. Events that mean different things across pages. Goals that change mid-quarter. Or metrics that mix users, sessions, and conversions without clarity.

Mistakes to avoid:

  • Treating time on page as a universal “good” signal
  • Measuring lead quality with only volume metrics
  • Asking confidence questions too early in the journey

If your measurement is unstable, fix the system first. That is usually a governance and implementation issue, not a reporting issue. It is also a reason brands bring in an SEO agency or analytics support to align tracking with growth goals.

Benchmarks and Targets: What “Good” Looks Like

Benchmarks are useful when they create direction, not when they create false certainty. UX metrics that matter should be tracked against your own baseline and improved quarter over quarter.

That said, it helps to set targets. Task success rate should be high for core tasks. Lead quality should improve as the experience clarifies fit. User confidence should trend upward as the brand reduces unanswered questions.

Practical target guidance:

  • Task success rate: improve the weakest task first, not the easiest
  • Lead quality: measure quality rate, not only total leads
  • User confidence: look for steady gains, not perfection

If task success falls while traffic grows, investigate the audience mix, the journey, and the measurement setup. A tracking change or a different study sample can also affect the result. Compare like with like before assigning a cause or selecting a fix.

An Illustrative Example: Turning UX Metrics Into a Test Plan

Consider a lead-generation site whose conversion rate appears acceptable, but sales receives many poor-fit enquiries. Increasing traffic alone may increase the volume without resolving the quality problem. This is an illustrative scenario, not a reported client result.

Use the three measures to investigate together. Observe task success on the path from service overview to form submission or booking. Connect valid enquiries to a defined qualified stage. Then ask about confidence at a consistent evaluation point, including feedback from participants who choose not to submit.

Changes to test against the baseline:

  • Raise task success rate by reducing decision friction in the flow
  • Improve lead quality by clarifying fit and routing users to the right action
  • Increase user confidence by adding proof, clarity, and control

The investigation might identify unclear pricing, confusing fields, or an early request for too much information. Test the relevant change, then review completion, qualified-enquiry rate, and confidence together. A clearer step may help, but improvement needs to be measured rather than assumed.

When To Bring In Outside Support

Most teams can start this scorecard internally. Outside support can help when measurement gaps or recurring usability issues extend beyond a single page. That might involve a redesign, an analytics cleanup, or a brand repositioning that changes how the funnel should work.

Outside support is also useful when teams are stuck in opinion loops. A neutral audit can turn debates into measurements, and measurements into a prioritized plan.

If you need help aligning measurement, UX, and brand execution, ask a branding agency such as Brand Vision how the brand promise will carry through messaging and interface decisions. The scorecard should connect that work to defined user outcomes, not just visual preferences.

A Scorecard Your Brand Can Stand Behind

The best UX metrics do not make reports longer. They make decisions clearer. Task success rate shows whether users complete a defined task. Lead quality shows whether enquiries meet agreed criteria. User confidence captures how people feel about their choice, adding context to what they do.

Track the three consistently, keep their limitations visible, and use the findings to decide what to test next. That is what a practical UX scorecard is for.
