What is Email Automation and Why Does It Matter?

Email automation is the ability to send customized, individualized emails to the subscribers seeking special attention according to the specific triggers, actions, or timelines without any manual operation. It will be like having a personal marketing assistant that never goes off duty but keeps an eye on all the customer activities, and when the customer does something wrong, then it sends the right message at the right time.

The technology operates on a high-level trigger-based system designed to understand user behavior, preference, and active patterns. 

When a subscriber does a particular thing like a purchase, leaving a shopping cart, or clicking a certain link, the automation platform can instantly send a corresponding email. Superior segmentation options enable such platforms to segment subscribers by multiple demographics, purchase and usage history and levels of engagement, and a myriad of other ways, so that the message will always be meaningful to the intended recipient.

The Role of Email Automation for Businesses

Email automation evens the playing field regardless of the size of the business, giving small companies the ability to deliver enterprise-quality customer experiences. 

  • It increases efficiency – Automatically sends the messages, thus it saves on the manual work.
  • Personalizes at scale – Personalizes content to audiences and improves engagement.
  • Enhances timing – Sends messages at their most opportune times.
  • Enhances customer relationships – Strengthens leads and sustains loyalty down the line.

How to Choose the Right Email Automation Platform for Your Goals

Choosing an email automation platform may involve paying close attention to various aspects that are in line with your business goals and objectives that are important to the operations of your business.

Step 1: Set Your Budget and ROI Goals

First, determine the specific budget that covers not only the platform cost, but the implementation working hours, training materials, and the possible integration costs, as well. Take into consideration the anticipated ROI—costlier platforms commonly are worth the investment in the form of a better deliverability rate, better segmentation, and analytics that directly relate to revenue creation.

Step 2: Evaluate Desired Capabilities/Functionality

Develop a list of desired capabilities/functionality and v. nice-to-have capabilities. Crucial capabilities tend to consist of automation‐based workstreams, segmentation tools, analytics reporting, and template libraries. More advanced ones may be predictive analytics, AI or machine learning optimization, or specific e-commerce connectivity.

Step 3: Grade Ease of Use and Learning Curve

Take into account the technical skills of your staff and the amount of time that your staff has to invest in learning the platform. It also has some platforms with drag-and-drop format that is easy to understand by the amateur and others with advanced customization where one has to know technical skills and hence is more elaborate.

Step 4: Consider Integration Ability

Look at the level of integration of potential platforms with other technology used such as CRM systems, e-commerce systems, analytics, and social media control software. Smooth integrations will avoid data silos and maintain the same customer experience across the touchpoints.

Step 5: Think About Scalability and Scaling Potential

Pick a platform that can scale with your business, dealing with higher subscriber loads, more complicated automation processes and other enhancements as your requirements expand. Think about pricing levels and other factors that can be a constraint in the future growth.

Step 6: Quantify Deliverability and Support Qualify

Research the deliverability levels, spam block capabilities, and reputation methodologies used on any given platform. Also, assess the level of customer support, what channels are available, what are the response times, and how thorough the supporting documentation and training material is.

FAQ

Q: What's the difference between email marketing and email automation platforms?

The platforms used in email marketing are aimed at designing and delivering newsletter emails to a subscriber list, and the workflow features commonly found in email automation tools contain advanced capabilities designed to drive the delivery of a customized email. More advanced segmentation, behavioral tracking, and sequences of multiple stages of campaign are usually available through automation platforms.

Q: How much do email automation platforms typically cost?

The rates depend largely upon the number of the subscribers and other functionalities. Small companies begin with basic plans that cost about 10-30 dollars a month, up to enterprise packages that could cost hundreds or even thousands of dollars a month. All the platforms present tiered pricing, depending on the number of subscribers to their services, as well as higher costs of other features such as predictive analytics or high-end integrations.

Q: Can small businesses benefit from email automation platforms?

Absolutely. Automation emails help bring a given field to the same playing field, as small businesses are now able to reach high levels of personalization in terms of providing professional customer experiences on par with larger businesses. Automation saves time and boosts engagement, as well as helps smaller businesses nurture leads without large marketing teams.

Q: Are there any industries where email automation doesn't work well?

The acceptance of email automation in different industries is high in general; however, the efficacy of the process depends on the audience and regulators it needs to comply with. Strictly-compliant industry (healthcare, finance) can require the specific platforms with higher freedom of security. B2B industries may not display the same levels of engagement as B2C and thus demand adjusted strategies and not a change of platforms.

Conclusion

The 2025 world of email automation presents unexplored potentials in building a significant customer relationship on a large scale with a crucial non-compromising aspect of personalization. Whether we think of a turnkey solution such as EngageLab that offers an omnichannel toolset, or a more niche platform that caters to particular business types like an online store or a particular industry like hospitality, the choices have never been more abundant when it comes to tools to revolutionize your marketing tactic.

Regardless of what feature is at the top of your list, be it advanced behavioral targeting, an integration with your e-commerce, or something user-friendly, the platforms mentioned in this guide are the most suitable for any contemporary marketer who wishes to make the most out of their email marketing.

Starting a business in the United States does not come with a guaranteed success rate. A more useful way to compare opportunities is to look at current demand, recurring-revenue potential, startup complexity, regulation, and whether the founder has a real advantage in the market. This 2026 list keeps the original ten business models, but treats them as ideas to evaluate rather than a ranking of guaranteed winners.

The U.S. Small Business Administration notes that location, structure, startup costs, taxes, zoning, and licenses and permits can all change what it takes to launch. Before committing capital, validate demand in your market and build a realistic cost model.

1. E-Commerce Store

An e-commerce business remains accessible because a founder can begin with a narrow product line, marketplace storefront, print-on-demand model, or direct-to-consumer site. U.S. Census Bureau data show that e-commerce accounted for 17.1% of total U.S. retail sales in the second quarter of 2026, with adjusted e-commerce sales up 12.2% from a year earlier.

The opportunity is not unlimited, and low setup friction can also mean heavy competition. A founder still needs product economics, reliable fulfillment, customer acquisition, and a reason to build a niche brand that shoppers can remember. Strong B2C marketing also matters once the store needs to move beyond marketplace traffic. For categories that payment processors treat cautiously, the original guide also pointed to a high-risk merchant account with instant approval as a specialized payment-processing option; terms and risk rules should be reviewed separately.

  • Best for founders who can differentiate a product, audience, or distribution angle.
  • Watch inventory, fulfillment, return rates, payment costs, and customer-acquisition economics.

2. Cleaning & Home Organization Services

Residential and commercial cleaning can be started with less fixed infrastructure than many storefront businesses, and recurring contracts can create predictable work. The older article linked a service-industry source arguing that consumers valuing cleanliness more than ever supported demand after the pandemic. More recent Bureau of Labor Statistics data are more measured: janitorial and building-cleaning employment is projected to grow 2% from 2025 to 2035, with about 321,800 openings per year largely because workers leave the occupation.

Home organization can be a related premium service for the right customer base, including clients influenced by systems such as Marie Kondo. The business case depends on local density, route efficiency, labor availability, insurance, and the ability to win repeat customers rather than a national growth headline.

  • Lower equipment needs than many physical businesses.
  • Recurring residential, rental, or commercial contracts can improve scheduling stability.

3. Real Estate Investing & Property Management

Real estate can produce rental income, service revenue, or long-term asset appreciation, but the capital requirements and risk are much higher than in service businesses. An existing roundup calls real estate one of the most successful businesses to start in 2026, while another source argues that Section 8 housing continue to be profitable niches. Those are third-party viewpoints, not guaranteed returns.

A lower-capital path is property management rather than property ownership. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects property, real estate, and community-association manager employment to grow 4% from 2025 to 2035, with about 36,900 openings per year. Operators still need to understand state licensing, landlord-tenant rules, insurance, local market conditions, and tenant acquisition. Our real estate marketing page covers the positioning side of the category. The original guide also points readers here for room-listing examples.

  • Property management can create service revenue without owning every property.
  • Investment returns depend on financing, occupancy, maintenance, regulation, and purchase price.

4. Technology & SaaS Startups

Software-as-a-Service can create recurring revenue when the product solves a specific problem and customers keep paying for it. That recurring model is attractive, but it does not make SaaS automatically low-cost or high-margin. Development, cloud infrastructure, security, support, sales, and churn can become significant costs.

Demand for software skills remains a real signal. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects software-developer employment to grow 16% from 2024 to 2034. Founders entering this category should pair product expertise with positioning and a clear route to market; technology marketing becomes important when technical capability alone is not enough to create demand.

  • Recurring revenue can improve forecasting when retention is strong.
  • Validate the customer problem and willingness to pay before overbuilding the product.

5. App Development & Tech Consulting

App development and technology consulting can be launched as expertise-led services before becoming a larger agency or product company. One existing industry source describes providers as seeing skyrocketing demand from both startups and established brands; the BLS software outlook provides a more conservative demand signal, with software-developer employment projected to grow substantially over the decade.

Two early investments still matter: professional web design that makes the service credible and a brand strategy that explains why a client should choose one consultancy over another. Once projects multiply, our guide to project management tools can help compare systems for owners, deadlines, and client handoffs.

  • Can start as a specialized consultancy before adding staff.
  • Scope control, sales pipeline, and repeatable delivery matter as much as technical skill.

6. Health & Wellness Services

Health and wellness includes very different businesses, from personal training and fitness studios to wellness software and regulated clinical services. The original article used health-spending research to support the view that Americans are spending more on feeling better. For a more direct operating signal, the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects fitness-trainer and instructor employment to grow 7% from 2025 to 2035, with about 68,000 openings per year.

Founders should separate general wellness services from regulated healthcare, nutrition, therapy, or telehealth activities that can require professional credentials, privacy controls, insurance, or state-specific licenses. The opportunity is strongest when expertise and compliance are clear. Health and wellness marketing also needs extra care around claims and customer trust.

  • Works across in-person, membership, coaching, and digital-service formats.
  • Check professional, privacy, advertising, and state licensing requirements before launch.

7. Home Services & Skilled Trades

Home services can benefit from local, recurring needs that cannot be fully digitized. The original article points to plumbing, HVAC, roofing, electrical work, along with window washing and general contracting. Current BLS projections support strong demand in several licensed trades: electricians are projected to grow 9%, plumbers 7%, and HVAC mechanics/installers 11% from 2025 to 2035.

These businesses are not low-barrier in the same way as freelancing. Many trades require apprenticeships, certifications, insurance, or state and local licensing. Once qualified, strong reviews, referrals, route density, and local search visibility can become major acquisition channels.

  • Demand is tied to maintenance, repair, construction, and replacement cycles.
  • Licensing, labor availability, equipment, vehicles, and insurance can create meaningful startup costs.

8. Food Services & Meal Prep

Food businesses can build repeat purchase, but margins and regulation can be demanding. The existing guide highlights Health-based meal prep kits, gourmet food trucks, and pop-up concepts as niche options. The better question is whether the menu, location, production model, and price point can support repeat demand after labor, ingredients, packaging, rent, delivery, and spoilage are included.

The FDA's food-business guidance notes that requirements vary by product and facility, with additional state and local permits often applying. Retail food establishments and food trucks are commonly regulated at the state or local level. Once the operating model works, clear food and beverage marketing can help turn a niche into repeat demand.

  • Strong product quality and repeat purchase matter more than novelty alone.
  • Model permits, food safety, labor, delivery, and waste before assuming attractive margins.

9. Creative & Digital Freelance Services

Graphic design, copywriting, video editing, branding, and virtual assistance can be started with relatively little equipment when the founder already has the skill. Platforms such as Upwork, Fiverr, and direct networking can help with early client acquisition, but platform access does not guarantee profitable work.

The main challenge is moving from selling hours to a repeatable offer with clear scope, pricing, and proof. Freelancers who later hire subcontractors should treat the transition like any other startup marketing problem: define the customer, sharpen the offer, and build a consistent acquisition channel.

  • Low fixed overhead for skill-based services.
  • Margins depend on pricing discipline, utilization, client concentration, and scope control.

10. Eco-Friendly & Niche Subscription Boxes

Subscription boxes can create recurring revenue, but retention, shipping, product sourcing, and churn determine whether the model is actually attractive. The existing guide describes them as easy to start, brandable, and profitable with recurring revenue; in practice, profitability depends on acquisition cost and how long customers remain subscribed.

A focused category, strong product curation, and reliable fulfillment can make the model easier to explain than a general marketplace. Founders should still test demand before committing to inventory and make cancellation, renewal, and subscription terms clear.

  • Recurring billing can improve revenue visibility.
  • Watch churn, shipping costs, inventory risk, and paid-acquisition efficiency.

Choosing the Right Business for 2026

The strongest opportunity is the one that matches real demand with your skills, capital, risk tolerance, and ability to reach customers. The SBA recommends market research and a startup-cost model that includes equipment, licenses, insurance, salaries, marketing, and website costs. Do that work before treating any "top business" list as a forecast.

For U.S. founders, it can also help to separate the business model from the go-to-market plan. A US branding and marketing agency can support positioning and customer acquisition, but the underlying unit economics still need to work first.

FAQ: Businesses to Start in 2026

What are 10 business ideas to consider in 2026?

This guide covers e-commerce, cleaning and organization, property management and real estate, SaaS, app development and tech consulting, health and wellness, home services and skilled trades, food services, creative freelancing, and niche subscription boxes.

Which business has the highest profit potential?

There is no universal answer. Profitability depends on pricing, labor, customer-acquisition cost, capital needs, regulation, competition, retention, and owner expertise. SaaS can scale well but has product and sales risk; trades can have strong demand but require training, equipment, and licensing; real estate can create asset value but needs capital and carries market risk.

Can these businesses be started with low capital?

Some skill-based services, consulting, cleaning, and certain online businesses can begin with modest equipment, but the original blanket claim that they can all be launched for under $5,000 is not supported. Estimate costs for your exact location and business model before launch.

What makes a business idea promising in 2026?

Look for validated customer demand, defensible positioning, workable unit economics, realistic startup costs, and a path to repeat or referral business. Growth trends are useful context, but they do not replace local research and financial planning.

If you’re looking for a way to boost your site’s SEO performance, then guest posting could present a great opportunity. If you can find the right sites relevant to your industry, you could generate traffic and authority within your industry very quickly.

Here are some top tips on how to find those guest posting opportunities.

‍

What are the benefits of guest posting?

Guest posting can have a number of benefits for you and your website. Not only is it an effective way of getting high-quality backlinks pointing to your site, it can also be a great way of building your brand awareness within your chosen field. If you can secure a guest posting opportunity on a site with a strong reputation within your industry, you could see a big improvement in your brand's visibility, along with the strong SEO benefits that come from securing a high authority backlink.

Tip 1: Use Google search to find sites

The first tip is really quite simple. Just search for the industry you work in (e.g. health, jewellery making, etc.) and then add phrases like ‘write for us’ or ‘submit guest post’ and then see what results you get. You could also try adding phrases like ‘guest blogging guidelines’ or even just ‘guest post’. There are many options you can try.

Once you have the results, start searching through them to see if any decent opportunities are available. Don’t restrict yourself to the first page of results. Go all the way through to page 5 or even page 10. Not all sites prioritise optimising their contributors or submission guideline pages, so you don’t want to miss out on a really good opportunity just because it didn’t appear straight away.

Tip 2: Check guest posting directories

Searching for guest posting directories is another quick and easy way to find opportunities. Simply do a quick search in Google and see what directories you can find. Many of the results will have been compiled by actual bloggers, and they may even include some tips and advice on how to get a guest post accepted.

The only thing to be cautious of is if the listings are out of date. Make sure that you double-check all opportunities before you try submitting a guest post to avoid wasting your time on an opportunity that doesn’t exist anymore.

Tip 3: Learn from successful guest bloggers

As you’re searching through Google results and directories for opportunities, you might find that you come across the same author names a lot. If you do, make sure you keep a note of them as they may well guide you towards some good guest posting opportunities.

As you go through established blogs in your niche, check those big-name authors and see if they have written guest posts anywhere else. Simply search for their name and then ‘guest post’ and see what appears. Given that you will be looking for the work of some established names in your industry, chances are that the sites they have posted on carry a lot of authority.

Tip 4: Find your competitor’s guest posts

Depending on your industry, you may have some competitors who are already writing and submitting guest posts. If they are, it can present a good opportunity to get some of your content on those sites as well.

Simply use an SEO tool like Ahrefs to find all the backlinks your competitors have. Then, as you comb through those links, you should be able to find the sites where they have published guest posts. Simply add those to your list of opportunities and reach out to them.

‍

Tip 5: Use a guest posting service

If you’re struggling to find guest posting opportunities by yourself, you can always look at a guest posting service or blogger outreach service. By going to a professional provider, they can handle the sourcing of your guest posts for you. Many services will also write the content for you, ensuring that it’s relevant to your industry and the keywords that you want to target. This can be a great option if you’re finding searching for the right sites too difficult or too time-consuming.

By following the above steps, you should find an absolute treasure trove of guest posting opportunities. If you can successfully get content on those sites, you could find your website shooting up the search rankings in no time at all.

Adidas has spent decades connecting sport with fashion, music, and culture, and its advertising is one of the clearest ways to see that positioning at work. From campaigns built around star athletes to films centered on creativity and social purpose, the best Adidas ads do more than introduce a shoe or jersey. They repeat a recognizable point of view while adapting it to a new audience or moment. From an agency perspective, that consistency is the useful lesson: strong branding services connect positioning, identity, and campaign execution so each new piece still feels like the same brand. Below are nine Adidas ads that show how the company has done that in different eras.

Impossible Is Nothing (2004)

In 2004, “Impossible Is Nothing” gave Adidas a campaign platform broad enough to work across sports and generations. Drawing inspiration from legendary athletes such as Muhammad Ali, the creative framed performance through adversity rather than victory alone. That made the slogan useful well beyond a single product launch: it could carry stories about limits, setbacks, and progress while remaining recognizably Adidas.

That flexibility helped the idea last. Adidas brought it back in 2021 for a new generation, while keeping the same core theme of seeing possibility where others see limits. The lesson for a brand strategy is simple: a durable platform gives a company room to refresh the cast, format, and context without rebuilding its message from scratch.

Adidas Is All In (2011)

“Adidas Is All In” widened the brand’s world in 2011 by bringing sport, music, and fashion into one campaign. These Adidas ads starred icons such as Lionel Messi, Derrick Rose, and pop sensation Katy Perry, giving the idea enough range to move from stadiums to stages without losing the central message about commitment. The campaign showed how celebrity casting can support a brand platform when each person represents a different expression of the same idea.

The rollout also carried the same campaign idea across television, cinema, digital content, and social channels. Shorter edits created reach while longer and behind-the-scenes pieces gave audiences more ways to stay with the campaign. Instead of changing the message for every channel, Adidas changed the format while keeping “all in” as the organizing idea. That consistency made the launch feel larger without fragmenting recognition, because each execution added a new layer to the same campaign rather than competing for attention with a different message.

Unite All Originals (2013)

By 2013, Adidas ads had already carved out a place in both sports and culture, but “Unite All Originals” took that blend to another level. These Adidas ads didn’t just rely on star athletes; they also tapped Run-D.M.C. and DJ A-Trak for a fresh spin on music, fusing old-school hip-hop with modern EDM. It was a bold statement that Adidas could speak to different generations without missing a beat. The interactive component was a fun extra, inviting users online to mix beats and visuals, which gave everyone a shot at co-creating part of the experience.

The campaign balanced nostalgia with a format built for contemporary digital participation. Run-D.M.C.’s history with the brand gave the collaboration credibility, while A-Trak and the interactive execution made it feel current. For brands working across music, media, and culture, that is a useful entertainment marketing principle: the partner should expand the brand story rather than replace it. The interactive component also gave the audience a role, turning the collaboration from something people only watched into something they could manipulate and explore.

Original Is Never Finished (2017)

In 2017, Adidas ads reached an almost cinematic level with “Original Is Never Finished.” Using surreal visuals and a reimagined version of Frank Sinatra’s “My Way,” these Adidas ads led viewers through a dreamlike sequence that blended high fashion, art references, and sports into one extravagant feast for the eyes. Scenes of Kendall Jenner and James Harden were intercut with moments referencing classic artworks, underscoring how style and culture constantly get reshaped.

The campaign’s visual identity did more than make the film distinctive. Its art references, fashion styling, symmetry, and recurring compositions gave viewers a set of cues to recognize and reinterpret. By remixing familiar imagery instead of simply repeating old work, Adidas made “originality” feel like an ongoing process rather than a fixed aesthetic.

Run for the Oceans (2018)

“Run for the Oceans” connected participation with Adidas’s sustainability partnership with Parley for the Oceans. “Run for the Oceans” in 2018 spotlighted plastic pollution, proving that a sports brand can help drive change. People were invited to log their runs, turning a campaign message into a measurable action. For every kilometer logged, Adidas contributed funds to cleanup efforts, with the 2018 release specifying $1 per kilometer for the first one million kilometers to support the Parley Ocean Plastic Program, particularly Ocean School education.

The campaign worked because the action matched the brand’s existing relationship with sport. Running was not bolted onto the idea; it was the mechanism that let people participate. That made the sustainability message more concrete and gave Adidas a way to connect product culture, community, and environmental education in the same campaign.

José +10 (2006)

“José +10” approached star power from a child’s point of view. Centered around a neighborhood match, it captured two kids “recruiting” legends like David Beckham and Zinedine Zidane into an imaginary game of pick-up soccer. The idea kept elite athletes recognizable while making the story feel playful and accessible, a useful contrast to sports advertising built only around spectacle or competition.

Because these Adidas ads appeared around the 2006 World Cup, they garnered massive attention and tapped into the global excitement for the tournament. Yet the charm went beyond hype: these Adidas ads had a playful spirit that reminded us sports should be accessible, imaginative, and joyful. Even after the World Cup ended, people kept talking about José and his larger-than-life lineup, cementing these Adidas ads as timeless fan favorites.

Take the Stage (2012)

During the 2012 London Olympics, “Take the Stage” arrived as a patriotic reminder that big dreams can spring from humble places. These Adidas ads focused on British athletes and even spotlighted music figures, weaving in everyday individuals who were stepping up to show their talents. The campaign felt like an open invitation for everyone to chase their goals, whether in an Olympic venue or a local neighborhood.

The visual style was bold and energetic, with quick cuts that reflected London during the Games. By blending athletic achievements with stories of regular people, the campaign widened the meaning of “taking the stage” beyond Olympic competition. The result was a simple participation idea: the stage could be a stadium, a performance venue, or a local neighborhood. That made the Olympic connection useful without making the campaign feel limited to elite competition, which helped the idea travel beyond the Games themselves.

Calling All Creators (2017)

By 2017, the brand was fully embracing the idea that creativity resonates well beyond the sports arena. “Calling All Creators” was a prime example: these Adidas ads brought household names from different industries together around a large table, where they casually chatted about what it means to create. The vibe was almost like eavesdropping on a cool brainstorming session where Lionel Messi, Pharrell Williams, and other big names discussed pushing boundaries in their crafts.

Instead of using famous names only as visual shorthand, the campaign centered the conversation on how people create and push their disciplines forward. The relaxed, dialogue-driven format also gave Adidas material that could extend beyond one hero film. That is one reason video marketing works best as a system of adaptable formats rather than a single upload.

‍

Predator Boot Launch (Various Years)

The Predator boot series has been a staple in many Adidas ads since the mid-’90s, each launch greeted by soccer fans around the world. Star players, from David Beckham to newer icons, laced up these boots and showed off swerving free kicks and pinpoint passes, making these Adidas ads a longtime favorite among football enthusiasts. There was something almost magical about seeing the ball bend in midair, hinting that the right gear could give you near-superhuman skills on the pitch.

Each iteration’s rollout came with fresh visuals or behind-the-scenes glimpses of development, and these Adidas ads consistently stirred up excitement for the next big thing in footwear. By putting the spotlight on both style and cutting-edge tech, Adidas secured its place in the hearts of aspiring players. It’s not every day a sports shoe crosses into pop culture, but these Predator-themed Adidas ads did exactly that, and they did it time after time.

Where Sport and Style Collide

Across these campaigns, the recurring strength is not one visual style or one celebrity formula. Adidas repeatedly connects products to a larger idea, then gives that idea a format suited to the moment. Some campaigns use athlete stories, others use music, participation, sustainability, or surreal art, but the brand rarely abandons its broader themes of performance, creativity, and self-expression.

That is what makes the best Adidas ads useful as marketing case studies: the creative can change dramatically while the brand remains recognizable. For businesses trying to build the same kind of continuity between strategy and campaigns, you can talk with Brand Vision about the positioning and identity behind the work.

As new digital technologies move fast, organizations want mobile apps that can run on Android and iOS without any differences. But it is costly, time-consuming, and wasteful to develop and maintain two applications. That is why companies are turning to cross-platform development — an approach wherein developers develop applications by employing a shared codebase that can run on both platforms.

By using a single codebase, developers code once and execute it on numerous operating systems with no duplication and faster time to market. Technologies like Flutter, React Native, and Xamarin enabled this with uniformity, offering nearly native performance and flexibility.

1. Faster Development and Time-to-Market

One of the biggest advantages of a shared codebase is speed. In the past, companies had to maintain two development teams — one for iOS (Objective-C or Swift) and one for Android (Java or Kotlin). They had to write, test, and maintain two distinct codebases.

With a shared codebase, developers can:

  • Write once and deploy on both platforms.
  • Avoid being stuck in infinite development loops.
  • Do changes and patches at the same time for everyone.

Therefore, businesses can deploy their apps quicker and be quick to react to market changes or customer feedback. This advantage is even more valuable to small start-ups or teams with limited budgets and deadlines.

2. Cost Savings and Easier Maintenance

Having two independent mobile apps means doubling your development and maintenance expenses. There are separate versions of updates, bug-fixture, and testing cycles in each platform.

Having a shared codebase, these costs are lessened exponentially. Rather than having two teams working on the same challenges, one team can share updates for both platforms at once. This is cost-effective:

  • Reduced development costs
  • Less maintenance work
  • Easier project management

This efficiency not only saves money but also consistency — your Android and iOS users experience the same features and performance at the same moment.

3. Same User Experience Across Platforms

Users expect the app's appearance and behavior to remain consistent when they move between Android and iOS devices. Having a second, different app sometimes creates visual or functional inconsistencies.

Sharing a single codebase ensures that the design and performance are the same on each platform. Platforms such as Flutter provide support for widgets that are customizable and appear as native widgets, with the platform's design language being preserved while providing consistency of experience. Consistency is helpful:

  • Fostering brand identity stronger
  • Fostering user trust and familiarity
  • Eliminating confusion caused by variant interfaces

Having a uniform experience on all devices is imperative, especially for those brands that value visual consistency and usability. 

4. Rapid Testing and Quality Assurance

Quality assurance (QA) is probably the most labor-intensive aspect of app building. Double testing must be performed with two apps separately — one for each app — so both apps are working properly.

With a unified codebase, QA teams must:

  • Test only one version of the app
  • Catch bugs earlier
  • Automatically implement fixes that touch both platforms

With the solitary strategy, there is better testing optimized, reduced release cycles, and greater assurance overall app stability.

Automated testing tools are also rapidly integrated into cross-platform frameworks, again aiding efficiency.

5. Access to a Greater Talent Pool

It is hard to hire seasoned native iOS and Android developers. Cross-platform technologies like Flutter and React Native have immense and thriving user bases with great support behind them having flawless documentation, open-source libraries, and business forums. 

Working with an experienced flutter app development company gives businesses access to professionals who specialize in creating high-performance apps from a single codebase.  They understand design, performance, and scalability management — so your app will work just as well on all devices.

They also have existing solutions and solutions learned from past projects that can avoid you from potential pitfalls and reduce development time.

6. Easy Integration and Future Scalability

A single codebase simplifies third-party solution integration such as APIs, analytics services, or payment gateways. Through shared logic, developers code these features once versus twice.

Secondly, as your business expands and user requirements shift, utilizing a single codebase implies updates and expansions are faster. You can easily add new features, add support for new devices, or shift to new technology without having to re-write.

This scalability also keeps your app on par as the mobile world evolves — guaranteeing long-term growth and responsiveness.

7. Simpler Post-Launch Maintenance

Releasing an app is only the beginning. Regular updates, feature additions, and user feedback integration are all the signature of long-term success.

With a unified codebase, post-launch maintenance is significantly simpler:

  • Updates and patches are pushed once.
  • Android and iOS users are updated simultaneously.
  • The chances of version conflict or incompatibilities are reduced.

This single maintenance cycle keeps both versions of your app up to date, reducing the developer burden and delivering a smoother experience to end users.

8. Improved Performance with New Frameworks

Earlier cross-platform solutions lagged behind in performance or offered incomplete access to native functionality. But newer frameworks like Flutter have bridged that gap to a large extent.

Flutter, for example, supports native code compilation natively as well as a high-performance rendering engine. This leads to smooth animations, zero load time, and great responsiveness.

Native APIs and device hardware are accessible to developers at hand without sacrificing performance, and one codebase is not just an exercise in cost-cutting but an exercise in performance too.

Conclusion

The demand for high-quality, fast mobile apps continues to grow — and maintaining two separate native codebases for iOS and Android can drain both budget and time.

A shared codebase offers a smarter approach: faster development, homogeneous experience, cost savings, and eased maintenance. Solutions like Flutter allow the user to get speed, quality, and cross-platform reach without sacrificing anything.

For those organizations seeking to launch feature-packed, high-performance mobile apps on multiple platforms, partnering with an experienced flutter app development company is one of the most effective ways of achieving this goal. Proper guidance and right tools help you future-proof your mobile strategy and stay ahead of the app game.

The branding trends of 2025 offered several contrasting directions: dessert-inspired imagery, hand-drawn illustration, restrained minimalism, expressive typography and fluid shapes. The useful question is not which style every business should adopt. It is which creative idea expresses your positioning, works across your materials and gives your audience a clear way to recognize you.

This guide examines ten directions as design options, not a measured ranking of their popularity. Canva's 2025 design forecast, informed by searches and design activity on its platform, highlighted handcrafted textures, modular shapes, nostalgia and motion. That provides context for the period, not proof that a particular aesthetic improves sales.

Effective branding starts with the business and audience before the visual treatment. Use the ideas below to explore a direction, then test it against your brand strategy. The reference images illustrate styles; they are not presented as a catalogue of campaigns launched in 2025.

1. Dessert-Inspired Product Branding

Candy colors, glossy textures and café or bakery imagery give a product a sensory setting. Think bubblegum pink, mint tones, frosting-like surfaces or a warm espresso palette. The creative connection should come from something specific about the product, such as its shade, texture or the occasion for using it.

Rhode's food-associated beauty marketing is a useful reference for this approach. Study how the product and surrounding props share a visual vocabulary rather than copying a dessert photograph. The image credit below concerns the article visual, not the creation of Rhode's brand identity.

For a hypothetical body-care launch, a cream-colored backdrop and soft lighting might communicate texture without suggesting the product is edible. Keep the product name and purpose obvious. Food imagery is not evidence that a cosmetic is safer, more natural or more effective, and the visual association does not establish why someone buys it.

Try the idea in a limited campaign before changing the permanent packaging or logo. In consumer-product marketing, the same concept should remain understandable on a product page, a shelf and a small social image. A prop that overwhelms the product is a reason to simplify the composition.

2. Hand-Drawn Motifs and the Handmade Digital Aesthetic

The handmade digital aesthetic fuses raw sketches, crayon-like textures, and imperfect strokes with refined typography. A loose illustration can introduce warmth or humor into an otherwise precise layout. The contrast is often the useful part: an informal drawing next to clear type, not an entire page that looks unfinished.

Define the illustration rules before expanding the style. Decide on stroke weight, texture, color, subject matter and how much imperfection is intentional. Give contributors approved examples so future drawings belong to the same family. A set of unrelated stock doodles is not a coherent illustration system.

This direction can support a personal or craft-led story, but rough lines do not prove that a product is handmade or a company is authentic. Use accurate descriptions of the actual process. Keep instructions, prices and long paragraphs in readable typography, and test fine details at the smallest print or screen size required.

Once the rules are clear, campaign graphics and packaging design can carry them into repeatable applications. The hand-drawn element should have a job, such as explaining a process or framing a message, rather than filling every empty corner.

3. Minimalism With a Recognizable Point of Difference

Minimalism reduces competing elements so the important ones have room to work. That may mean a limited palette, fewer type styles, controlled photography or a simple layout. It does not require a beige identity, an anonymous wordmark or removing information customers need.

A possible creative brief is: Clean logos or packaging emphasize calm, confident visuals that stand out in loud digital feeds. Treat that as an intended design effect, not a guaranteed audience response. Compare the result with its real surroundings: a quiet pack can be distinctive in one category and almost indistinguishable from its neighbors in another.

Decide which features still identify the business after the decoration is removed. A particular color relationship, typographic detail, crop or composition can provide continuity. Test those choices as a complete visual identity system, not only as a logo on a blank slide.

Watch for over-simplification. A product range still needs clear differences between variants; a website still needs useful navigation and supporting details. Minimalism works as a design discipline when it reduces noise without reducing understanding.

4. Naturalism Without Unsupported Environmental Claims

Earthy palettes, textured papers, botanical drawings and outdoor photography can establish a nature-led visual direction. Unlike a perfectly smooth digital finish, naturalism embraces small imperfections, including irregular edges or visible material texture. The important decision is which details connect to the actual product or story.

Photography of ingredients, landscapes or materials can suggest a brand’s alignment with nature. But a leaf icon, green palette or brown package does not verify environmental benefits, ethical production or a particular material composition. Separate the visual association from any claim the business needs to support.

For U.S. marketing, the FTC's Green Guides summary cautions against broad, unqualified claims such as “green” or “eco-friendly” and calls for clear, specific qualifications. Check the requirements in the markets where the product is sold rather than treating natural-looking design as substantiation.

Brief the design and product teams together. Confirm what the package is made from, what any certification covers and which information belongs on the label. A nature-inspired campaign can be visually appealing without making an environmental claim at all.

5. Negative Space That Still Reads Clearly

Negative space is the area around and between visual elements. In a logo, a gap can form a second shape or reveal a subtle idea. In a layout, it can separate information and direct attention without adding more lines, boxes or symbols.

A hidden detail should reward a closer look, not be necessary to understand the business name or offer. Start by checking the primary silhouette and legibility. Then ask whether the secondary shape remains visible when the mark is reduced, reversed onto a dark background or reproduced in one color.

For logo design, compare the concept at actual application sizes, including an avatar, website header and printed item. A clever gap that closes at small sizes needs adjustment. Do not add a complicated explanation to rescue a mark that people cannot read.

Negative space and minimalism are not interchangeable. A detailed composition can have well-managed spacing, and a sparse composition can still feel cramped. Judge the relationship between elements, not simply how few elements appear.

6. Wordmarks and Expressive Typography

A text-only logo is still a logo. A wordmark uses the business name as its identifying form, with character coming from the letterforms, spacing, proportions or custom details. This approach shifts the design work toward the name rather than removing the need for an identity.

Choosing a name and drawing a wordmark are separate tasks. Resolve brand naming before refining letterforms; typography cannot fix a name that is unclear for the intended audience.

Separate the wordmark from the typography used for ordinary content. A distinctive display treatment may work for a short brand name but become tiring across a paragraph. Document typography rules for headlines, body copy, captions and practical information.

Check the limits before retiring a symbol. A long name may not fit a small profile image or narrow product label. Develop a deliberate compact version when needed, and define where it may appear. Neither a wordmark nor a symbol is automatically clearer at every scale.

Try unfamiliar names, numbers and required languages in the supporting type system. Review font permissions for the actual applications and contributors. The goal is a recognizable typographic system that other people can use consistently, not a typeface chosen only because it looks unusual.

7. Shape-Driven Branding as a Repeatable System

Circles, blocks, frames and repeating geometric forms can connect a brand's materials without repeating the logo everywhere. A shape might frame photography, divide a presentation or provide a consistent background for a campaign. Its usefulness comes from how the system is applied.

Define a small set of rules: which shapes are permitted, their proportions, how they overlap and when they act as decoration rather than information. Give each element enough flexibility to work on packaging, web design and print without forcing an identical composition.

A circle does not inherently prove inclusivity, and a triangle does not automatically communicate innovation. Treat those associations as creative hypotheses. Review the shapes with the name, message, audience and category to see whether the whole composition expresses the intended idea.

Test a dense information layout as well as a promotional image. If the pattern competes with text, makes charts confusing or crowds the product, reduce its role. A repeatable graphic language should help contributors organize content, not require them to fit every message into the same decorative frame.

8. Nostalgic Aesthetics, Including 1960s References

Swirling lettering, psychedelic color combinations and vintage photographic treatments offer one route into nostalgia. The 1960s album covers linked here are useful visual references, not a template for every retro identity. Identify whether you are borrowing a typographic treatment, a palette or a particular cultural association.

Nostalgia was also part of Adobe's 2025 forecast. Its explanation of the Time Warp design direction describes remixing historical eras with futuristic elements, rather than treating one decade as the only reference point. That is a helpful distinction when choosing between a faithful revival and a contemporary interpretation.

Start with the audience's relationship to the reference. A familiar brand archive and a borrowed vintage aesthetic are different creative resources. The nostalgic marketing campaigns of 2023 illustrate how an older reference can support a new campaign idea; they are historical examples, not 2025 launches.

Keep the present-day offer legible. Use expressive lettering where it can be read comfortably, and let simpler type carry essential details. Copying a past era wholesale can make a new product difficult to understand or leave the business looking like an imitation of an established brand.

9. Fluid and Liquid Visuals With Controlled Motion

Flowing shapes, gradients and liquid-like surfaces create a visual contrast with rigid grids. They can appear as static illustrations or become animated elements. A liquid aesthetic is not the same as a flexible identity system: the latter needs rules for variation, whether or not anything looks fluid.

Choose the constants before creating variations. Keep a recognizable palette, wordmark or framing rule so each execution still belongs to the same business. Test the design in a static format first; a print advertisement or an email should not need animation to make sense.

For digital work, treat motion as part of interaction design, not a layer of decoration added at the end. Define what starts the movement, whether it communicates useful information and what happens when someone needs it to stop.

W3C's Pause, Stop, Hide guidance requires a way to pause, stop or hide automatically starting moving content that lasts more than five seconds and runs alongside other content, unless the movement is essential. Review that requirement alongside reduced-motion preferences and readability. Visual energy should not make the message or controls harder to use. Include these checks in website accessibility testing before launch.

10. Anti-Branding as a Deliberate Identity Choice

Anti-branding describes an intentionally restrained or apparently unpolished presentation: plain packaging, modest typography, sparse layouts or an everyday photographic style. It is not the absence of design. The repeated choices still communicate an identity, even when they avoid conventional promotional polish.

Distinguish it from minimalism by its intended attitude. Minimalism can look highly refined; anti-branding may deliberately resemble something ordinary, utilitarian or provisional. Both need a clear hierarchy and recognizable cues.

For a less-established business, stripping away the name or distinctive features can leave people unsure who is speaking. Test whether the packaging, product page and order email still connect. A deliberately plain wrapper should not obscure the product, necessary information or the route to customer support.

Do not use an understated appearance as a claim of honesty, superior quality or lower environmental impact. Those qualities depend on the business and evidence behind the presentation. An anti-branding direction is useful only when its restraint serves the audience and the offer.

How to Choose and Apply a Branding Direction

Decide Whether You Need a Campaign, Refresh or Rebrand

Branding is more than a collection of visuals or short-lived campaigns. Before choosing a trend, name the problem: unclear positioning, inconsistent materials, weak product differentiation or an identity that no longer fits the offer. These problems do not all require the same response.

A seasonal illustration style might be a campaign treatment. Better templates may resolve inconsistency without changing the identity. Broader rebranding ideas deserve consideration when the business, audience or positioning has changed, not merely because a new aesthetic is fashionable.

Use brand and audience research to identify what customers already recognize and where they are confused. Preserve useful identifying features rather than replacing every element at once. Record which assumptions still need testing.

Compare Directions on the Same Real Applications

Give each concept the same copy, product and required formats. Review a small digital placement, a content-heavy page and a physical item where relevant. A moodboard can explain an idea, but it cannot demonstrate whether the design works in those settings.

For example, a fictional bakery might compare hand-drawn illustrations with a typography-led direction using the same menu, box and ordering page. Ask whether customers can find the product and price, identify the business and understand the offer. Do not judge solely by which concept looks most impressive on a presentation cover. Use task-based usability testing for the ordering page, rather than asking only which visual style people prefer.

  • Check fit with the positioning and audience before considering novelty.
  • Test legibility, recognition, accessibility and production constraints in the actual formats.
  • Identify which elements stay fixed and which can change for campaigns or product variants.
  • Record the cost and ownership of photography, illustration, templates and future updates.
  • Set an observable review question, such as whether users can distinguish two variants, instead of promising a sales increase.

Document the Rules and Review the Rollout

Turn the selected direction into usable guidance for typography, color, imagery, spacing and applications. The guide to building a visual identity explains how those elements form a system. Include correct examples, common mistakes and approved files, then ask someone outside the design team to produce a routine asset.

After rollout, review customer feedback and the tasks the design was meant to support. Keep changes in price, distribution, campaigns and product availability separate from visual changes when interpreting results. A different outcome after a redesign does not, by itself, identify what caused it.

The most useful lesson from these branding trends of 2025 is to borrow selectively. Keep the parts that express the business clearly and reject the ones that only make it resemble the current moodboard.

Looking ahead from late 2024 to 2025, email remained a direct way to speak with subscribers about offers, services and useful updates. Segmentation, mobile-ready design and automation could make messages more relevant, but no tactic guaranteed a revenue lift. Email worked best as part of a wider digital marketing services plan rather than a standalone campaign.

The most useful trends for 2025 planning were better use of permissioned subscriber data, practical automation, accessible design and stronger measurement. Interactive features also deserved attention, provided a message still worked in email clients that did not support them. The sections below explain what to test and where older performance claims need context.

‍

Personalization and Segmentation for Relevant Emails

Generic campaigns leave little room for different needs. For 2025 planning, hyper-personalization meant adapting offers, educational content and timing to relevant subscriber groups. Its value depended on the quality of data and how well the message matched what a recipient had chosen to receive.

Leveraging AI for Personalized Content

AI tools could help teams draft content variants and identify patterns in consented subscriber data, but human review remained important for accuracy and brand voice. The linked Gartner report discusses AI-driven marketing; it does not establish a universal 15% revenue uplift from email personalization. Before scaling any variant, review sensitive data use, tone and results. For perspectives on tactics and tools, some email marketing podcasts may be useful, but discussions are not substitutes for campaign evidence.

Segmentation and Targeted Messaging

Segmentation groups subscribers by relevant interests, purchase history or customer stage so each email has a clearer purpose. Campaign Monitor's older research circulated the headline claim that email campaigns achieve a 760% increase in revenue. The linked article describes gains of as much as 760% among some marketers, not an average result or a forecast for a particular business. A maintained company contacts database can support accurate preferences. For a business briefing a marketing agency in Montreal, that may also mean testing appropriate English and French messaging rather than sending one version indiscriminately.

Useful personalization should improve relevance, not simply insert a name into a subject line. Start with a small set of meaningful segments, confirm the data is permitted and accurate, and compare responses before expanding the program.

Interactive Emails and Inbox Compatibility

Interactive email designs attracted attention in 2025 planning, but support differed between inbox providers and devices. Polls, image carousels and other features needed functional static alternatives so recipients could still understand the message and take the next step.

Key Interactive Features

  • A short poll or quiz can collect stated preferences when the email client supports it. Otherwise, link to an accessible web form. Avoid treating broad engagement percentages from unrelated interactive campaigns as a reliable email benchmark.
  • Carousels can show several products where supported, but fallback layouts are essential. Litmus provides format examples; its linked page does not substantiate the widely repeated 65% boost in user engagement as a general result. Test rendering, accessibility and actual click behavior.

The goal is a better user experience, not interaction for its own sake. If an element fails in some clients, a clear image, description and ordinary link should still communicate the offer.

‍

Mobile-Friendly Email Design

Mobile-friendly templates help readers scan content, recognize the brand and use the main call to action. An older Adobe measurement resource is sometimes linked to a 15% lower click-through rate, but its landing page does not substantiate that precise figure. Check actual device reports and clicks instead. Consistent visual identity design makes emails recognizable across screen sizes. Flodesk is one example of an email marketing platform; verify features and plan limits before assuming specific automation or A/B testing behavior.

Best Practices for Mobile Email Design

  • Keep subject lines concise enough to communicate the main value on small screens; test how they render rather than relying on an inflexible character limit.
  • Use short paragraphs, descriptive headings and readable spacing. Readers scan at different speeds, so make the main action obvious without assuming a universal reading time.
  • Use clear, accessible CTA buttons with sufficient contrast and tap space. Evaluate clicks and downstream outcomes rather than expecting a guaranteed lift from size alone.

Email Automation and Lead Nurturing

Automated welcome, onboarding and re-engagement sequences, including drip emails, could help teams deliver timely messages when subscribers took a relevant action. Triggers, frequency and exit rules mattered as much as the software. Test that every sequence reflects the recipient's status and preferences.

Drip Campaigns for Lead Nurturing

Drip campaigns send a series of useful messages based on a schedule or customer action. HubSpot's practical guide is sometimes cited for a 320% increase in lead conversion rates, but the linked article does not support a universal 320% conversion gain. In B2B marketing, nurturing should answer evaluation questions before asking for a sales conversation. Brand Vision’s guide to email sequences for service businesses offers practical ways to structure the next step.

‍

Consent, Privacy and Sender Trust

For teams planning 2025 campaigns, consent, data transparency and unsubscribe handling were central to subscriber trust. GDPR and CCPA requirements depend on how and where a business operates. Google also introduced 2024 Gmail sender requirements for authentication and, for applicable bulk marketing mail, easy one-click unsubscribe. Confirm the rules relevant to each audience and sending volume.

Best Practices for Compliance

  • Explain what subscribers are joining and obtain consent appropriate to the purpose and jurisdiction. Make preferences and unsubscribe choices accessible rather than assuming every contact wants every message.
  • Explain what customer data is collected, why it is used and how people can change their preferences. Cisco's privacy benchmark is sometimes cited for a 40% higher customer retention rate, but the linked study does not substantiate that specific retention gain from email transparency.

Privacy practices support trust and sound list management. They do not remove the need to evaluate delivery, complaints, preferences and customer experience alongside applicable legal requirements.

Measuring Email Performance Beyond Opens

Open rates can be misleading when privacy tools prefetch email images. Apple's Mail Privacy Protection can prevent senders from knowing whether a message was opened. Measure clicks, qualified responses, conversions, unsubscribe rates and revenue where appropriate, and separate useful signals from automatic image loading.

‍

The Importance of A/B Testing

A/B testing can help compare one meaningful change at a time, such as a subject line, CTA or layout. Optimizely publishes useful ideas for what to test, but no fixed conversion lift can be assumed. Define the audience, outcome and adequate sample before deciding which version worked better.

What Marketers Could Prioritize for 2025

For 2025 planning, personalization, mobile usability, respectful automation and measurement were more useful priorities than chasing every new email feature. Effective B2C email marketing should still reflect the customer relationship and a recognizable brand. Top national TV ad spenders are difficult to rank across history because the public sources measure different things. Kantar’s annual advertiser lists cover total U.S. advertising across media, iSpot estimates national TV spend, category reports isolate specific windows, and Super Bowl prices describe a single event. This guide keeps those numbers separate instead of treating them as one audited leaderboard.

Historic all-media rankings still show which companies had the scale to support heavy television, while current TV datasets show where national spend is concentrating now. From a planning standpoint, the useful question is not who spent the most in absolute terms, but how reach, timing, brand strategy, and measurement worked together. Kantar’s 2018 ranking provides the historical advertiser context (Marketing Dive), while Amazon’s 2019 jump shows how quickly that context can change (Axios).

At a glance

  • Historical advertiser scale: Kantar ranked P&G as the largest U.S. advertiser in 2018 at $2.9 billion across measured media. That is an all-media figure, not a TV-only total (Marketing Dive).

  • Amazon’s jump: Amazon became the largest U.S. advertiser in 2019 at nearly $7 billion in total advertising. The figure should not be read as $7 billion of television spend (Axios).

  • National TV now: iSpot publishes estimated national TV spend based on impressions and CPM assumptions, so its weekly leaderboard is a TV-specific snapshot rather than an audited company-wide advertising total (iSpot).

  • Event economics: Super Bowl LIX in 2025 averaged a record 127.7 million viewers on the single-network telecast, with 30-second units reported as high as $8 million (Reuters). Super Bowl LX in 2026 averaged nearly 125 million viewers, while some 30-second units reached $10 million (Reuters 2026).

1) Procter & Gamble: the historic scale benchmark

Procter & Gamble is a useful starting point because it has spent at enormous scale for decades across consumer categories built on broad reach and repeated brand memory. Kantar put P&G at $2.9 billion in U.S. advertising in 2018, but that number covers measured media broadly and should not be presented as national TV spend. Its television importance is better understood through the company’s long history of mass-reach creative and the continuing visibility of brands such as Tide, Febreze, and Pampers on national schedules (Marketing Dive, Wired).

  • Use P&G’s $2.9 billion figure as evidence of advertiser scale, not as a TV-only total.
  • Its longevity shows why television has historically fit brands that need broad awareness and repeated creative assets.

2) Amazon: a digital-first advertiser reaches mass scale

Amazon’s 2019 surge is another case where the denominator matters. Axios reported nearly $7 billion in U.S. advertising and the No. 1 advertiser position for the year, but that was total advertising, not a disclosed national TV budget. Prime, devices, retail promotions, and entertainment made mass reach strategically useful as Amazon moved deeper into mainstream households. The lesson for B2C marketing is that television can complement digital distribution when a consumer proposition needs rapid national awareness; for technology marketing, it also shows how a digital-native company can use traditional reach without abandoning digital acquisition (Axios, The Guardian).

  • Amazon’s nearly $7 billion figure describes total U.S. advertising in 2019, not TV alone.
  • The strategic takeaway is channel expansion at scale, not proof that television replaced digital media.

3) Telecom and media: large advertisers with built-in reach needs

Telecom and media companies regularly appear near the top of large-advertiser lists because they sell national connectivity, programming, subscriptions, and bundles. In Kantar’s 2018 all-media ranking, AT&T, Comcast, and other major corporate advertisers were among the country’s largest spenders (Marketing Dive). That does not establish a TV-only ranking, but it explains why these businesses have the scale and product cadence to remain visible on national television. For organizations coordinating national reach with a US marketing agency, the practical lesson is to treat TV as one part of a broader media system rather than using total corporate ad spend as a proxy for TV investment.

  • All-media corporate rankings provide scale context, not channel-specific totals.
  • Telecom and media brands have recurring reasons to advertise nationally: plans, launches, streaming, sports rights, and bundles.

4) Insurance: one of national TV’s most persistent categories

Insurance remains a particularly clear national TV category because the largest carriers compete for broad awareness in a market where many customers shop only at specific moments. iSpot’s weekly leaderboard regularly surfaces insurance advertisers (iSpot). Looking at a completed period rather than a single week, iSpot reported that insurance led linear-TV industry share of voice in the first half of 2026 and accounted for more than $1.32 billion in estimated national TV spend; Progressive ranked first among linear advertisers by share of voice (iSpot H1 2026).

That persistence does not mean every insurance brand should copy the same frequency. TV should sit inside a broader paid media plan that distinguishes reach, response, and incremental business outcomes.

  • Insurance is a documented high-spend national TV category in current iSpot estimates.
  • Frequency is useful only when creative recognition and measurement justify the repeated exposure.

5) Household products and healthcare: keep the categories separate

The pandemic-era evidence in this article covers two different advertiser groups. Household CPG brands such as Tide, Downy, and Febreze were visible national TV buyers in 2021; Adweek reported substantial spending for those P&G brands during the period (Adweek). They should not be labeled as pharma or healthcare advertisers.

Separately, the Center for Media Engagement studied advertising on nightly network and primetime cable news from January 2020 through June 2021. It found healthcare advertisers spent $307 million across that news inventory. The study’s $132 million figure refers to the top five healthcare advertisers per network across six networks, not total healthcare advertising. It is also a news-programming study, not a measure of all national TV (PDF). For health and wellness marketing, the broader lesson is to keep the category, period, and inventory definition attached to every spending claim.

  • Household CPG and healthcare are separate categories and should not be combined in one spend total.
  • The $307 million healthcare figure covers specific news inventory over an 18-month pandemic window.

6) Automotive: a large category with visible cycles

Automotive remains an important national TV category, but its spending moves with inventory, launches, incentives, and macro conditions. An earlier MediaPost report documented a sharp April 2025 decline in national TV activity (MediaPost). A year later, MediaPost reported $131.9 million in April 2026 national linear TV spend, down 18% from the prior April, reinforcing the point that even large traditional categories can contract materially from one period to the next (MediaPost 2026). Weekly rankings can then shift toward other categories as available inventory and campaigns change (iSpot).

  • Automotive is strategically important to national TV, but its spend should be read by period rather than treated as constant.
  • Year-over-year category changes can be large enough to reshape weekly advertiser rankings.

7) Retail and ecommerce: event-driven national reach

Retailers often increase mass-reach advertising around periods when demand is already elevated, including back-to-school, Black Friday, and the holiday season. Amazon’s 2019 all-media surge is useful context for how a retail platform can dramatically increase total advertising when Prime, devices, and entertainment all need support, but it should not be converted into a TV-only number (Axios). National TV can still be valuable in those windows when the goal is to make a promotion or brand message visible at scale.

  • Retail TV budgets are often tied to calendar moments, launches, and promotions rather than a flat year-round level.
  • Judge the channel by incremental reach and business response, not by the size of another retailer’s total advertising budget.
